items.exact_text: Difficilis in perfecto mora est; naturaliterque, quod procedere non potest, recedit; et ut primo ad consequendos, quos priores ducimus, accendimur: ita, ubi aut praeteriri, aut aequari cos posse desperavimus, studium cum spe senescit; et quod adsequi non potest, sequi desinit; et, velut occupatam relinquens materiam, quaerit novam: praeteritoque eo in quo eminere non possumus, aliquid in quo nitamur conquirimus; sequiturque, ut frequens ac mobilis transitus maximum perfecti operis impedimentum sit.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Velleius Paterculus, Historia Romana, Book 1, Chapter 17.
Translation: “It is difficult to stand still at the point of perfection; and naturally, that which cannot advance, recedes. And just as we are at first fired with the ambition of overtaking those whom we regard as leaders, so, when we have despaired of being able either to surpass or to equal them, our enthusiasm languishes along with our hope; it ceases to follow what it cannot overtake, and, abandoning the field as if it were already occupied, it seeks a new one. Passing over that in which we cannot excel, we look for some other object for our efforts; and it follows that this frequent and restless changing of direction is the greatest impediment to the perfection of any work.”

items.exact_text: Haec est mea sententia de Messia, seu rege illo promisso, et haec est mea religio, quam coram vobis ingenue profiteor.
items.translation_text: Translation: “For the rest, that you may know of what religion I am, although I have shown it in my writing which you have, yet I will briefly repeat it here. And first, indeed, the doctrine concerning the Messiah, or that promised king, belongs in no way to my religion: for that king was promised only to the Jews, just as also those good things of Canaan. So also circumcision, sacrifices, and the remaining ceremonies of Moses do not belong to me, but were promised, given, and commanded only to the Jewish people. Nor were those things the worship of God among the Jews, but they served divine worship, and led the Jews to divine worship. But the true worship of God, which I call my religion, is the Decalogue [the Ten Commandments], which is the eternal and unchangeable will of God; which Decalogue therefore belongs to me, because it has also been given to me by God, not indeed by a voice sounding from heaven, as to the Jewish people, but is implanted in my mind by creation; but because the implanted Decalogue, through the corruption of human nature and wicked customs, has been obscured in some part, therefore to illustrate it, I employ the vocal [written] Decalogue, which vocal Decalogue therefore also belongs to me, and to all peoples, because it agrees with the Decalogue implanted in us, nay, it is that very same Decalogue. This is my opinion concerning the Messiah, or that promised king, and this is my religion, which I ingenuously profess before you.” — Martin Seidelius of Olawa, Silesia.

items.exact_text: Haereo lac inter meditans, interque cruorem;
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Carolus Scribanius (writing under the pseudonym Clarus Bonarscius), Amphitheatrum Honoris (Antwerp, 1605), Book 3, Chapter 6 ("Ad Divinam Virginem Hallensem & Puerum Iesum").
Translation: “I cling, meditating, between milk and blood; between the delights of the breast and of the side. And I say (if by chance I stretch my eye upon the breast), 'O divine Parent, I demand the joys of your breast.' But I say (if then I turn my eyes to the wounds), 'O Jesus, I prefer the joys of your side.' One thing I know: I will grasp the breast with my right hand if it be allowed, and I will grasp the wounds with my left if it be granted. I wish to mix the mother's milk with the son's blood; I could not enjoy a nobler antidote. Let the wounds restore the beggar foul with ulcers, whom a shard alone can scrape of his corruption. Let the breasts refresh the thirsting Ishmael, whom Sarah does not tolerate, and whom Hagar does not nourish. These things for me, to drive the pestilence far, far away; these things for me, to prevail against long fevers. Anger vomits flames, and the Etna of lust smokes; I am able to suffocate them with blood, I am able with milk. Envy rages in the limbs with unquenched rust; I am able to wipe it away with milk, I am able with blood. Vain honor tempts me with perpetual itching; I am able to satisfy it with blood, I am able with milk. Therefore, parent and son, attend to my prayers: I seek milk, I desperately long for blood, I want both. O, yet I thirst! O, thirst cuts off my voice! O Son, quench my thirst with blood; parent, with milk. Say to the mother: 'This brother of mine is thirsty, best mother; deign to draw from your fountain, and from mine.' Say to the son: 'This brother of yours, my honeyed son, shows his chains as a captive, you have the ransom.' Therefore, show, O Redeemer, that you are rightly called so, if nobler blood than the rest is in you. And you, parent, show that you are rightly called mother, if you bear breasts richer than the rest. O when shall I be suckled from the breast, and fed from the wound? And enjoy the delights of both your breast and side.”

items.exact_text: Ubera me matris, nati me vulnera pascunt
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Franciscus de Mendoza, Viridarium Utriusque Eruditionis, Christiana et Ethico-Politica (Cologne, 1633), Book 2, Problem 2 ("De fletu Christi et Mariae Virginis").
Translation: “The breasts of the mother, the wounds of the son feed me; doubtless these are the medicine of my soul. For while love draws tears from me, I suck the breasts, that sorrow, sad with sweet love, may smile. But while joys thrill me, I lick the wounds, so that glad things, mixed with pious sorrow, may delight me. Thus I suck the wounds of the son, thus the breasts of the parent, so that my varied fortunes may be secure. Who, I pray, could live without milk, or who without blood? By your milk, O mother; by your blood, O son. Let milk be instead of ambrosia, and blood instead of sweet nectar; thus the perpetual wound and breast nourish me.”

items.exact_text: Quid est Deus? Mens universi. Quid est Deus? Quod vides totum, et quod non vides totum. Sic demure magnitude sua illi redditur, qua nihil majus excogitari potest, si solus est omnia, opus suum et extra et intra tenet. Quid ergo interest inter naturam Dei et nostram? Nostri melior pars animus est, in illo nulla pars extra animum.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: What is God? The mind of the universe. What is God? The whole of what you see, and the whole of what you do not see. Thus finally his true magnitude is restored to him, than which nothing greater can be conceived, if he alone is all things, and holds his work both outside and inside. What then is the difference between the nature of God and ours? Our better part is the mind; in him there is no part outside the mind. (Seneca, Naturales Quaestiones, 1.Pref.13)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text:
Apparet Paulum absolute intelligere opera quaecunque ilia tandem sint. Quod tamen non eam vim habet, ut a causa justificationis nostrae omnino quaecunque opera, et quocunque modo considerata, excludere velit. Sed serums ipsius est, nulla esso opera quae tanti sint, ut propter ipsorum meritum justificari possimus. Quando scilicet nemo est qui perfectissime et integerrime per totam vitam ea opera faciat quae sub vetere sive sub novo testamento praescripta sunt, id quod tamen omnino

[[BLOCKQUOTE]] requiritur, sive requiretur ad hoc, ut per ipsa opera tanquam ejus rei aliquo modo meritoria, justificatio contingeret. Diximus autem aliquo modo meritoria, ut ab ipsis operibus excludamus, non modo absolutum et maxime proprium meritum, quod oritur ex ipsa operum praestantia per se considerata; sed etiam illud, quod minus proprie et respective meritum est, . . . . . quod ex solo Dei promisso oritur ac proficiscitur, adeo ut nemo nec per illud neque per hoc meritum suorum operum justificationem et absolutionem a peccatis suis adipiscatur,
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: It is clear that Paul absolutely understands works, whatever they may ultimately be. Which, however, does not have the force that he wishes to exclude from the cause of our justification all works whatsoever, and considered in whatever way. But his discourse is, that there are no works which are of such value, that on account of their merit we can be justified. Since, evidently, there is no one who most perfectly and most entirely throughout his whole life does those works which are prescribed under the old or under the new testament, a thing which is nevertheless altogether required, or will be required to this end, that through the works themselves, as in some way meritorious of that thing, justification should happen. But we have said in some way meritorious, that we may exclude from the works themselves, not only absolute and most proper merit, which arises from the excellence of the works themselves considered in themselves; but also that which is less properly and respectively merit, which arises and proceeds solely from the promise of God, so that no one, neither through that nor through this merit of his works, obtains justification and absolution from his sins. (Faustus Socinus, De Justificatione, Tractatus)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Cum Paulus negat nos ex operibus justificari, considerat opera tanquam meritoria, et sua ipserum vi hominem justificantia, et consequenter ejusmodi, quibus si ad Dei praeceptum examinentur, nihil prorsus desit; at Jacobus operum nomine eam obedientiam intelligit, sine qua Deus hominem sibi carum habere non vult; seu mavis opera ejusmodi sine quibus dici nequeat, ulla ratione hominem Deo obedire Ex hac collatione istorum duorum Pauli et Jacobi locorum et sententiarum manifestum est, quemadmodum ad justificationem nostram non requiritur necessario perfecta obedientia mandatorum Dei, sic ad eandem justificationem omnino requiri, ut Dei mandata ita conservarenius, ut merito dici possit nos Deo obedientes esse.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: When Paul denies that we are justified by works, he considers works as meritorious, and by their own power justifying a man, and consequently of such a kind, which if they are examined according to the precept of God, are entirely lacking nothing; but James by the name of works understands that obedience, without which God does not wish to hold a man dear to himself; or if you prefer, works of such a kind without which it cannot be said, by any reason, that a man obeys God. From this comparison of these two passages and sentences of Paul and James it is manifest, that just as perfect obedience to the commands of God is not necessarily required for our justification, so for the same justification it is altogether required, that we so keep the commands of God, that it may be deservedly said that we are obedient to God. (Conrad Vorstius or Faustus Socinus, On Justification, Arminian/Socinian Controversy)

(Conrad Vorstius or Faustus Socinus, On Justification, Arminian/Socinian Controversy)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Secunda controversia capitalis quae Christianismo cum quidusdam heterodoxis (Remonstrantibus scilicet in Belgio, viris, si non Socinianae, saltem dubliae theologiae) intercedit, est de merito Christi pro nobis hoc est, vice et loco nostro, et sic in bonum nostrum actualiter praestito, seu de satisfactione plena ac proprie dicta a Christo sponsore, loco nostro justitiae divinae praestita: illi satisfactionem et meritum sic accipiunt quasi nihil aliud sit, quam partis offensae talis placatio qua offenso hactenus satisfit, ut in gratiam redire velit cum eo qui offendit, et per quam Christus Deo Patri jus et voluntatem acquisiverit novum foedus ineundi cum hominibus.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: The second major controversy that Christianity has with certain heterodox individuals (namely, the Remonstrants in the Netherlands—men of doubtful, if not entirely Socinian, theology) concerns the merit of Christ on our behalf; that is, what He actually accomplished in our place and stead, and thus for our good, or concerning the full and properly so-called satisfaction rendered to divine justice by Christ the guarantor in our place. They understand satisfaction and merit merely as a kind of pacification of the offended party, whereby the offended one is sufficiently satisfied to be willing to return to favor with the offender, and through which Christ is said to have acquired for God the Father the right and will to enter into a new covenant with men. (Gisbertus Voetius, Selectae Disputationes Theologicae, De Merito Christi)

They understand satisfaction and merit merely as a kind of pacification of the offended party, whereby the offended one is sufficiently satisfied to be willing to return to favor with the offender, and through which Christ is said to have acquired for God the Father the right and will to enter into a new covenant with men. (Gisbertus Voetius, Selectae Disputationes Theologicae, De Merito Christi)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Fides justificationem non meretur, neque est ejus causa efficiens; non ignoramus fidei nostrae nequaquam esse ea merita, quibus justificatio qua sempiterna continetur felicitas, tanquam merces debita, sit tribuenda. Hinc porro consequitur, fidem istam, quamvis obedientiam et pietatem in se comprehendat, nequaquam tamen per se, et principaliter efficere, ut justificationis beneficium consequamur.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: Faith does not merit justification, nor is it its efficient cause; we are not unaware that our faith by no means possesses such merits that justification, which contains eternal happiness, should be granted to it as a due reward. From this it further follows that this faith, even though it includes obedience and piety within itself, by no means brings it about by itself and as a primary cause that we obtain the benefit of justification. (Simon Episcopius / Remonstrants, Confession of the Remonstrants, Chapter 18)
items.note_html: Modern Translation: Faith does not merit justification, nor is it its efficient cause; we are not unaware that our faith by no means possesses such merits that justification, which contains eternal happiness, should be granted to it as a due reward. items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Ne admittam culpam, ego meo sum promus pectori, Suspicio est in pectore alieno sita. Nam nunc ego to si surripuisse suspicer Jovi coronam de capite e Capitolio, Quod in culmine astat summo; si non id feceris, Atque id tamen mihi lubeat suspicarier, Qui tu id prohibere me potes ne suspicer?
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: Lest I commit a fault, I am the steward of my own breast; suspicion is situated in another's breast. For now, if I should suspect you of having stolen the crown from the head of Jupiter from the Capitol, which stands on the highest summit; if you have not done it, and yet it pleases me to suspect it, how can you prevent me from suspecting? (Plautus, Trinummus, Act 1, Scene 2)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Interim tamen sic habendum est, cum Deus non nisi illis, qui fidem virtutemque pro sua virili parte colunt, vitam sempiternam designaverit, fiduciam istam ne quidem causam meritoriam, aut principaliter efficientem, sed causam sine qua non (ut loquuntur) justificationis nostrae esse.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: Meanwhile, however, it must be held thus, since God has not appointed eternal life except for those who cultivate faith and virtue according to their manly portion, that this trust is not indeed the meritorious cause, or principally efficient cause, but the cause without which not (as they say) of our justification. (Arminian Theologian, Unknown, Location)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Imputatur nebis a Deo id quod revera in nobis est, non aliquid quod a nobis absit vel in alio sit, nempe quod firmiter in animo decreverimus nihil dubitantes de Dei promissionibus, neque considerantes nostram infirmitatem, nos propositum fidei certamen decurrere velle.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: That which is truly in us is imputed to us by God, not something that is absent from us or resides in another, namely, that we have firmly resolved in our mind, not doubting God's promises, nor considering our infirmity, to desire to run the proposed race of faith. (Johannes Völkel, De vera religione, N/A)
items.note_html: Modern Translation: That which is truly in us is imputed to us by God, not something that is absent from us or resides in another, namely, that we have firmly resolved in our mind, not doubting God's promises, nor considering our infirmity, to desire to run the proposed race of faith. items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Sunt enim opera nostra, id est, ut dictum fuit, obedientia, quam Christo praestamus, licet nec efficiens nec meritoria, tamen causa (ut vocant) sine qua non justificationis coram Deo, atque aeternae salutis nostrae.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: For our works, that is, as it has been said, the obedience which we render to Christ, although they are neither efficient nor meritorious, are nevertheless the cause (as they call it) sine qua non of our justification before God and of our eternal salvation. (Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore, Part 4)
items.note_html: Modern Translation: For our works, that is, as it has been said, the obedience which we render to Christ, although they are neither efficient nor meritorious, are nevertheless the cause (as they call it) sine qua non of our justification before God and of our eternal salvation. (Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore, Part 4)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: O Nam qui lepide postulat alterum frustrari, Quem frustratur, frustra eum dicit frustra esse. Nam qui sese frustrari quem frustra, sentit, Qui frustatur is frustra est, si non, ille est frustra.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: For he who pleasantly demands to deceive another, whom he deceives, he says in vain that he is in vain. For he who feels himself deceiving someone in vain, he who deceives is in vain; if not, the other is in vain. (Plautus, Captivi, 2.2.82)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Certum est ex sacris literis requiri ad hoc, ut quis consequatur apud Deum remissionem peccatorum, et ita coram Deo justificetur, ut de illo merito dici possit, quod pactum Dei servet.

(Socinian or Arminian Author, On Justification, Soteriology)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text:
Fides est fiducia per Deum in Christum, unde apparet eam in Christo fidem duo comprehendere: unum, ut non solum Deo, verum et Christo confidamus; deinde ut

Deo obtemperemus,
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: Faith is trust through God in Christ, from which it appears that this faith in Christ comprehends two things: one, that we not only trust God, but also Christ; and then that we obey God. (Faustus Socinus, De Justificatione, Unknown)
items.note_html: Modern Translation: Faith is trust through God in Christ, from which it appears that this faith in Christ comprehends two things: one, that we not only trust God, but also Christ; and then that we obey God. (Faustus Socinus, De Justificatione, Unknown)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Itaque nemo justificatus est coram Deo nisi prius Christo confidat, eique obediat; quae obedientia sunt illa opera ex quibus nos justificari Jacobus apostolus affirmat.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: Therefore no one is justified before God unless he first trusts in Christ, and obeys him; which obedience are those works by which the apostle James affirms we are justified. (Faustus Socinus, De Justificatione, Socinian Tracts)
items.note_html: Modern Translation: Therefore no one is justified before God unless he first trusts in Christ, and obeys him; which obedience are those works by which the apostle James affirms we are justified. (Faustus Socinus, De Justificatione, Socinian Tracts)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Quod vero ad nos pertinet, non aliter reipsa justi coram Deo habemur, et delictorum nostrorum veniam ab ipso consequimur, quam si in Jes. Christ. credamus.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: As far as it concerns us, we are not in reality accounted righteous before God, nor do we obtain pardon for our sins from Him, in any other way than if we believe in Jesus Christ. (Remonstrants, Apology or Confession, Unknown)
items.note_html: Modern Translation: As far as it concerns us, we are not in reality accounted righteous before God, nor do we obtain pardon for our sins from Him, in any other way than if we believe in Jesus Christ. (Remonstrants, Apology or Confession, Unknown)

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Id a nobis revera exegit, ut in Christum credamus, vitam emendaremus (quam conditionem salva sanctitate et majestate sua non poterat non exigere).
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: He indeed demanded this of us, that we believe in Christ and amend our life (which condition, saving His holiness and majesty, He could not but demand). (Theological Maxim, Various, )

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:
items.exact_text: Placeat tibi, Domine, liberare me a lite difficili, et ab adversario difficili, sive is ad foedus tuum pertineat sive non pertineat.

items.chapter: Of the Death of Christ, and of Justification:

items.chapter: A Second Consideration of the Annotations of Hugo Grotius.
items.exact_text: Καὶ λούσαντι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὑτοῦ. Sanguine suo, id est, morte tolerata, certos nos reddidit veriatis eorum quae docuerat, quae talia sunt, ut nihil sit aptius ad purgandos a vitiis animos. Humidae naturae, sub qua est et sanguis, proprium est lavare. Id vero per egregiam ἀλληγορίαν ad animam transfertur. Dicitur autem Christus suo sanguine nos lavasse, quia et ipse omnia praestitit quae ad id requirebantur et apparet secutum in plurimis effectum.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: 'And having washed us from our sins in his own blood.' In his own blood, that is, by the death he endured, he made us certain of the truth of the things he had taught, which are such that nothing is more apt to purge minds from vices. It is the property of a wet substance, under which blood is also included, to wash. But this is transferred to the soul by an excellent allegory. Moreover, Christ is said to have washed us in his blood, because he himself performed all things that were required for this, and the effect is seen to have followed in many. (Hugo Grotius, Annotations on the New Testament, Revelation 1:5)

items.chapter: A Second Consideration of the Annotations of Hugo Grotius.
items.exact_text: Bene autem in epistola tua quae mihi longe gratissima advenit, de me judicas, non esse me eorum in numero qui ob sententias saiva pietate dissidentes alieno a quoquam sim animo, aut boni alicuius amicitiam repudiem. Equidem in libro "De Vera Religione," quem jam percurri, relecturus et posthac, multa invenio summo cum judicio observats.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Hugo Grotius, Epistle to Johannes Crellius (with printed text's typo saiva for salva, and observats for observata).
Translation: “But in your letter, which came to me as by far the most welcome, you judge well of me, that I am not of the number of those who, on account of opinions that differ without harming piety, am of an estranged mind toward anyone, or would reject the friendship of any good man. Indeed, in the book ‘On the True Religion,’ which I have already run through and shall reread hereafter, I find many things observed with the highest judgment.”
items.note_html:

items.chapter: A Second Consideration of the Annotations of Hugo Grotius.
items.exact_text: Primo, quod non tantum humane, sed et valde officiose mecum egeris, ita ut queri nihil possim, nisi quod in me praediando, modum interdum excedis, deinde vero, quod multa me docueris, partita utilia, partim jucunda scitu, meque exemplo tuo incitaveris ad penitius expenden. dum sensus sacrorum librorum.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Hugo Grotius, Epistle to Johannes Crellius (with printed text's typo praediando for praedicando, and partita for partim, and expenden. dum for expendendum).
Translation: “First, because you dealt with me not only humanely but also very courteously, so that I can complain of nothing, except that in praising me you sometimes exceed the limit; and next indeed, because you have taught me many things, partly useful, partly pleasant to know, and by your example have incited me to weigh more deeply the meaning of the sacred books.”
items.note_html:

"Necessarium est hoc tristi tempore, quo Sociniana pestis, quam haud immerito dixeris omnis impietatis ἀκρόπολιν, videtur nune in vicina Anglia sedem aibi metropolitanam fixisse, nisi quod isthic cile admittat et bells cruent3, et Judicia capita!is severissima, sub quorum umbone crevit, lNam inter varias haereses, quibus felix ilia quondam insula et orthodoxiae tenacissima hodie conspurcatur, tantum eminet Socinianismus, quantum 'lenta solent inter viburna Cupressi;' nec enim amplius ibi horrenda sua mysteria mussitat in angulis, sed sub dio explicat omnia vexilla suaae iniquitatis: non loquor incomperta, benevole lector. Modo enim ex Anglia allatus eat Anglica lingua conscriptus Catechismus duplex, major et minor, Londini publice excusus, hoc anno 1654, spud Jac. Coterell, et Rich. Moone, etc., authore Johane Bidello, magistro artium Oxoniensi, etc." — Sam. Mares. Hyd. Socin. Refut. tom. ii. praefat. ad lect.
items.modern_reference:
Translation: “There appeared this year in England, authored by John Biddle, Master of Arts, fighter against the Spirit [pneumatomacho], a twofold Scriptural Catechism, published in English, by which he strives to force upon the Christian world, under the name of the Christian religion, pure and unadulterated Socinianism. Although, however, he does not seem to wish to be considered a Socinian; nevertheless, he reveals of what disposition he is toward the end of the booklet, when he commends the book entitled, ‘The life of that incomparable man, Faustus Socinus Senensis,’ and so distorts the phrase of Scripture to merely Socinian dogmas that no one before him has instilled that heresy so fraudulently; it is my intention, with God's help, to pull off his mask after the dog days.”
“It is necessary in this sad time, when the Socinian plague, which you might not undeservedly call the citadel [ἀκρόπολιν] of all impiety, seems now to have fixed its metropolitan seat in neighboring England, except that there it easily admits both bloody wars and most severe capital judgments, under the shield of which it has grown. For among the various heresies with which that once happy island, and most tenacious of orthodoxy, is defiled today, Socinianism stands out as much as ‘cypresses are wont to do among pliant viburnums’ [Virgil, Eclogues 1.25]; for no longer does it mutter its horrendous mysteries there in corners, but under the open sky it unfurls all the banners of its iniquity. I do not speak of things undiscovered, benevolent reader. For just recently there was brought from England a twofold Catechism, major and minor, written in the English tongue, publicly printed in London, this year 1654, by James Coterell, and Richard Moone, etc., authored by John Biddle, Master of Arts at Oxford, etc.”

items.modern_reference: Translation: “Grotius, in book 5 of On the Truth of the Christian Religion, in the notes adduces R. Solomon, Aben Ezra, and Onkelos. items.modern_reference: Translation: “Reverend sir, I am often compelled to be troublesome to you. items.exact_text: "Ariani Christo divinum cultum non.tribuerunt. Atqui longe praestat Trinitarium esse quam Christo divinum cultum non tribuere. Imo Trinitarius (meo quidem judicio) modo alioqui Christi praecepta conserver, nec ulla ratione eos persequatur, qui Trinitarii non sunt sed potius cum ipsis fraterne conferre, ac veritatem inquirere non recuset, merito Christianus dici debet. Qui vero Christum divina ratione non colit, is hullo mode Christianus dici potest: Quocirca non est dubitandum, quin Deo minus displicuerunt Homo-ousiani Trinitarii, quam vulgus Arianorum. Quid igitur mirum, si cum totus fere orbis Christianus in has duas (ut ita dicam) factiones divisus esset Deus visionibus et miraculis testari voluisset utram ipsarum viam salutis vel adhuc retineret, vel jam abjecisset. Adde Arianos acerrime tunc persecutos fuisse miseros Homo-ousianos, idque diu et variis in locis: 825 quare merito se Deus Arianis iratum ostendit." — Socin. ad Weik, p. 452.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “The Arians did not attribute divine worship to Christ. But it is far better to be a Trinitarian than not to attribute divine worship to Christ. Indeed a Trinitarian (in my judgment at least), provided he otherwise keeps the precepts of Christ, and by no means persecutes those who are not Trinitarians, but rather does not refuse to confer fraternally with them and seek the truth, ought deservedly to be called a Christian. But he who does not worship Christ in a divine manner, can in no way be called a Christian: Wherefore it is not to be doubted that the Homoousian Trinitarians displeased God less than the rabble of the Arians. What wonder then, if when almost the whole Christian world was divided into these two factions (so to speak), God willed to testify by visions and miracles which of them either still retained the way of salvation, or had already cast it away. Add that the Arians then most bitterly persecuted the miserable Homoousians, and that for a long time and in various places: wherefore God deservedly showed himself angry with the Arians.”

items.exact_text: "De tribus in una divina essentia personis anno 1562 controversiam moverunt, in Min. Pol. Itali quidam advenae; praecipui autem assertores contra S. S. Trinitatem fuere, Georgius Blandrata theologus ac medicus, Petrus Statorius, Tonvillanus, Franciscus Lismaninus theologiae doctor, quorum tamen ab initio opera reformationis valde fuit ecclesiae Dei procliva." — Hist. Ecclesiastes Slavon lib 1:p 84
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Some Italian immigrants in 1562 stirred up a controversy in Minor Poland concerning the three persons in one divine essence; the principal assertors against the Holy Trinity were George Blandrata, theologian and physician, Peter Statorius, Tonvillanus, and Francis Lismaninus, doctor of theology, whose work of reformation, however, from the beginning was very favorable to the church of God.”

items.exact_text: "Propheticam et apestolicam doctrinam, quae veram Dei Patris, Filii, et Spiritus Sancti cognitionem continet, amplector ac veneror parique religione Deum Pattrem, Filium et Spiritum Sanctum distincte secundum sacrarum literarum veritatem colendum, implo-randumque precibus, libere profiteor. Denique omnem haereticam de Deo Patre, Fitio, et Spiritu Sancto blasphemiam, plane detestor, sire Ariana ilia. sive Servetiana, sive Euno-miana, sive Stancariana" — Act. Ecclesiastes Min. Pol. Syn. Pinczov. anno 1559.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I embrace and venerate the prophetic and apostolic doctrine, which contains the true knowledge of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and I freely profess that God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are to be worshipped with equal religion, distinctly, according to the truth of the sacred letters, and to be implored in prayers. Finally, I plainly detest all heretical blasphemy concerning God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whether it be that of Arius, or Servetus, or Eunomius, or Stancarus.”

items.exact_text: "De Georgio Blandrata, pro singulari suo in ecclesiam Dei amore praemonuit Polonoe Cl. vir Johan. Cal. quinetiam illustrissimum principem palatinum, Vilocensem, Nicolaum Radzivilium, cujus patrocinio Blandrata tum utebatur. Subolfecerat enim vir doctus Blandratae ingenium ad Serveti sententiam esse compositum: itaque serius prin-cipi suasor fuit, ut sibi ab eo caveret: sed homo ille facile, technis suis fallacibus, optimo principi fucum fecit, adeo ut ille iratus Johanni Calvino, Blandratam nomine suo ad Synodum Pinckzoviensem anno 1561, 25 Jun. habitam, delegaret cum literis, quibus serio postulabat in causa Blandratae, cum ecclesia, dicebatque male et praecipitanter egisse Calvinum, quod Blandratam traduceret, et Servetismi notaret." — Regen. Hist. lib. 1:p. 85.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Concerning George Blandrata, out of his singular love for the church of God, the celebrated man John Calvin forewarned the Poles; and furthermore the most illustrious palatine prince of Vilna, Nicholas Radziwiłł, whose patronage Blandrata then used. For the learned man had smelled out that the disposition of Blandrata was composed toward the opinion of Servetus: therefore he earnestly advised the prince to beware of him: but that man easily, by his fallacious tricks, painted a false picture for the excellent prince, so that he, angry at John Calvin, delegated Blandrata in his own name to the Synod of Pińczów held in the year 1561, on June 25, with letters in which he seriously made demands in the case of Blandrata with the church, and said that Calvin had acted badly and precipitately in slandering Blandrata and branding him with Servetism.”

items.exact_text: "Fateor me credere in unum Deum Patrem, et in unum Dominum Jesum Christum Filium ejus, et in unum Spiritum Sanctum, quorum quilibet est essentialiter Deus. Deo-rum pluralitatem detestor, cum unus tantum sit nobis Deus, essentia indivisibilis. Fateor tres esse distinctas hypostases; et aeternam Christi divinitatem et generationem; et Spiritum Sanctum, unum et aeteruum Deum, ab utroque procedentem." — Act. Syn. Pinckzov. anno 1561. 826
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I confess that I believe in one God the Father, and in one Lord Jesus Christ his Son, and in one Holy Spirit, any one of whom is essentially God. I detest a plurality of Gods, since there is only one God to us, indivisible in essence. I confess that there are three distinct hypostases; and the eternal divinity and generation of Christ; and the Holy Spirit, one and eternal God, proceeding from both.”

items.exact_text: "Dixit heri vir amplissimus Blandrata, librum se tuum contra Palaeologum accepisse. Habes tu unum saltem cui sis charissimus, cui omnia debes, qui judicio maxime polleat: cur tantum studium, consiliique pondus neglexisti? poteras non tantum ejus censuram absoluti jam libri petere, sed consilium postulare de subeundo non levi labore. lit possum affirmare senis consilium tibi sine dubio, si petivisti, profuturum fuisse." — Ep. Marcel Squarc. ad Faust. Socin.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “The most distinguished man Blandrata said yesterday that he had received your book against Palaeologus. You have at least one to whom you are very dear, to whom you owe everything, who is very powerful in judgment: why have you neglected so much zeal, and weight of counsel? You could not only have sought his censure of the already completed book, but have asked his counsel about undergoing no light labor. And I can affirm that the old man's counsel would without a doubt have been profitable to you, if you had sought it.”

items.exact_text: b "Fuit is Laelius nobili honestaque familia natus, bene Graece et Hebraice doctus, vitaeque etiam.externae inculpatae, quarum rerum causa mihi quoque intercesserat cumillo non vulgaris amicitia; sed homo fuit plenus diversarum haeresium, quas tamen mihi -nunquam proponebat nisi disputandi causa, et semper interrogans, quasi cuperet doceri. Hanc vero Samosatenianam imprimis annos multos fovit, et quoscunque potuit pertraxit in eundem errorem; pertraxit autem non paucos: me quoque ut dixi diversis tentabat rationibus, si eodem possit errore simul, et aeterno exitio secum involvere." — Zanch. Pre-fat. ad lib. de Tribus Elohim.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “This Laelius was born of a noble and honest family, well learned in Greek and Hebrew, and also of a blameless external life, for which reasons an uncommon friendship had arisen between me and him; but he was a man full of diverse heresies, which however he never proposed to me except for the sake of disputing, and always questioning, as if he desired to be taught. But this Samosatenian one especially he fostered for many years, and drew over whomever he could into the same error; and he drew over not a few: me also, as I have said, he tempted with diverse arguments, if he might be able to involve me simultaneously in the same error, and eternal destruction with himself.”

items.exact_text: "Nos quidem o amici haud difficulter poterimus vobiscum earn rem transigere, nam ubi primum Biblia aperueritis, et initium veteris et novae legis consideraveritis, statim offendetis, id ibi asseri quod vos pernegatis, sic enim Geneseos primo Scriptura loquitur, Faciamus 828 hominem ad imaginem nostram. Nostram, inquit, non meam. Postea vero addit, Fecit Deus. Novae autem legis initium hoc est, Verbum erat apud Deum, et Verbum erat Deus. Videtis ut in veteri lege loquatur unus Deus tanquam de tribus; hic vero quod filius veroum sete. rnum (nam quod ab initio erat, ternum est) erat apud Deum, et erat aem, non anus, ut yes perram mterpretamini, Deus"
items.modern_reference: Translation: “We indeed, O friends, will be able to settle this matter with you without difficulty, for as soon as you open the Bibles and consider the beginning of the old and new law, you will immediately encounter that being asserted there which you utterly deny. For thus Scripture speaks in the first chapter of Genesis: 'Let us make man in our image.' 'Our,' it says, not 'my.' But afterwards it adds: 'God made.' Now the beginning of the new law is this: 'The Word was with God, and the Word was God.' You see how in the old law one God speaks as if of three; but here, that the Son, the eternal Word (for what was from the beginning, is eternal) was with God, and was God, not another God, as you wrongly interpret.”

items.exact_text: "Homo ille Jes. Nazarenus qui Christus appellatur, non per spiritum propheticum, sed per Spiritum Sanctum locutus est; id est, quamvis a Deo legatus fuerit, non tamen quaecunque verba ex ipsius Dei ore provenisse censenda sunt. 2. Hinc fit ut illius et apostolorum ejus verba, ad Mosaicae legis et aliorum propheticorum oraculorum normam expendenda sint, et siquid contrarium vel diversum ab his in illis reperitur, aut reperiri videtur, id aut rejiciendum, aut certe ita in terpretandum sit, ut cum Mosis et prophet-arum doctrina consentiat quae sola morum et divini cultus regula est"
items.modern_reference: Translation: “That man Jesus of Nazareth, who is called the Christ, spoke not by a prophetic spirit, but by the Holy Spirit; that is, although he was sent as an ambassador by God, yet not all his words are to be considered as having proceeded from the mouth of God Himself. 2. Hence it follows that his words and those of his apostles must be weighed according to the standard of the Mosaic law and other prophetic oracles, and if anything contrary to or different from these is found, or seems to be found in them, it must either be rejected, or at least so interpreted that it agrees with the doctrine of Moses and the prophets, which alone is the rule of morals and divine worship.”

items.exact_text: "Quod-si Weikus intelligit damnandi verbo nostros ministros censuisse illum aliqua sfficiendum, aut vuit fallere, aut egregie fallitur: nam certum est, in judicio illo, cum minister quidam Calvinianus Christophero, Principi, qui toti actioni interfuit, et praefuit, satis longa oratione persuasisset, ut talem, hominem e medio tolleret, minitans everenter illi supplicasse, ut miseri hominis misereri vellet et clementem et benignum se erga illum praebere." — Socin, ad Weik cap. 2 p. 47
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But if Weick understands by the word 'condemned' that our ministers thought he should be subjected to some punishment, he either wishes to deceive, or is egregiously deceived: for it is certain that in that trial, when a certain Calvinist minister had persuaded Prince Christopher, who was present at and presided over the whole proceeding, in a rather long speech, to remove such a man from their midst with threats, [we] reverently entreated him that he would have mercy on the wretched man and show himself merciful and kind towards him.”

items.exact_text: "Imo plusquam haereticum eum (ecclesiae nostrae) judicaverunt, nam talem hominem indignum Christiano nomme esse dixerunt; quippe qui Christo invocationis cultum prorsus detrahendo, et eum curam ecclesiae gerere negando, simul reipsa negaret eum ease Christum." — Idem ubi supra.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Nay, they (of our church) judged him to be more than a heretic, for they said such a man was unworthy of the Christian name; seeing that by utterly taking away the worship of invocation from Christ, and denying that he takes care of the church, he at the same time practically denied that he is the Christ.”

items.exact_text: Duces hujus agminis Anabaptistici, et Antitrinitarii erant Gregorius Paulus, Daniel Bielenscius, et alii, quorum tandem aliqui fanatico proposito relicto, ad ecclesiam evangelicam redierunt, ut Daniel Bielenscius, qui Cracoviae omnium suorum errorum publice poenitentiam egit, ibidemque, ecclesiae Dei commode praefuit." — Adrian. Regen. Hist. Ecclesiastes Slavon lib. 1 p. 90.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “The leaders of this Anabaptist and Antitrinitarian host were Gregory Paul, Daniel Bieliński, and others, some of whom at length, abandoning their fanatical purpose, returned to the evangelical church, as did Daniel Bieliński, who at Krakow publicly repented of all his errors, and in the same place properly presided over the church of God.”

items.exact_text: "Ita argumentor, quoties regnum Davidi usque in seculum promissum est tale necesse fuit, ut posteri ejus, in quibus haec promissio impleri debebat, haberent: sed regnum mundanum Davidi usque in seculum promissum est, ergo regnum mundanum posteri Davidis ut haberent necesse est: et per consequens, rex file, quem prophetae ex hac promissione post captivitatem Babylonicam regnaturum promiserunt, perinde ut caeteri posteri Davidis, mundanum regnum debuit habere. Quod quia Jesus ille non habuit (non enim regnavit ut David et posteri ejus), sed dicitur habere coeleste regnum, quod est diversum a mundano regno; ergo Jesus ille non est rex quem prophetae promiserunt." — Martin Seidelius, Ep. 1 ad Socin.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Thus I argue: as often as a kingdom was promised to David forever, it was necessary that his descendants, in whom this promise was to be fulfilled, should have it: but a worldly kingdom was promised to David forever, therefore it is necessary that the descendants of David should have a worldly kingdom: and consequently, that king, whom the prophets promised from this promise would reign after the Babylonian captivity, just as the rest of the descendants of David, ought to have had a worldly kingdom. Which because that Jesus did not have (for he did not reign as David and his descendants), but is said to have a heavenly kingdom, which is different from a worldly kingdom; therefore that Jesus is not the king whom the prophets promised.”

items.exact_text: "Nam quod dicimus, si Deus mundanum regem mundanumque regnum promisit, coelestem autem regein, coeleste, regnum reipsa praestitit plus eum. praestitisse quam promiserit, recte omimino dicimus, nam qui plus praestat quam promisit, suis promissis non modo non stetisse sed ea etiam cumulate praestitisse est agnoscendus." — Socin. Ep. ad Seidelium, p. 20.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “For as to what we say, if God promised a worldly king and a worldly kingdom, but in reality provided a heavenly king and a heavenly kingdom, that he provided more than he promised, we say altogether rightly; for he who provides more than he promised is to be acknowledged not only not to have stood by his promises, but even to have provided them abundantly.”

items.exact_text: "Extat apud me ipsius Blandratae epistola, non tamen scripta sine Theseo (Statorto) si Blandratum bene novi, in qua Gregorium Paulum a Tritheismo ad Samosateni dogma revocare nititur. Incidit enim Blandrata in Transylvaniam rediens in quendam Fran-ciscum David, paulo magis, quam superiores illi ut aiunt providum." — Beza, Ep. 81.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “There is extant with me a letter of Blandrata himself, yet not written without his Theseus (Statorius), if I know Blandrata well, in which he strives to call back Gregory Paul from Tritheism to the dogma of Samosatenus. For Blandrata, returning to Transylvania, fell in with a certain Francis David, a little more provident, as they say, than those former ones.”

items.exact_text: "Ecclesiis Polonicis, quae solum Patrem Domini Jesu summum Deum agnoscunt, publice adjungi ambivit, sed satis acerbe atque diu repulsam passus est, qua tamen ignominia minime accensus, vir, non tam indole quam anir, instituto, ad patientiam compositus, nulla unquam alienati animi vestigia dedit." — Vita Faust. Socin.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “He sought to be publicly joined to the Polish churches, which acknowledge only the Father of the Lord Jesus as the supreme God, but he suffered a rather bitter and prolonged rejection; yet being not at all inflamed by this disgrace, the man, being composed to patience not so much by his nature as by the purpose of his mind, never gave any signs of an alienated mind.”

items.exact_text: Nam quod mihi objicis .me communionem.cum. fratribus, et Christi fidelibus spernere nec cuare ut cum ipsis coenam Domini celebrem, respondeo, me postquam in Poloniam veni, nihil antiquius habuisse, quam ut me quam maxime fratribus conjungerem, licet invenissem illos in non parvis religionis nostrae capitibus, a me diversum sentire; quemadmodum multi hodieque sentiunt: quod si nihilominus aquas baptismum una cum illis non accipio, hoc praeterea fit, quia id bona conscientia facere nequeo, nisi publice ante protestor, me non quod censeam baptismum aquae mihi meique similibus ullo modo necessarium esse, etc." — Ep, ad Sophiam Siemichoviam feminam nobilem. — Ep. 11 ad Valent. Smalc. anno 1604.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “For as to your objection to me, that I despise communion with the brethren and the faithful of Christ, and do not care to celebrate the Lord's supper with them, I answer, that after I came to Poland, I accounted nothing more important than to join myself as much as possible to the brethren, although I found them to think differently from me in no small heads of our religion; just as many still think today: but if nevertheless I do not receive the baptism of water together with them, this happens moreover because I cannot do it with a good conscience, unless I publicly protest beforehand, not that I think the baptism of water is in any way necessary for me and those like me, etc.”

items.exact_text: "Dico secessionem Racoviensium ac delirium, esse ab ecclesia rati o sejungendum, nisi velis conciliabula quaeque amentium anicularum partes ecclesiae a Christianae ut ecclesiam appellare " — Mar Squarcialup Ep. ad faust Socin. p. 8.

Translation: “I say that the secession and madness of the Racovians must be separated from the account of the church, unless you wish to call any assemblies of mad old women parts of the Christian church, or to call them the church.”

items.exact_text: Huc accedit, quod Racovienses isti, sive coetus Racoviensis, quem tu petis atque oppugnas, vel non amplius extat, vel ita hodie mutatus est, et in aliam quodammodo formam versus, ut agnosci non queat." — Socin. Praefat. ad Palaeolog.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “To this is added, that those Racovians, or the Racovian congregation, which you attack and assail, either no longer exists, or is so changed today, and turned into another form in a certain measure, that it cannot be recognized.”

items.exact_text: " Dolerem quidem mirum., in in odum si disputatio ista sic habita fuisset, ut adversarii susplcor tamen nihfiommus, quatenus diputationem ab ipsis editam percurrendo animadvertere ac consequi conjectura potui, Licinii antagonistam arte dispu-tandi et ipso 834 superiorem esse, et id in ista ipsa disputatione facile plerisque constitisse: nam etsi (ni fallor) Licinius noster neutiquam in ea haeresi est, in qua non pauci ex nostris sunt, non esse Christiano homini dandam operam dialecticae," etc. — Ep. ad Balcerovicium, p. 358.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I should indeed be wonderfully grieved, if that disputation had been so held, as the adversaries [claim]; nevertheless I suspect, as far as I could observe and conclude by conjecture in running through the disputation published by them, that the antagonist of Licinius was superior to him in the art of disputing, and that this was easily apparent to most in that very disputation: for although (unless I am mistaken) our Licinius is by no means in that heresy in which not a few of our men are, that a Christian man should not give attention to dialectics, etc.”

items.exact_text: "Quod totum fere pondus illius disputationis, adversus eos qui Christum adhuc ignorare dici possunt, sustinueris, vehementer tibi gratulor: nihil mihi novum fuit, ex narratione ista percipere, pastores illos Lithuanicos ab ejusmodi ignoratione minime li-beros deprehensos fuisse." — Ep. 5 ad Smalc.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “That you have sustained almost the whole weight of that disputation, against those who can be said still to be ignorant of Christ, I vehemently congratulate you: it was nothing new to me to perceive from that narrative, that those Lithuanian pastors were discovered to be by no means free from such ignorance.”

items.exact_text: "Me imitari noli, qui nescio quo malo genio ductore, cum jam divinae veritatis fontes degustassem, ita sum abreptus, ut majorem et potiorem juventutis meae partem, inanibus quibusdam aliis studiis, imo inertiae atque otio dederim, quod cum mecum ipse reputo, reputo autem saepissime, tanto dolore afficior, ut me vivere quodam modo pi-gear. — Ep. ad Smalc. p. 513.
items.modern_reference:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, Letter to Valentinus Smalcius, p. 513 [Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, 1:513].
Translation: “Do not imitate me, who, led by I know not what evil genius as a guide, when I had already tasted the fountains of divine truth, was so carried away that I gave the greater and better part of my youth to certain other empty studies, indeed to sluggishness and leisure; which when I consider with myself—and I consider it very frequently—I am affected by such great grief that in a certain way it irks me to live.”

items.exact_text: "Ad te quod attinet, amino es tu quidem ad omnem doctrinae rationem, ac veritatis investigationem nato, magna rerum, sophisticarum cognitio, orator summus, et theologus cum proipuis totius Europae ingeniis certare." — Marcel. Squarcialup. Ep. ad. Faust. Socin.
items.modern_reference:
Modern Citation: Marcellus Squarcialupus, Letter to Faustus Socinus [Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, 1:8].
Translation: “As far as you are concerned, you indeed have a mind born for every method of doctrine and investigation of truth, a great knowledge of sophisticated matters, a supreme orator, and a theologian fit to compete with the foremost intellects of all Europe.”

items.exact_text: "Tibi significo me ni fallor invenisse viam quomodo verum esse possit, quod Christus plane libere et citra omnem necessitatem Deo perfectissime obediret et tamen necessarium omnino fuerit ut sic obediret; quaenam ista via sit, nisi eam ipse per te (ut plane spero) inveneeris, postea tibi aperiam: volo enim prius tuum hosae iin re et Statorii mgenium experiri, tametsi vereor ne ja, eam illi indicaverim." Ep. 4 ad Ostorod. P. 472. 835
items.modern_reference:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, Letter 4 to Christopher Ostorod, p. 472 [Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, 1:472].
Translation: “I signify to you that, unless I am mistaken, I have found a way in which it can be true that Christ obeyed God most perfectly, completely freely and without any necessity, and yet it was entirely necessary that He should so obey. What that way is, unless you find it yourself (as indeed I hope you will), I will reveal to you later; for I wish first to test your genius and that of Statorius in this matter, though I fear I may have already indicated it to them.”

items.exact_text: "Perlecto scripto tuo contra Volanum animadverti argumenta ejus satis accurate a te refutata, locaque scripturae pleraque examinata, ac elucidata, verum no sine maerore (ne quid gravius addam) incidi inter legendum in quoddam paradoxon, Scripturae sacrae contrarium ac plane horrendum, dum Christum in morte sua sive in cruce, sacrificium obtulisse pernegas, miror quid tibi in mentem venerit, ut tam confidenter (ne quid aliud dicam) contra manifesta sacrae Scripturae testimonia pugnare, contrariamque sententiam tueri non timeas." — Ep. 1 Joh. Niemojev. ad Faust. Socin. p. 196
items.modern_reference:
Modern Citation: John Niemojevus (Niemojewski), Letter 1 to Faustus Socinus [Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, Faustus Socinus Opera, 1:196].
Translation: “Having thoroughly read your writing against Volanus, I noticed that his arguments were refuted by you with sufficient accuracy, and most passages of Scripture were examined and elucidated. However, not without grief (to add nothing more serious), I stumbled while reading upon a certain paradox, contrary to the Holy Scripture and plainly horrible: namely, that you deny Christ offered a sacrifice in His death or on the cross. I wonder what came into your mind, that you do not fear to fight so confidently (to say nothing else) against the manifest testimonies of the Holy Scripture, and to defend a contrary opinion.”

items.exact_text: Denique Socinistae recensendi mihi veniunt quia Fausto Socino, per Polooniam et Transylvaniam virus suum disseminante, tum nomen tum doctrinam sumpsere; atque hi soli, extinctis Farnesianis, Anabaptistis, et Francisci Davidis sectatoribus supersunt; homines ad fallacias et sophismata facti." — Hist. items.modern_reference: Translation: “Finally, I must review the Socinians, because when Faustus Socinus disseminated his poison through Poland and Transylvania, they took both their name and their doctrine from him; and these alone survive, after the Farnesians, Anabaptists, and the followers of Francis David have been extinguished; men made for fallacies and sophisms.”

items.exact_text: "Palaeologus praecipuus fuit ex Antesignanis illorum qui Christum nec invocandum, nec adorandum esse hodie affirmant et interim tamen se Christianos esse impudenter profitentur, quo vix quidquam scelestius in religione nostra depravanda excogitari posse existimo." — Socin. ad Weik. Ref. ad cap. 4:cap. 2:p. 42. 836
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Palaeologus was the chief among the vanguard of those who affirm today that Christ is neither to be invoked nor adored, and yet meanwhile impudently profess themselves to be Christians, than which I think scarcely anything more wicked could be devised for corrupting our religion.”

items.exact_text: "Notatu vero dignissimum est hisce novis Arianis ad apostasiam seu Arianismum occasionem fuisse, doctrinam Calvinistarum, id quod ipsi Ariani haud obscure professi sunt. Recitabo hujus rei exemplum memorabile de Adamo Neusero ante paucos annos Ecclesiae Heidelbergensis ad S. S. primario pastore nobilissimo sacramentario. Hic ex Zvinglianisimo per Ariauismum ad Mahometismum usque, cum aliis non paucis Calvinistis Constantinopolin circumcisionem judaicam recipiens et veritatem agnitam abnegans progressus est Hic Adamus sequentia verba dedit Constantinopol. D. Gerlachio, anne 1574, 'nullus nostro tempore mihi notus factus est Arianus qui non antea fuerit Calvinista. Servetus, etc., igitur qui sibi timet ne incidat in Arianismum, caveat Calvinismum.'"
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Indeed, it is most worthy of note that the doctrine of the Calvinists was the occasion for these new Arians to apostatize to Arianism, a fact which the Arians themselves have not obscurely professed. I will recite a memorable example of this concerning Adam Neuser, who a few years ago was the primary and most noble sacramentarian pastor of the Church of Heidelberg at the Holy Spirit. He progressed from Zwinglianism through Arianism all the way to Mohammedanism, receiving Jewish circumcision in Constantinople along with not a few other Calvinists, and denying the recognized truth. This Adam gave the following words to D. Gerlach at Constantinople in the year 1574: ‘No one in our time known to me has become an Arian who was not previously a Calvinist. Servetus, etc., therefore whoever fears for himself lest he fall into Arianism, let him beware of Calvinism.’”

items.exact_text: "Hoc tantum dicam, cum nuper Bellarmini disputationum primum tomum evolverem, supra modum me miratum fuisse, quod ad finem fere singularum controversiarum homo alioqui acutus ac sagax ea verba aut curaverit aut permiserut adscrubu; Laus Deo, virginique matri; quibus verbis manifeste Virfini Mariae divinus cultus, aut ex sequo cum ipso Deo, aut certe secundum Deum exhibetur." — Socin. Ad Weik. Cap. i. p. 22
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I will say only this: when I recently unrolled the first volume of Bellarmine's disputations, I was beyond measure amazed that at the end of almost every single controversy a man otherwise acute and sagacious either took care or allowed these words to be appended: ‘Praise be to God and to the Virgin Mother’; by which words divine worship is manifestly exhibited to the Virgin Mary, either on an equal footing with God himself, or certainly second to God.”

items.exact_text: "Nam ego quidem sic statuok etsi non pendent aliuude rerum sacrarum veritas quam ab unico Dei verbo, et sedul vitanda est nobis omnis κενοφωνία: tamen sublato essentiae et hypostasewn discrimine (quibuscumque tandem verbis utaris) et abrogato ὁμοουσίῳ, vix ac ne vix quidem istorum blasphemorum fraudes detegi, et errores satis perspicue coargui posse. Nego quoque sublatis vocabulis naturae, proprietatis, hypostaticae unionis, ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνίας posse Nestorii et Eutychei blasphemias commode a quoquam refelli: qua in re si forte hallucinor, hoc age, nobis demonstret qui potest, et nos illum coronabimus." — Beza, Ep. 81.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “For I indeed determine thus: although the truth of sacred matters depends on nothing else than the unique word of God, and we must diligently avoid all empty babbling, nevertheless, if the distinction of essence and hypostases is removed (whatever words you may finally use) and the consubstantial is abrogated, the frauds of those blasphemers can scarcely, if at all, be detected and their errors sufficiently clearly refuted. I also deny that, if the words of nature, property, hypostatic union, and communion of properties are removed, the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches can be conveniently refuted by anyone. In this matter, if perchance I am hallucinating, come now, let him who can demonstrate it to us, and we will crown him.”

items.exact_text: "Ais igitur adversus id quod a me affirmatum fuerat, in controversis dogmatibus probandis, aut improbandis, necesse esse literam adferre, et id quod asseritur manifeste demonstrare: id quod asseritur manifeste demonstrari debere plane concede; literam autem adferre necesse esse prorsus nego; me autem jure hoc facere id aperte confirmat, quod quaedam dogmata in Christi ecclesia receptissima, non solum per expressam literam non probantur, sed ipsam sibi contrariam habent. 837 Exempli causa, inter omnes fete Christiani nominis heroines receptissimum est, Deum non habere aliqua membra corporis, ut aures, oculos, nares, brachia, pedes, marius, et tamen non mode expresse et literaliter (ut vocant) id scripture in sacris libris non est: verum etiam contrarium omnino passim diserte scriptum extat." — Faust. Socin. Frag. Disput. de Ador. Christi cum Fran. David, cap. 10 p. 59.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “You say, therefore, against what had been affirmed by me, that in proving or disproving controversial dogmas, it is necessary to bring forward the letter, and to manifest clearly what is asserted: I plainly concede that what is asserted ought to be manifestly demonstrated; but I utterly deny that it is necessary to bring forward the letter. That I do this by right is openly confirmed by the fact that certain dogmas most widely received in the church of Christ are not only not proved by the express letter, but have the letter itself contrary to them. For example, among almost all men of the Christian name it is most highly received that God does not have any bodily members, such as ears, eyes, nostrils, arms, feet, hands, and yet not only is this not expressly and literally (as they call it) written in the sacred books, but even the exact opposite is expressly written everywhere.”

items.exact_text: "Simile quod affers de vocabulis "essentiae," et "personarum" a nobis repudiatis, quia in sanctis literis non inveniantur, non est admittendum, nemini enim vere cordato persuadebitis id quod per ea vocabuli adversarii significare voluerunt, idcirco repudiandum esse, quia ipsa vocabula scripta non inveniantur, imo quicunque ex nobis hac ratione sunt usi, suspectam apud nonnullos, alioquin ingenio, et eruditione praestantes viros, causam nostram reddidere." — Idem, ubi sup. p. 62.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “The similarity you bring up about the words ‘essence’ and ‘persons’ being repudiated by us, because they are not found in the holy letters, is not to be admitted; for you will persuade no truly sensible person that what the adversaries wished to signify by these words is to be repudiated on the grounds that the words themselves are not found written; indeed, whoever among us has used this reasoning has rendered our cause suspect among some men, otherwise outstanding in genius and erudition.”

items.exact_text: "Quotquot hactenus theologica tractarunt, id sibi negotii crediderunt solum dari, ut quam sive sors illis obtulerat, sive judicio amplexi erant sententiam, totis illam viribus tuerentur." — Curcellaeus Praesat. ad Opera Episcop.
items.modern_reference:
Modern Citation: Etienne de Courcelles (Curcellaeus), Preface to the *Works of Simon Episcopius* (Amsterdam, 1650).
Translation: “As many as have flourished in treating theology believed that this task alone was given to them: that they should defend with all their strength whatever opinion either chance had offered them, or they had embraced by their judgment.”

items.modern_reference: Translation: “In athletes, states of supreme physical fitness are dangerous, if they are at the extreme. items.exact_text: "Quicunque sacras literas assidua manu versat, quantumvis nescio quos catechismos, vel locos communes et commentarios quam familiarissimos sibi reddiderit, is statim cum nostrorum libros vel semel inspexerit, intelliget quantum distant aera lupinis." — Valent. Smalc. Res. Orat. Vogel et Peuschel. Rac. anno 1617, p. 34. "Scripta haec, Dei gloriam et Christi Domini nostri honorem, ac ipsam nostram salutem, ab omni traditionum humanarum labe, ipsa divina veritate literis sacris comprehensa repurgare nituntur, et expeditissima explicandae Dei gloriae, honoris Christo Domino nostro asserendi, et salutis consequendae ratione excerpta, ac omnibus proposita eam ipsissima sacrarum literarum authoritate sancire et stabilire conantur." — Hieron. Moscorov. Ep. Dedic. Cat. Rac. ad Jacob. in B. R. nomine et jussu Ecclesiae Polon. "Neque porro quemquam ease arbitror, qui in tot ac tantis Christianae religionis placitis, a reliquis homimbus dissentiat, in 838 quot quantisque ego dissentio." — Socin. Ep. ad Squarcialup. anno 1581.
items.modern_reference:
Translation: “Whoever turns the sacred letters with a constant hand, however much he may have made familiar to himself I know not what catechisms, or commonplaces and commentaries, as soon as he has inspected our books even once, will understand how much true coin differs from lupines [i.e., real money from fake].”
“These writings strive to purge the glory of God and the honor of Christ our Lord, and our very salvation, from every stain of human traditions, by the very divine truth comprehended in the sacred letters, and they endeavor to sanction and establish with the very authority of the sacred letters the most expedient method, excerpted and proposed to all, of explaining the glory of God, of asserting the honor to Christ our Lord, and of obtaining salvation.”
“Nor furthermore do I think there is anyone who dissents from the rest of men in so many and such great tenets of the Christian religion, in as many and as great ones as I dissent.”

items.exact_text: "Via remotionis utendum est, in Dei consideratione: nam divina suhstantia sua immensitate excedit omnem formam, quam intellectus noster intelligit, unde ipsum non possumus exacte cognoscere quid sit, sed quid non sit." — Thom. Con. Gentes, lib..1, cap; 14:"Merito dictum est a veteribus, potius in hac vita de Deo a nobis cognosci quid non sit, quam quid sit; ut enim cognoscamus quid Deus non sit, negatione nimirum aliqua, quae propria sit divinae essentiae, satis est unica negatio dependentiae," etc. — Socin. ad lib. 2:cap 1; Metaph. Arist. q. 2, sect 4. ftt119 Suarez. Metaph. tom. 2:disput. 30, sect. 3; Cajetan. de Ente et Essen. cap ii.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa contra Gentiles, I.14.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa contra Gentiles, I.14.
Translation: “The way of remotion is to be used especially in the consideration of God: for the divine substance by its immensity exceeds every form which our intellect understands, whence we cannot know exactly what He is, but what He is not.” — Thomas Aquinas.
“It was rightly said by the ancients, that in this life it is better known by us concerning God what He is not, rather than what He is; for in order that we may know what God is not, by some negation indeed, which is proper to the divine essence, a single negation of dependence is sufficient, etc.” — Socinus. [With references to Aristotle's Metaphysics, Francisco Suárez's Metaphysical Disputations, and Thomas Cajetan's On Being and Essence].

Serm. 3:de Nat. 840

Translation: “Not so that God would be a dweller, and human nature a dwelling place: but that one nature should be so mingled with the other, that although the one which is taken up is different from the one which takes it up, the diversity of both should nevertheless meet in such a great unity, that it is one and the same Son, who, both according to the fact that He is man, calls Himself lesser than the Father, and according to the fact that He is one God, professes Himself equal to the Father.”

items.exact_text: "Exposuisti quae cognitu ad salutem de essentia Dei sunt prorsus necessaria, expone quae ad eam rem vehementer utilia esse censeas. R. Id quidem est ut cognoscamus in essentia Dei unam tantum personam esse. Demonstra hoc ipsum. R. Hoc sane vel hinc patere potest, quod essentia Dei sit una numero; quapropter plures numero personae, in ea esse nullo pacto possunt. Quaenam est haec una Persona divina? Est ille Deus unus, Domini nostri Jesu Christi Pater, 1 Corinthians 8:6." — Cat. Rac cap. i., de Cognit. Dei, de Dei Essentita.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “‘You have explained those things concerning the essence of God which are absolutely necessary to be known for salvation, explain those things which you think to be very useful for that matter.’ Answer: ‘It is indeed this, that we may know that there is only one person in the essence of God.’ ‘Demonstrate this very thing.’ Answer: ‘This indeed can be evident even from this, that the essence of God is one in number; on which account several persons in number can by no means be in it. Who is this one divine Person? It is that one God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 8:6.’”

items.exact_text: "Significat enim Christus id, quod ratio ilia dictat, Deum, cum spiritus sit, non spiritualibus revera delectari." — Crell. de Deo: seu de Vera Relig. lib. i, cap. 15. p. 108. "Spiritus est Deus: animadverterunt ibi omnes prope S. literarum interpretes, Dei nomen, quod articulo est in Graeco notatum, Subjecti locum tenere: vocem, spiritus, quae articulo caret, praedicati: et spiritualem significare substautiam, Ita perinde est ac si dictum fuisset, Deus est spiritus, seu spiritualis substantia" — Idem ibid, Ira. 107.

items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Johannes Crellius, De Deo et ejus Attributis, I.15.
Translation: “‘For Christ signifies that which reason dictates, that God, since He is a spirit, is truly not delighted with non-spiritual things.’ — Crellius. ‘God is spirit: almost all interpreters of the Sacred letters have noticed there, that the name of God, which is marked with an article in Greek, takes the place of the subject; the word spirit, which lacks an article, of the predicate; and that it signifies a spiritual substance. Thus it is exactly as if it had been said, God is a spirit, or a spiritual substance.’”

items.exact_text: "Ex his autem intelligitur, membra humani corperis, quae Deo in sacris literis ascribuntur, uti et partes quaedam aliarum animantium, quales sunt alae non nisi improprie Deo tribui; siquidem a spiritus natura prorsus abhorrent. Tribuuntur autem Deo per metaphoram cum metonymia conjunctam. Nempe quis facultates vel actiones Deo conveniunt, illarum similes, quae membris illis, aut insunt, aut per ea exercentur." — Crell. de Deo, sire de Vera Relig. lib. 1:cap. 15:p. 107.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “‘From these things it is understood that the members of the human body which are ascribed to God in the sacred scriptures, just as certain parts of other living creatures, such as wings, are attributed to God only improperly; since indeed they are utterly foreign to the nature of a spirit. They are attributed to God by a metaphor joined with metonymy. For certain faculties or actions are suitable to God, similar to those which are either in those members or are exercised by them.’ — Crellius, De Deo et ejus Attributis (or De Vera Religione), bk. 1, ch. 15, p. 107.”

items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Stobaeus, Eclogae Physicae, I.1, I.3.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Stobaeus, Eclogae Physicae, I.1, I.3.
Translation: “‘God is an intellectual spirit, not having a form.’ — Posidonius in Stobaeus; Eclogae Physicae, bk. 1, ch. 1, p. 2. I confess Epicurus said, ‘The gods are in the form of humans.’ — Stobaeus, ibidem. ch. 3, p. 5. And possibly Mr B. might borrow his misshapen divinity from him and the Anthropomorphites; and then we have the pedigree of his wild positions. But the more sober philosophers (as Stobaeus there tells us) held otherwise: ‘God is neither tangible nor visible nor measurable nor extended, nor similar to any other body’; which Guil. Canterus renders thus, ‘God can neither be touched nor seen, nor does he fall under measurement or boundary, nor is he similar to any body.’”

items.exact_text: Theodoret on this place tells us, "Οὐ μὴν ώς τινες φασίν, etc. Non autem ut fuerunt quidam" (so that Mr B. is not the first that held this opinion), "ita quadam et poenitentia ductus Deus haec egit: Ταῦτα γάρ τοι ἀνθρώπινα ἡ δὲ θέια φύσις ἐλευθέρα παθῶν." And then he adds, "Τί δήποτε τοίνυν, etc. Quomodo ergo poenitentia cadat in Deum?" His answer is, "Οὐκ οῦν ἐπὶ Θεοῦ μεταμέλεια, etc. Quare paenitentia Dei nihil aliud est, quam mutatio dispensationis ejus. Paenitet me (inquit) quod Saul regem, pro eo quod est, statui illum deponere. Sic in hoc loco ( Genesis 6:6), Paenitet fecisse hominem; hoc est, decrevi perdere humanum genus." — Theod. in Genesis quaest 50, tom 1:pp. 41, 42.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Theodoret of Cyrus, Quaestiones in Genesin (PG 80).
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Theodoret of Cyrus, Quaestiones in Genesin (PG 80).
Translation: “Theodoret on this place tells us, ‘Not indeed as some say,’ [Greek and Latin], (so that Mr B. is not the first that held this opinion), ‘so God did these things led by a certain repentance. For these things indeed are human, but the divine nature is free from passions.’ And then he adds, ‘Why then... How therefore does repentance apply to God?’ His answer is, ‘Therefore there is no repentance in God... Therefore the repentance of God is nothing else than a change of his dispensation. He repents (he says) concerning Saul the king, which stands for: I have decided to depose him. So in this place (Genesis 6:6), He repents of having made man; that is, I have decreed to destroy the human race.’ — Theodoret on Genesis, Question 50, vol. 1, pp. 41, 42.”

items.exact_text: "Ut ad rationem istam non minus plene quam plane respondeamus, animadvertendum est, infallibilem istam Dei praenotionem, quam pro re concessa adversarii sumunt, a nobis non admitti." — Socin Praelec. cap. 8 p. 25. "Cure igitur nulla ratio, nullus sacrarum literarum locus sit, ex quo aperte colligi possit, Deum omnia quae fiunt, scivisse antequam fierent, concludendum est, minime asserendam esse a nobis istam Dei praescientiam: praesertim, cum et rationes non paucae, et sacra testimonia non desint, unde eam plane negandam esse apparet." — Idem, cap. 11:p. 38.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “‘That we may answer this reason no less fully than plainly, it must be observed that this infallible foreknowledge of God, which our adversaries take for granted, is not admitted by us.’ — Socinus, Praelectiones Theologicae, ch. 8, p. 25. ‘Since therefore there is no reason, no place in the sacred letters, from which it can be openly gathered that God knew all things that happen before they happened, it must be concluded that this prescience of God is by no means to be asserted by us: especially since both not a few reasons, and sacred testimonies, are not lacking, from which it appears that it is plainly to be denied.’ — Idem, ch. 11, p. 38.”

items.exact_text: "Itaque inconsiderate illi faciunt, qui futura contingentia Deum determinate scire aiunt, quia alias non esset omniscius: cum potius, ideo illa determinate futura non concipiat, quia est omniscius." — Crell. de Vera Relig. lib. 1:cap. 24 p. 201.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Johannes Crellius, De Vera Religione, Book 1, Chapter 24, p. 201.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Johannes Crellius, De Vera Religione, Book 1, Chapter 24, p. 201.
Translation: “Therefore they act inconsiderately who say that God determinately knows future contingent events, because otherwise He would not be omniscient; whereas on the contrary, He does not conceive of those events as determinately future precisely because He is omniscient.”

items.exact_text: "Nam si omnia futura, qualiacunque sunt, Deo ab omni aeternitate determinate cognita fuisse contendas; necesse est statuere omnia necessario fieri, ac futura esse Unde sequitur, nullam esse, aut fuisse unquam, humanae voluntatis libertatem, ac porro nec religionem." — Idem ibid, p. 202. Smalcius Refut. Thes. Franz. disput. 1, de Trinitat. p. 3, disput. 12, de Caus. Peccat. p. 428, 429, etc., 435.

items.exact_text: "Poenitentia infert ignorantiam praeteriti, presentis, et futuri, mutationem voluntatis, et errorem in consiliis, quorum nihil in Deum cadere potest: dicitur tamen ille metaphorice poenitentia duci, quemadmodum nos, quando alicujus rei poenitet, abolemus id quod antea feceramus: quod fieri potest sine tali mutatione voluntatis, qua nunc homo aliquid facit, quod post mutate animo, destruit" — Manasseh Ben. Israel conciliat. in Genesis 6:q. 23. "Poenitentia, cum mutabilitatem importet, non potest esse in Deo, dicitur tamen poenitere, eo quod ad modum poenitentis se habet, quando destruit quod fecerat." — Lyra ad 1 Samuel 15:85.

Modern Citation: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book 12, Chapter 7 (1072b); Maximus of Tyre, Dissertations, 1; Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book 5, Metrum 2.

items.exact_text: Τί δὲ μέλλω φρένα δῖαν Καθορᾷν ὄψιν ἄβυσσον — AEsehyl. Supp. 1071, 2. 846 Δοκέει δέ μοι ὁ καλέομεν θερμὸν ἀθάνατόν τε εῖναι καὶ νοεῖν πάντα καὶ ὁρᾷν καὶ ἀκούειν καὶ εἰδέναι τὰ ὄντα καὶ τὰ μέλλοντα ἔσεσθαι. — Hippoc. de Princip. To the same purpose is that of Epicharmus, Οὐδὲν ἐκφεύγει τὸ θεῖον αὐτὸς ἐσθ ἁμῶν ἐπόπτας, etc. And the anonymous author in Stobaeus (vid. Excerpta Stobaei, p.l17), speaking of God, adds, Ον οὐδὲ εῖς λέληθεν οὐδε ἑ͂ν ποιῶν οὐδ ἆν ποιήσων οὐδὲ πεποιηκὼς ππάλαι ὁ δὲ παρὼν ἁπανταχοῦ πάντ ἐξ ἀνάγκης οῖδε, etc. In short, the Pagans' generally received custom of consulting oracles, of using their οἰωνοσκοπία, their auguria, and auspicia, etc., by which they expected answers from their gods, and significations of their will concerning future things, are evident demonstrations that they believed their gods knew future contingents.

items.exact_text: Οὐκοῦν ὡς μὲν καὶ Ελληνες καὶ βάρβαροι τοὺς θεοὺς ἡγοῦνται πάντα εἰδέναι πάντα εἰδέναι τά τε ὄντα καὶ τὰ μέλλοντα εὐδηλον. Πᾶσαι γοῦν αἱ πόλεις καὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη διὰ μαντικῆς ἐπερωτῶσι τοὺς θεοὺς τίτε χρὴ καὶ τί οὐ χρὴ ποιεῖν. Καὶ μὴν ὅτι νομίζομέν γε δύνασθαι αὐτοὺς καὶ εῦ καὶ κακῶς ποιεῖν καὶ τοῦτο σαφές Πάντες γοῦν αἰτοῦνται τοὺς θεοὺς τὰ μὲν φαῦλα ἀποτρέπειν τἀγαθὰ δὲ διδόναι Οῦτοι τοίνυν οἱ πάντα μὲν εἰδότες κ.τ.λ. Διὰ δὲ τὸ προειδέναι καὶ ὅ τι ἐξ ἑκάστου ἀποβήσεται κ.τ.λ.. — Xenoph. ΣΥΜΠΟΕ. cap. 4:47.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Therefore it is clear that both Greeks and barbarians believe that the gods know all things, both present and future: at any rate, all cities and all nations inquire of the gods by divination what they should and should not do. And furthermore, it is also clear that they believe the gods have the power to do both good and evil: at any rate, all men beg the gods to avert evil things and to grant good things. These gods, then, who know all things, etc. And because they foreknow what will result from every action, etc.” — Xenophon, Symposium, chap. 4:47.

items.exact_text: "Cum ergo Deus omnia prout reipsa se habent cognoscat, ἐσόμενα seu certo futura cognoscit ut talia, similiter et μέλλοντα ut μέλλοντα, seu verisimiliter eventura, pro ratione causarum unde pendent." — Crell, de Vera Relig. lib. 1:cap. 24:p. 201.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Therefore, since God knows all things just as they are in themselves, He knows things that will be (εσομενα) or are certainly future as such, and similarly things that are about to be (μελλοντα) as things that are about to be, or things that are likely to happen, in proportion to the causes on which they depend.” — Crell, De Vera Religione, book 1, chap. 24, p. 201.
