items.exact_text: "Sciendum, quod omnino aliter se habet antiqua vel aeterna scientia ad ea quae fiunt et facta sunt, et aliter recens scientia: esse namque rei entis est causa scientiae nostrae, scientia vero aeterna est causa ut ipsa res sit. Si vero quando res est postquam non erat, contingeret noviter in ipsa scientia antiqua, scientia superaddita, quemadmodum contingit hoc in scientia nova, sequeretur utique quod ipsa scientia antiqua esset causata ab ipso ente: et non esset causa ipsius, oportet ergo quod non contingat ibi mutatio, scilicet in antiqua scientia, quemadmodum contingit in nova: sciendum autem, quod hic error idcirco accidit, quia scientia antiqua mensuratur ab imperitis cum scientia nova, cujus 847 mensurationis modus vitiosissimus est: projicit quippe quandoque hominem in barathrum, unde nunquam est egressurus." — Rab. Aben. Rost. Interpret. Raymund. Martin. Pugi. Fidei. P. P., cap. 25:sect. 4, 5, p. 201.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “It should be known that ancient or eternal knowledge relates in one way to things that are coming to be and have been done, and recent knowledge in another way: for the being of an existing thing is the cause of our knowledge, but eternal knowledge is the cause that the thing itself exists. But if, when a thing comes to be after it was not, a new, superadded knowledge should occur in ancient knowledge itself, just as this occurs in new knowledge, it would certainly follow that the ancient knowledge itself would be caused by the being itself: and it would not be its cause. Therefore, there must be no change there, namely in ancient knowledge, just as there is in new knowledge. But it must be known that this error happens for this reason, because ancient knowledge is measured by the unskilled alongside new knowledge, and this manner of measurement is most vicious: for it sometimes throws a man into an abyss from which he will never emerge.” — Rab. Aben. Rost. (Averroes), interpreted by Raymundus Martinus, Pugio Fidei P. P., chap. 25, sect. 4, 5, p. 201.

items.exact_text: "Dixit R. Juchanan: Omnia videntu uno intuitu. Dixit Rab, Nachman filius Isaaci: Sic etiam nos didicimus; quod scripture est Psalm 33:15, Formans simul cor eorum, intelligent omnia opera corum: quomodo inteillgendum est? Dicendmn est, dici, Deum adunare simul corda totius mundi? Ecce, videmus non ita rem se habere: sed sic dicendum est, Formans sive Creator videt simul cor eorum, et intelliget omnia opera eorum." — Talmud. Rosch. Haschana: interpret. Joseph, de Voysin.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “R. Jochanan said: All things are seen in a single glance. Rab Nachman the son of Isaac said: Thus we also have learned; because it is written in Psalm 33:15, ‘He fashions their hearts together, he understands all their works’: how is this to be understood? Are we to say that God unites together the hearts of the whole world? Behold, we see that this is not the case: but it is to be stated thus: ‘The Fashioner or Creator sees their heart at the same time, and understands all their works.’” — Talmud, Rosh Hashanah; interpreted by Joseph de Voysin.

items.exact_text: Speciem et pondus videtur habere haec objectio; nec pauci sunt, qui ejus vi adeo moventur, ut divinam futurorum contingentium praescientiam negate, et quae pro ea facere videntur loca, atque argumenta, magno conatu torquere malint, et flectere in sensus, non minus periculosos quam difficiles. Ad me quod attinet, ego hactenus sive religione quadam animi, sive divinae majestatis reverentia, non 849 potui prorsus in animum meum inducere, rationem istam allegatam tanti esse, ut propter eam Deo futurorum contingentium praescientia detrahenda sit; maxime cum vix videam, quomodo alioquin divinarum praedictionum veritas salvari possit, sine aliqua aut incertitudinis macula, aut falsi possibilis suspicione." — Sim. Episcop. Respons. ad 2 Ep. Johau. Beverovic.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “This objection seems to have some appearance and weight; nor are there few who are so moved by its force that they prefer to deny the divine foreknowledge of future contingencies, and to twist with great effort the passages and arguments that seem to support it, and bend them into meanings that are no less dangerous than difficult. As for me, up to this point, whether by a certain religious feeling of the mind or by reverence for the divine majesty, I have not been able entirely to persuade my mind that this alleged reasoning is of such great value that on its account the foreknowledge of future contingencies should be taken away from God; especially since I can hardly see how otherwise the truth of divine predictions could be saved, without some stain of uncertainty or suspicion of a possible falsehood.” — Simon Episcopius, Responsio ad II Epistolam Johannis Beverovicii.

items.exact_text: "Poterat et illud de angelis intelligi, Faciamus hominem, etc., sed quia sequitur, ad imaginem nostram, nefas est credere, ad imagines angelorum hominem esse factum, aut eandem esse imaginem angelorum et Dei. Et ideo recte intelligitur pluralitas Trinitatiis. Quae tamen Trinitas, quia unus est Deus, etiam cum dixisset, faciamus, et fecit, inquit, Deus hominem ad imaginem Dei: non veto dixit, fecerunt Dii ad Deorum." — Aug. de Civil Dei, lib. 16:cap. 6.

items.translation_text:

Translation: “That could also be understood of the angels, 'Let us make man,' etc., but because it is followed by, 'in our image,' it is wicked to believe that man was made in the images of angels, or that the image of angels and of God is the same. And therefore the plurality of the Trinity is rightly understood. Yet this Trinity, because God is one, even though he had said, 'Let us make,' it is said, 'And God made man in the image of God': he did not indeed say, 'the Gods made in the image of the Gods.'”

items.exact_text: "Illud corpus ante peccatum, et mortale secundum aliam, et immortale secundum aliam causam dici poterat; id est, mortale quia poterat mori, immortale quia poterat non mori. Aliud est enim non posse mori, sicut quasdam naturas immortales creavit Deus, aliud est autem posse non mori; secundum quem modum primus creatus est homo immortalis, quod ei praestabatur de ligno vitae, non de constitutione naturae; a quo ligno separatus est cum peccasset, ut posset mori, qui nisi peccasset posset non mori. Mortalis ergo erat conditione corporis animalls, immortalis autem beneficio conditoris. Si enim corpus animale, utique et mortale, quia et mori poterat, quamvis et immortale dico, quia et mori non poterat." — Aug, tom. 3:de Genesi ad literam, lib. 6:cap. xxiv.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram, VI.25.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram, VI.25.
Translation: “That body before the sin could be called both mortal for one reason, and immortal for another; that is, mortal because it was able to die, and immortal because it was able not to die. For it is one thing not to be able to die, just as God created certain immortal natures; but it is another thing to be able not to die, according to which manner the first man was created immortal. This was provided for him from the tree of life, not from the constitution of his nature. From this tree he was separated when he sinned, so that he might be able to die, who, had he not sinned, might have been able not to die. Therefore he was mortal by the condition of his animal body, but immortal by the benefit of his Creator. For if it was an animal body, it was certainly also mortal, because it was able to die, although I also call it immortal, because it was able not to die.”

items.exact_text: "Fit mentio destitutionis vel carentiae divinae gloriae, ergo privationis imaginis Dei et justitiae et sanctitatis, ejusque originalis; fit mentio carentiae divinae gloriae, ergo in creatione cum homine fuit communicata: o ineptias!" — Smalc. Refut. Thes. de Peccat. Orig. disput. 2, p. 42. "Porto sit Franzius, Paulum mox e vestigio imaginem Dei, seu novum hominem its explicare, quod fuerit conditus primus homo ad justitiam es sanctimoniam veram. Hic cum erroribus fallaciae, etiam et fortassis voluntariae, sunt commixtae Videat lector benevolus quanti sit facienda illatio Franzii, dum sit, ergo imago Dei in homine ante lapsum consistebat in concreata justitia et vera sanctimonia primorum parentum. Si haec non sunt scopae dissolutae, equidem nescio quid eas tandem nominabimur." — Smalc, ubi sup. pp. 50, 51.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Valentin Schmalz, Refutatio thesium Wolfgangi Franzii de peccato originali, disp. 2.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Valentin Schmalz, Refutatio thesium Wolfgangi Franzii de peccato originali, disp. 2.
Translation: “There is mention made of a destitution or lack of divine glory, therefore of a privation of the image of God and of righteousness and holiness, and that original; there is mention made of a lack of divine glory, therefore it was communicated to man in creation: O absurdities!” . . . “Furthermore, Franzius says that Paul presently on the spot explains the image of God, or the new man, in this way, that the first man was created in righteousness and true holiness. Here fallacies, even and perhaps voluntary ones, are mixed with errors. Let the benevolent reader see of how much value the inference of Franzius is to be made, when he says, therefore the image of God in man before the fall consisted in the concreated righteousness and true holiness of our first parents. If these are not a bundle of loose twigs [i.e., nonsense], I truly do not know what we shall finally call them.”

items.exact_text: "Etenim unum illud peccatum per se, non modo universes posteros, sed ne ipsum quidem Adamum, corrumpendi vim habere potuit. Dei vero consilio, in peccati illius paenam id factum fuisse, nec usquam legitur, et plane incredibile est, imo impium id cogitare." — Socin. Praelect.. cap. 4:see. 4, p. 18. "Lapsus Adami, cum unus actus fuerit, vim eam, quae depravare ipsam naturam Adami, multo minus posterorum ipsius posset, habere non potuit. Ipsi veto in paenam irrogatum fuisse, nec Scriptura doect, ut superius exposuimus, et Deum ilium, qui omnis sequitatis fons est, incredibile prorsus est id facere voluisse." — Cat. Rac. de Cognit. Christ. cap. 10:ques. 2.

items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, Praelectiones Theologicae, chap. 4, sect. 4; Racovian Catechism, De Cognitione Christi, chap. 10, q. 2.
Translation: “For indeed that one single sin by itself could not have the power of corrupting not only all his posterity, but not even Adam himself. But that this was done by the counsel of God, as a punishment for that sin, is nowhere read, and is plainly incredible, indeed impious to think it.” . . . “The fall of Adam, since it was a single act, could not have that power which could deprave the very nature of Adam, much less that of his posterity. But that it was inflicted on him as a punishment, the Scripture neither teaches, as we have explained above, and it is altogether incredible that God, who is the fountain of all equity, willed to do this.”

items.exact_text: "Concludimus igitur, nullum, improprie etiam loquendo, peccatum originale esse; id est, ex peccato illo primi parentis nullam labem aut pravitatem universo humano generi necessario ingenitam esse, sive inflictam quodammodo fuisse." — Socin. Praelect. cap. 4:sect. 4, pp. 13, 14. "Peccatum originis nullum prorsus est, quare nec liberum arbitrium vitiare potuit, Nec enim e Scriptura id peccatum originis doceri potest." — Cat. Rac. de Cognit. Christ. cap. 10:de Lib. Arbit. "Quaedam ex falsissimis prin- cipiis deducuntur. In illo genere illud potissimum est, quod ex peccato (ut vocant) originali depromitur: de quo ita disputant, ut crimen a primo parente conceptum, in sobolem derivatum esse defendant, ejusque contagione, tum omnes humanas vires corruptas et depravatas, tum potissimum voluntatis libertatem destructam esse asserant, quae omnia nos pernegamus, utpote et sanae mentis rationi, et divinae Scripturae contraria." — Volkel. de Vera Relig. lib. 5:cap. 18:pp. 547, 548. "Prior pars thesis Franzii falsa est. Nam nullum individuum unquam peccato originis fuit infectum. Quia peccatum illud mera est fabula, quam tanquam foetum alienum fovent Lutherani, et alii." — Smalc. Refut. Thes. Franz. disput. 2, p. 46, 47. Vid. Compend. Socin. cap. in.; Smalc. de Vera Divin. Jes. Christ. cap. 7: — Putas Adami peccatum et inobedientiam ejus posteritati imputari. At hoc aeque tibi negamus, quam Christi obedientiam credentibus imputari." — Jonas Schlichtingius, disput, pro Socino adversus Meisnerum, p. 251; vide etiam p. 100. "Quibus ita explicatis, facile eos qui ... onmem Adami posteritatem, in ipso Adamo parente suo peccasse, et mortis supplicium vere fuisse commeritum." — Idem, Comment. in Epist. ad Hebraeos ad cap. 7:p. 296.

items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, Praelectiones Theologicae, chap. 4, sect. 4; Racovian Catechism, De Cognitione Christi, chap. 10; Johannes Völkel, De Vera Religione, V.18; Valentin Schmalz, Refutatio thesium Wolfgangi Franzii, disp. 2; Jonas Schlichting, Disputatio pro Socino adversus Meisnerum, p. 251; Jonas Schlichting, Commentaria in Epistolam ad Hebraeos, on chap. 7.
Translation: “We conclude therefore, that even speaking improperly, there is no original sin; that is, from that sin of the first parent no stain or depravity was necessarily innate to the whole human race, or was in some way inflicted upon it.” . . . “There is absolutely no original sin, wherefore it could not vitiate free will. For neither can this original sin be taught from Scripture.” . . . “Certain things are deduced from the most false principles. In that class, that which is drawn from the (so-called) original sin is chief: concerning which they dispute in such a way as to defend that the crime conceived by the first parent was derived into his offspring, and by its contagion, they assert that not only were all human powers corrupted and depraved, but chiefly the liberty of the will was destroyed; all of which we vehemently deny, as being contrary to both the reason of a sound mind, and divine Scripture.” . . . “The prior part of Franzius's thesis is false. For no individual was ever infected with original sin. Because that sin is a mere fable, which Lutherans and others cherish as an alien fetus.” . . . “You think that Adam's sin and disobedience are imputed to his posterity. But we deny this to you just as much as we deny that Christ's obedience is imputed to believers.” . . . “With these things thus explained, it is easy [to refute] those who [think] . . . that all of Adam's posterity sinned in Adam himself, their parent, and truly deserved the punishment of death.”

items.exact_text: "Cum dixeris initio, hanc viam quae ad immortalitatem ducat esse divinitus patefactam, scire velim cur id abs to dictum sit? — Propterea, quia ut homo natura nihil habet commune cum immortalitate, ita eam ipse viam, quae nos ad immortalitatem duceret, nulla ratione per se cognoscere potuit" — Cat. Rac. de via salut, cap. 1.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
Translation: “Since you said at the beginning that this path which leads to immortality was divinely revealed, I would like to know why you spoke thus? — For the reason that before the coming of Christ this path was by no means so revealed that men could establish anything certain concerning it; for although some suspected that the souls of men do not perish after this life, and that it goes well with the good and ill with the bad, yet this was so weakly and doubtfully conceived by them that none of them could persuade others, nor could they fully satisfy themselves in it.”

items.exact_text: "Cur vero nihil commune habet homo cum immortalitate? — Idcireo, quod ab initio de humo formatus, proptereaque mortalis creatus fuerit; deinde vero, quod mandatum Dei, ipsi propositum, transgressus sit; ideoque decreto Dei ipsius in mandato expresso, aeternae morti necessario subjectus fuerit."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But why does man have nothing in common with immortality? — Therefore, because from the beginning he was formed from the ground, and on that account created mortal; but then, because he transgressed the command of God set before him; and therefore, by the decree of God Himself expressed in the command, he was necessarily subjected to eternal death.”

items.exact_text: "Qui vero id conveniet iis Scripturae locis in quibus scriptum extat, hominem ad imaginem Dei creatum esse, et creatum ad immortalitatem, et quod mors per peccatum in mundum introierit, Genesis 1:26, 27; Sap. 2:23; Romans 5:12? — Quod ad testimonium attinet, quod hominem creatum ad imaginem Dei pronunciat, sciendum est, imaginem Dei non significare immortalitatem (quod hinc patet, quod Scriptura, eo tempore quo homo aeternae morti subjectus erat, agnoscat in homine istam imaginem, Genesis 9:6, Jacob. 3:9), sed potestatem hominis, et dominium in omnes res a Deo conditas, supra terrain, designare; ut idem locus in quo de hac eadem imagine agitur, Genesis 1:26, aperte indicate"
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But how does this agree with those passages of Scripture where it is written that man was created in the image of God, and created for immortality, and that death entered the world through sin, Genesis 1:26, 27; Wisdom 2:23; Romans 5:12? — As far as the testimony is concerned which declares man created in the image of God, it must be known that the image of God does not mean immortality (which is evident from this, that Scripture recognizes that image in man at the very time when he was subjected to eternal death, Genesis 9:6, James 3:9), but designates the power of man, and his dominion over all things created by God upon the earth; as the same passage where this same image is discussed, Genesis 1:26, clearly indicates.”

items.exact_text: "Quae igitur est horum verborum sententia, quod mors per peccatum introierit in mundum? — Haec, quod Adamus ob peccatum, decreto et sententia Dei, aeternae morti subjectus est; proinde, omnes homines, eo quod ex eo nati sunt, eidem aeternae morti subjaceant. Rem ita esse, collatio Christi cum Adamo, quam apostolus eodem capite, a ver. 12 ad finem, instituit, indicio est." 854
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What then is the meaning of these words, that death entered the world through sin? — This, that Adam on account of sin, by the decree and sentence of God, was subjected to eternal death; accordingly, all men, because they are born from him, are subject to the same eternal death. items.exact_text: "Nonne peccato originis hoc liberum arbitrium vitiatum est? — Peccatum originis nullum prorsus est: quare nec liberum arbitrium vitiare potuit, nec enim e Scriptura id peccatum originis doceri potest; et lapsus Adae cum unus actus fuerit, vim eam quae depravare ipsam naturam Adami, multo minus vero posterorum ipsius posset, habere non potuit. Ipsi vero in poenam irrogatum fuisse, nec Scriptura docet, uti superius exposuimus; et Deum ilium, qui omnis aequitatis fons est, incredibile prorsus est, id facere voluisse." — Cap 10:de lib. arbit, q. 2.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Was not this free will corrupted by original sin? — There is no original sin at all: therefore it could not corrupt free will, for neither can that original sin be taught from Scripture; and the fall of Adam, since it was a single act, could not have had that power which could deprave the very nature of Adam, much less indeed that of his descendants. But that it was inflicted upon him as a punishment, Scripture does not teach, as we have explained above; and it is absolutely incredible that God, who is the fountain of all equity, wished to do this.” — Chapter 10, On Free Will, question 2.

items.exact_text: "Veruntamen esse peccatum originis illa testimonia docere videntur, Genesis 6:5, etc., 8:21. — Haec testimonia agunt de peccato voluntario; ex iis itaque effici nequit peccatum originis. Quod autem ad primum attinet, Moses id peccatum ejusmodi fuisse docet cujus causa poenituisse Deum quod hominem creasset, et eum diluvio punire decrevisset; quod certe de peccato quod homini natura inesset, quale peccatum originis censeat, affirmari nullo pacto potest. In altero vero testimonio docet, peccatum homi-nis eam vim habiturum non esse, ut Deus mundum diluvio propter illud puniret; quod etiam peccato originis nullo modo convenit."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Yet those testimonies seem to teach that there is an original sin, Genesis 6:5, etc., 8:21. — These testimonies deal with voluntary sin; therefore, original sin cannot be derived from them. As to the first, Moses teaches that the sin was of such a kind that on its account God repented that He had created man, and decreed to punish him with the flood; which certainly can by no means be affirmed of a sin which was inherent in man by nature, such as one considers original sin to be. In the other testimony, however, he teaches that the sin of man would not have such force that God would punish the world with a flood because of it; which also in no way suits original sin.”

items.exact_text: "Quid vero ea de re sentis quod David ait, Psalm 51:7? — Animadvertendum est, hic Davidem non agere de quibusvis hominibus, sed de se tantum, nec simpliciter, sed habita ratione lapsus sui; et eo loquendi modo usum esse, cujus exemplum apud eundem Davidem habes Psalm 58:3. Quamobrem neo eo testimonia effici prorsus potest peccatum originis."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what do you think about the matter which David states, Psalm 51:7? — It must be noticed that here David is not dealing with just any men, but with himself alone, nor absolutely, but with regard to his own fall; and that he used a manner of speaking, an example of which you have in the same David, Psalm 58:3. Therefore, original sin can absolutely not be established by that testimony.”

items.exact_text: "At Paulus ait Romans 5:12, In Adamo, etc. — Non habetur eo loco, In Adamo omnes peccasse; verum in Graeco verba sunt ἐφ ῷ, quae passim interpretes reddunt Latine, quo, quae tamen reddi possunt per particulas quoniam aut quatenus, ut e locis similibus, Romans 8:8, Philippians 3:12, Hebrews 2:18, 2 Corinthians 5:4, videre est. Apparet igitur neque ex hoc loco extrui posse peccatum originis."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But Paul says in Romans 5:12, In Adam, etc. — It is not held in that passage, that all sinned in Adam; but in Greek the words are eph' hō (εφ' ῶ), which everywhere interpreters render in Latin by quo, which nevertheless can be rendered by the particles 'since' or 'insofar as', as is to be seen from similar passages, Romans 8:8, Philippians 3:12, Hebrews 2:18, 2 Corinthians 5:4. It appears therefore that original sin cannot be built up from this passage either.”

items.exact_text: "Ergo Dominus Jesus est purus homo? — Ans. Nullo pacto; etenim est conceptus a Spiritu Sancto, natus ex Maria Virgine, eoque ab ipsa conceptione et ortu Filius Dei est, ut de ea re Luc. 1:35 legimus." — Cat. Rac. de persona Christi, cap. i.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Therefore is the Lord Jesus a mere man? — Ans. By no means; for He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, and therefore from His very conception and birth He is the Son of God, as we read concerning this matter in Luke 1:35.” — Racovian Catechism, On the Person of Christ, chapter 1.

Porto hunc Deum, et Filium Dei unigenitum esse docent tum ratione conceptionis a Spiritu Sancto," etc.. — Compendiolum Doctrinae Eccl. Christianae, etc., cap. i.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “They teach that Jesus Christ is that man conceived by the Holy Spirit, and born of the blessed Virgin; apart from or before whom they acknowledge no one to be (or) to have been actually existing as the only-begotten Son of God. items.exact_text: "Conceptus enim est de Spiritu Sancto, et natus ex Virgine Maria; ob id genus conceptionis, et nativitatis modum, Filius etiam Dei ab ipso angelo vocatus fuit, et ita naturalis Dei Filius (quia scilicet falls natus fuit) dici vere potest. Solus Jesus Christus a Deo Patre suo absque opera viri in lumen productus est." — Smalc. de Vera Divin. Jes. Christ. cap. 3.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “For He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and born of the Virgin Mary; on account of that kind of conception, and the manner of His birth, He was also called the Son of God by the angel himself, and so can truly be called the natural Son of God (because evidently He was born such). Jesus Christ alone was brought into the light by God His Father without the agency of a man.” — Smalcius, De Vera Divinitate Jesu Christi, chapter 3.

items.exact_text: "Dico igitur, Christum merito dici posse Filium Dei naturalem, quia natus est Dei Filius, tametsi ex ipsa Dei substantia non fuerit generatus. Natum autem illum sub alia ratione, quam per generationem ex ipsius Dei substantia, probant angeli verba, Mariae matri ejus dicta, Luc. 1:85. Quia igitur homo ille Jesus Nazarenus, qui dictus est Christus, non viri alicujus opera, sed Spiritus Sancti operatione generatus est in matris utero, propterea Filius Dei est vocatus." — Faust. Socin. Responsio ad Weik. cap. 4:p. 202.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I say therefore, that Christ can rightly be called the natural Son of God, because He was born the Son of God, even though He was not generated from the very substance of God. But that He was born under another condition than by generation from the very substance of God, the words of the angel, spoken to Mary His mother, prove, Luke 1:35. Because therefore that man Jesus of Nazareth, who is called the Christ, was generated in His mother's womb not by the agency of any man, but by the operation of the Holy Spirit, for that reason He is called the Son of God.” — Faustus Socinus, Responsio ad Weiekum, chapter 4, p. 202.

items.exact_text: "Sunt quidem plurima dicta quaae ostendunt Christum peculiari prorsus nec ulli alio communi ratione esse Dei Filium; non tamen hinc concludere licet eum ease naturali ratione filium, cum praeter hanc, et illam communem, alia dari possit, et in Christo reipsa locum habeat, Nonne singulari prorsus ratione, nec ulli com-muni, Dei Filius est 856 Christus, si ab ipso Deo, vi et efficacia Spiritus Sancti, in utero virginis conceptus fuit et genitus?" — Schlichting. ad Meisner. artic., de Trinit. p. 160.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “There are indeed many sayings which show that Christ is the Son of God by a reason entirely peculiar and common to no one else; yet one may not conclude from this that He is a son by natural reason, since besides this, and that common one, another can be given, and actually has place in Christ. Is not Christ the Son of God by a reason entirely singular, and common to no one, if He was conceived and generated by God Himself, by the power and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, in the womb of a virgin?” — Schlichting, Adversus Meisnerum, article on the Trinity, p. 160.

items.exact_text: "Nec enim omni tempore quo Christus Filius Dei fuit, Deus etiam fuit. Filium enim Dei esse, ad nativitatem etiam referri, et ob ortum ipsum aliquem Dei Filium appelari posse nemo non intelligit. At Deum (praeter unum illum Deum) nemo esse potest, nisi propter similtudinem cum Deo. Itaque tunc cum Christus Deo similis factus esset per divinas quae in ipso erant qualitates, summo jure eatenus Dei Filius, qua Deus, et vicissim eatenus Deus, qua Dei Filius. At ante obtentam illam cum Deo similitudinem Deus proprie dici non potuit." — Smalc. Respon. ad Smiglec. cap. 17 p. 154.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “For Christ was not also God at all times when He was the Son of God. For everyone understands that being the Son of God is also referred to birth, and that someone can be called the Son of God on account of his very origin. But no one can be God (except that one God), except on account of a likeness to God. Therefore then when Christ had been made like to God through the divine qualities which were in Him, with supreme right He was insofar the Son of God, as He was God, and conversely insofar God, as He was the Son of God. But before obtaining that likeness to God, He could not properly be called God.” — Smalcius, Responsio ad Smiglecium, chapter 17, p. 154.

items.exact_text: "Si quae sit vocabuli 'adoptivus' significatio ex mente sacrarum literarum consideretur, nos non inficiari Christum suo modo esse adoptivum Dei Filium; quia enim adoptivi filii ea est conditio et proprietas, ut talis non sit natus qualis factus est post adoptionem. Certe quia Christus talis natura, vel in ipsa conceptione et nativitate non fuit, qualis postea fuit aetate accedente, sine injuria adoptivus Dei Filius eo modo dici potest." — Smalc, ad Smiglec. cap. 20 p. 175.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “If what the meaning of the word 'adoptive' is according to the mind of sacred letters be considered, we do not deny that Christ in His own way is the adoptive Son of God; for because the condition and property of an adoptive son is this, that he was not born such as he was made after adoption. Certainly because Christ by nature, or in His very conception and birth, was not such as He later was as age advanced, without injury He can be called the adoptive Son of God in that way.” — Smalcius, Responsio ad Smiglecium, chapter 20, p. 175.

items.exact_text: "Primus modus est quis quatenus homo ex Spiritu Dei Sancto conceptus est, et ex virgine natus est. Nec dubium mihi est, quin ob hunc modum, Deus etiam κατ ἐξοχὴν vocetur Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Secundus modus est, quia Jesus Christus ratione muneris illius, quod a Patre speciali mandato impositum ei fuit, ut rex Israelis esset, promissus ille per prophetas, et praevisus ante secula Filius Dei vocatur. Tertius modus est, quia a Patre ex mortuis in vitam immortalem suscitatus, et veluti ex utero terrae, nulla mediante matre, denuo genitus est. Quartus modus est, quia Jesus Christus ex morte suscitatus, haeres ex asse constitutus est in domo Patris sui, ac proinde bonorum onmium coelestium, et Patris sui ministrorum omnium sive angelorum dominus." — Episcop. Instit. Theolog. lib. 4 cap. 33, sect 2, p. 195. 857
items.modern_reference: Translation: “The first manner is insofar as he, as a man, was conceived by the Holy Spirit of God and born of a virgin. And I have no doubt that on account of this manner, God is also called par excellence [κατ ἑξοχὴν] the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. The second manner is because Jesus Christ, by reason of that office which was imposed on him by the Father through a special mandate, that he might be king of Israel, the one promised by the prophets, and foreseen before the ages, is called the Son of God. The third manner is because he was raised by the Father from the dead to immortal life, and, as if from the womb of the earth with no mother intervening, he was begotten anew. The fourth manner is because Jesus Christ, raised from death, was constituted sole heir in the house of his Father, and accordingly the Lord of all heavenly goods and of all the ministers of his Father, or angels.”

items.exact_text: "Notemus igitur Christum Judaeos tanquam in verborum suorum intelligentia hallucinatos minime reprehendentem se naturalem Dei Filium clare professum ease. Deinde, quod isto modo colligunt Christum se Deo aequalem facere recte fecerunt; nec ideo a Christo refelluntur, aut vituperantur ab evangelista, qui in re tanta nos errare non fuerit passus." — Cartwrightus Har. Evan. in loc.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Let us note, therefore, that Christ by no means rebuked the Jews as if they were hallucinating in the understanding of his words, but clearly professed himself to be the natural Son of God. Next, that in gathering in this manner that Christ makes himself equal to God, they did rightly; nor are they refuted by Christ on that account, or reproached by the evangelist, who would not have suffered us to err in so great a matter.”

items.modern_reference: Translation: “He connects what he had said with the preceding words; If they cannot be snatched from the power of the Father, neither can they be snatched from mine: for my power emanates from the Father, and indeed in such a way that it avails just as much to be guarded by me, or by the Father. See Genesis 41:25, 27.”

items.exact_text: "Jesus Filius Dei multis modis dicitur; maxime populariter, ideo quod in regnum a Deo evectus est; quo sensu verba Psalmi secundi, de Davide dicta, cum ad regnum pervenit, Christo aptantur, Act. 13:33, et ad Hebraeos 1:5, et 5:5 Haec autem Filii sive regia dignitas Jesu praedestinabatur et praefigurabatur tum cum mortalem agens vitam magma ilia signa et prodigia ederet, quae δυνάμεων voce denotantur, saepe et singulariter δυνάμεως, ut Marci 6:5, 9:39; Luc. 4:36, 5:17, 6:19, 8:46, 9:1; Act. 3:12, 4:33, 6:8, 10:88. Haec signa edebat Jesus, per Spiritum illum sanctitas, id est, vim divinam, per quam ab initio conceptionis sanctificatus fuerat, Luc. 1:85; Marci 2:8; Joh. 9:36. Ostenditur ergo Jesus nobilis ex materna parte, utpete ex Rege terreno ortus; sed nobilior ex Paterna parte, quippe a Deo factus rex coelestis post resurrectionem, Hebrews 5:9; Act. 2:30, Acts 26:23." — Grot. Annot. in Romans 1:3, 4.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Jesus is called the Son of God in many ways; most popularly, for the reason that he was raised to the kingdom by God; in which sense the words of the second Psalm, spoken concerning David when he came to the kingdom, are applied to Christ in Acts 13:33, and in Hebrews 1:5 and 5:5. Now this dignity of the Son, or royal dignity of Jesus, was predestined and prefigured then when, living a mortal life, he produced those great signs and prodigies, which are denoted by the word dynameōn [powers], often and singularly dynameōs [power], as in Mark 6:5, 9:39; Luke 4:36, 5:17, 6:19, 8:46, 9:1; Acts 3:12, 4:33, 6:8, 10:38. Jesus produced these signs by that Spirit of holiness, that is, the divine power, by which from the beginning of his conception he had been sanctified, Luke 1:35; Mark 2:8; John 9:36. Therefore, Jesus is shown to be noble from his maternal side, inasmuch as he sprang from an earthly king; but more noble from his Paternal side, because he was made a heavenly king by God after the resurrection, Hebrews 5:9; Acts 2:30, 26:23.”

Now this dignity of the Son, or royal dignity of Jesus, was predestined and prefigured then when, living a mortal life, he produced those great signs and prodigies, which are denoted by the word dynameōn [powers], often and singularly dynameōs [power], as in Mark 6:5, 9:39; Luke 4:36, 5:17, 6:19, 8:46, 9:1; Acts 3:12, 4:33, 6:8, 10:38. items.exact_text: So that πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως is, ὁ τεχθεὶς πρὸ πάσης κτίσεως, qui genitus est prior onmi creatura, vel ante omnem creaturam, for so πρῶτος sometimes signifies comparatively. Arist. Avibus. 484, πρῶτον Δαρείου, id est, πρότερον, Johan. 1:15; πρῶτός μου ῆν, that is, πρότερος and 1 Johan. 4:19, πρῶτος ἠγάπησεν, that is, πρότερος. His generation was before the creation, indeed eternal. Tertullian saith so too, Lib. de Trinitate: "Quomodo primogenitus esse potuit, nisi quia secundum divinitatem ante omnem creaturam ex Deo Patre Sermo processit."
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Novatian, De Trinitate (PL 3), 16.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Novatian, De Trinitate (PL 3), 16.
Translation: “So that firstborn of all creation [πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως] is, the one begotten before all creation [ὁ τεχθεὶς πρὸ πάσης κτίσεως], who was begotten prior to every creature, or before every creature [qui genitus est prior onmi creatura, vel ante omnem creaturam], for so first [πρῶτος] sometimes signifies comparatively. Aristophanes The Birds 484, before Darius [πρῶτον Δαρείου], that is, before [πρότερον], John 1:15; he was before me [πρῶτός μου ἦν], that is, prior/before [πρότερος] and 1 John 4:19, first loved [πρῶτος ἠγάπησεν], that is, prior/before [πρότερος]. His generation was before the creation, indeed eternal. Tertullian saith so too, On the Trinity: ‘How could he be the firstborn, except because according to his divinity the Word proceeded from God the Father before every creature?’”

items.exact_text: "Ideo autem nusquam Scriptum est, quod Deus Pater major sit Spiritu Sancto, vel Spiritus Sanctus minor Deo Patre; quia non sic assumpta est creatura in qua appareret S. S. sicut assumptus est filius hominis, in qua forma ipsius Verbi Dei persona prae-entaretur." — August. lib. 1:de Trinit. cap. vi.

items.exact_text: "Hic primum ea vox in narratione Evangelica reperitur ab Apostolis Jesu tribute, postquam scilicet sua resurrectione probaverat, se esse a quo vita et quidem aeterna exspectari deberet, Vide supra, 11:25. Mansit deinde ille mos in ecclesia, ut apparet non tantum in scriptis Apostolicis ut, Romans 9:5, et veterum Christianorum, ut videre est apud Justinum Martyrem contra Tryphonem, sed et in Plinii ad Trajanum Epistola, ubi ait Christianos Christo, ut Deo, carmina cecinisse." — Grot, in loc.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Here first that word is found in the Evangelical narrative attributed to Jesus by the Apostles, evidently after he had proven by his resurrection that he is the one from whom life, and indeed eternal life, ought to be expected. See above, 11:25. That custom then remained in the church, as is apparent not only in the Apostolic writings such as Romans 9:5, and of the ancient Christians, as is to be seen in Justin Martyr against Trypho, but also in the Epistle of Pliny to Trajan, where he says that the Christians sang hymns to Christ as to God.”

items.exact_text: "Rogatum to velim, ut mihi ca de Jesu Christo exponas, quae me scire opertest? — Sciendum tibi est, quaedam sd essentiam Jesu Christi, quaedam ad illius munus referri, quae to scire oportet. "Quaenam ea sunt quae ad personam ipsius referuntur? — Id solum, quod natura sit homo verus, quemadmodum ea de re crebro Scripturae 859 sacrae testautur, inter alias, 1 Timothy 2:5, et 1 Corinthians 15:21; qualem olim Deus per prophetas promiserat, et qualem etiam esse testatur fidei symbolum, quod vulgo Apostolicum vocant, quod nobiscum universi Christiani amplectuntur."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I would like to ask you to explain to me those things concerning Jesus Christ which I ought to know? — You should know that some things refer to the essence of Jesus Christ, and some to his office, which you must know. What are those which refer to his person? — This alone: that by nature he is a true man, as the sacred Scriptures frequently testify concerning this matter, among others, 1 Timothy 2:5, and 1 Corinthians 15:21; such a one as God had formerly promised through the prophets, and such as the symbol of faith, which they commonly call the Apostles' Creed, and which all Christians universally embrace with us, also testifies him to be.”

items.exact_text: "Ergo Dominus Jesus est purus homo? — Nullo pacto; etenim est conceptus e Spiritu Sancto, natus ex Maria Virgine, eoque ab ipsa conceptione et ortu Filius Dei est, ut ea de re Luc. 1:35 legimus, ubi angelus Mariam ira alloquitur, Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in to, etc., ut alias causas non afferam, quas postmodum in Jesu Christi persona deprehendes, quae evidentisaime ostendunt Dominum Jesum pro pure heroine nullo modo accipi posse."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Therefore the Lord Jesus is a mere man? — By no means; for he was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, and for that reason from his very conception and birth he is the Son of God, as we read concerning this in Luke 1:35, where the angel addresses Mary thus: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, etc., not to adduce other reasons, which you will presently apprehend in the person of Jesus Christ, which most evidently show that the Lord Jesus can in no way be taken for a mere man.”

items.exact_text: "Dixeras paulo superius Dominum Jesum natura esse hominem; an idem habet naturam divinam? — Nequaquam; nam id non solum rationi sanae, verum etiam divinis literis repugnat."
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
Translation: “You said a little above that the Lord Jesus is by nature a man; does he also have a divine nature? — By no means; for that is repugnant not only to sound reason, but also to the holy Scriptures.”

Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.

items.exact_text: "Cedo qui rationi sanae repugnat? — Primo, ad eum modum, quod duae substantiae, proprietatibus adversae, coire in unam personam nequeant; ut sunt mortalem et immortalem esse, principium habere et principio carere, mutabilem et immutabilem existere. Deinde, quod dues natures, personam singulae constituentes, in unam personam convenire itidem nequeant; nam loco unius duas personas esse operteret, atque ita duos Christos existere, quem unum esse, et unam ipsius personam omnes citra omnem controversiam agnoscunt."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Tell me how it is repugnant to sound reason? — First, in this way: that two substances, opposite in their properties, cannot come together into one person; such as being mortal and immortal, having a beginning and lacking a beginning, existing mutable and immutable. Next, that two natures, each constituting a person, cannot likewise convene into one person; for in place of one there would have to be two persons, and thus two Christs would exist, whom all acknowledge without any controversy to be one, and his person to be one.”

items.exact_text: "Cum vero illi ostendunt, Christum sic ex natura divina et humana constare, quemadmodum homo ex animo et corpore constet, quid illis respondendum? — Permagnum hic esse discrimen; illi enim aiunt, duas naturas in Christo ita unitas esse, ut Christus sit Deus et homo. Anima vero et corpus ad eum modum in homine conjuneta sunt, ut nec anima nec corpus ipse homo sit, nec enim anima nec corpus sigillatim personam constituunt. At ut natura divina per se constituit personam, ita humana constituat per se necesse est."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But when they show that Christ so consists of a divine and human nature, just as a man consists of soul and body, what is to be answered to them? — That there is a very great difference here; for they say that the two natures are so united in Christ that Christ is God and man. But the soul and body are joined in man in such a way that neither the soul nor the body is the man himself, nor indeed do the soul or the body separately constitute a person. But as the divine nature by itself constitutes a person, so it is necessary that the human should constitute one by itself.”

items.exact_text: "Doce etiam, qui id repugnet Scripturae Christum habere divinam naturam. — Primum, ea ratione, quod Scriptura nobis unum tantum natura Deum proponat, quem superius demonstravimus esse Christi Patrem. Secundo, eadem Scriptura testatur, Jesum Christum natura esse hominem, ut superius ostensum est; quo ipso illi naturam adimit divinam. Tertio, quod quicquid divinum Christus habeat, Scriptura eum 860 Patris dono habere aperte doceat, Matthew 28:18; Philippians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 15:27; John 5:19, 10:25. Denique cum eadem Scriptura apertissime ostendat, Jesum Christum omnia sua facta divina non sibi, nec alicui naturae divinae suae, sed Patri suo vindicare solitum fuisse, planum facit, eam divinam in Christo naturam prorsus otiosam, ac sine omni causa futuram fuisse."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Teach me also how it is repugnant to Scripture that Christ has a divine nature. — First, by this reason, that Scripture proposes to us only one God by nature, whom we demonstrated above to be the Father of Christ. Secondly, the same Scripture testifies that Jesus Christ is by nature a man, as was shown above; by which very thing it takes away from him a divine nature. Thirdly, that whatever divine thing Christ has, Scripture openly teaches that he has it by the gift of the Father, Matthew 28:18; Philippians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 15:27; John 5:19, 10:25. Lastly, since the same Scripture most openly shows that Jesus Christ was accustomed to claim all his divine deeds not for himself, nor for any divine nature of his own, but for his Father, it makes it plain that that divine nature in Christ would have been utterly idle, and without any cause.”

items.exact_text: "Atqui illi e Scripturis illam divinam in Christo naturam asserere conantur? — Co. nantur quidem variis modis; idque dum student aut e scripturis quibusdam evincere quae in iis non habentur, aut dum ex iis quae in scripturis habentur perperam ratio-cinantur, ac male rem suam conficiunt."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But do they try to assert that divine nature in Christ from the Scriptures? — They indeed try in various ways; and this while they study either to prove from certain scriptures things which are not contained in them, or while they incorrectly reason from those things which are contained in the scriptures, and badly accomplish their purpose.”

items.exact_text: "Quae vero sunt ilia quae illi de Christo e Scripturis evincere laborant quae illic non habentur? — Est illius, ut loquuntur, praeaeternitas, quam duplici scripturarum genere approbare nituntur. Primum ejusmodi est, in quo prae-aeternitatem hanc expressam putant. Secundum, in quo licet expressa non sit, earn tamen colligi arbitrantur."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What then are those things which they labor to prove concerning Christ from the Scriptures, which are not contained there? — It is his pre-eternity, as they speak, which they strive to approve by a twofold kind of scriptures. The first is of such a kind in which they think this pre-eternity is expressed. The second, in which although it is not expressed, they nevertheless think it can be inferred.”

items.exact_text: "Quaenam sunt testimonia Scripturae quae videntur ipsis eam prae- aeternitatem ex-primere? — Sunt ea in quibus Scriptura testatur de Christo, ipsum fuisse in principio, fuisse in coelo, fuisse ante Abrahamum, Joh. 1:1, 6:62, 8:58."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What are the testimonies of Scripture which seem to them to express this pre-eternity? — They are those in which Scripture testifies concerning Christ, that he was in the beginning, that he was in heaven, that he was before Abraham, John 1:1, 6:62, 8:58.”

items.exact_text: "Quid vero ad primum respendes? — In loco citato nihil habetur de ista praeaeter-nitate, cum hic principii mentio fiat, quod prae- aeternitati oppenitur. Principii vero vox in Scripturis fere semper ad subjectam refertur materiam, ut videre est, Daniel 8:1; Joh. 15:27, Joh. 16:4; Act. 11:15: cum igitur hic subjecta sit materia evangelium, cujus descriptionem suscepit Johannes, sine dubio per vocem hanc principii, principium evangelii Johannes intellexit."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What then do you answer to the first? — In the place cited there is nothing contained about that pre-eternity, since here mention is made of a beginning, which is opposed to pre-eternity. But the word 'beginning' in the Scriptures is almost always referred to the subject matter, as is to be seen in Daniel 8:1; John 15:27, 16:4; Acts 11:15: since therefore the subject matter here is the gospel, the description of which John undertook, without doubt by this word 'beginning', John understood the beginning of the gospel.”

items.exact_text: "Novum Testamentum divinitus oblatum aperio. Aliud agenti exhibet se mihi aspectu primo augustissimum illud caput Johannis evangelistae et apostoli, In principio erat Verbum. Lego partem capitis, et ita commoveor legens, ut repente divinitatem argumenti, et scripti majestatem, auctoritatemque senserim, longo intervallo omnibus eloquentiae humanae viribus praeeuntem. Horrebat corpus, stupebat animus, et totum illum diem sic afiiciebar, ut qui essem, ipsi mihi incertus viderer esse." — Francisc. Junius.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Francis Junius the Elder, Vita ipsius (Leiden, 1595) [Junius's personal autobiography].
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Francis Junius the Elder, Vita ipsius (Leiden, 1595) [Junius's personal autobiography].
Translation: “I open the New Testament offered to me divinely. While I was doing something else, there presents itself to me at first sight that most august chapter of John the evangelist and apostle, 'In the beginning was the Word.' I read part of the chapter, and I am so moved as I read, that suddenly I felt the divinity of the subject, and the majesty and authority of the writing, leaving all the forces of human eloquence far behind. My body shuddered, my mind was astounded, and I was so affected all that day that I seemed uncertain to myself who I was.”

items.exact_text: "Expone igitur mihi quibus testimoniis approbare contendunt Christum coelum et terrain creasse? — his ubi scriptum extat, quod per eum omnia facta sint, et sine eo factum sit nihil quod factum sit, John 1:3; et iterum, Mundus per ipsum factus est, ver. 10, et rursus, quod in eo omnia sunt condita, etc., Colossians 1:16, et quod Deus per eum sacecula fecerit, Hebrews 1:2, denique, et ex co, Tu in principio, etc., ver. 10-12. "Qui vero ad primum testimonium respondes? — Primum, non habetur in primo testi-monio creata sunt, verum facta sunt. Deinde, ait Johannes, facta esse per eum, qui modus loquendi, non eum qui prima causa sit alicujus rei, velum causam secundam aut mediam exprimit. Denique, vox omnia non pro omnibus prorsus rebus hic sumitur, sed ad subjectam materiam restringitur omnino, quod frequentissimum est in libris divinis, praesertim Novi Testamenti, cujus rei exemplum singulare extat, 2 Corinthians 5:17, in quo habetur sermo de re, huic, de qua Johannes tractat, admodum simili, ubi dicitur, omnia nova facta esse, cum certum sit multa extare, quae nova facta non sunt. Cum veto subjecta apud Johannem materia sit evangelium, apparet vocem omnia de iis omnibus quae quoquo modo ad evangelium pertinent accipi debere. "Cur vero addidit Johannes, quod sine eo factum est nihil quod factum est? — Addidit haec Johannes, ut eo melius illustraret illa superiora, Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, quae eam vim habere videntur, per solum Verbum vel Filium Dei omnia illa facta esse, licet ejus generis qaedem, et quidem magni momenti, non per ipsum, verum per apostolos facta fuerint, — ut est vocatio Gentium, et legalium ceremoniarum abolitio: licet enim haec originem ab ipsis sermonibus et operibus Domini Jesu traxerint, ad effectum tamen non sunt perducta per ipsum Christum, 862 sed per ipsius apostolos, non tamen sine ipso; apostoli enim omnia nomine et authoritate ipsius administrarunt, ut etiam ipse Dominus ait, Sine me nihil facere potestis, John 15:5."

items.exact_text: "Quid vero respondes ad secundum? — Primum, quod hic non scribat Johannes mundum esse creatum, sed factum. Deinde, eo loquendi mode utitur, qui mediam causam designat, ait enim, mundum per eum factum. Denique, haec vox mundus, quemadmodum et aliae quae prorsus idem in Scripturis valent, non solum coelum et terram denotat, verum praeter alias significationes, vel genus humanum designat, un locus praesens ostendit, ubi ait, In mundo erat, et mundus eum non agnovit, John 1:10, et Mundus eum secutus est, John 12:19, aut etiam futuram immortalitatem, ut apparet, Hebrews 1:6, ubi ait, Et eum iterum introducit primogenitum in mundum, ait, Et adorent cum omnes angeli Dei, quod de futuro mundo accipi apparet e cap. 2:ejusdem epistolae, ubi ait, Etenim non angelis subjecit mundum futurum, de quo loquimur, at nusquam de eo locutus fuerat, nisi ver. 6, cap. 1:Praeterea, habes locum, cap. 10:ver. 5, ubi de Christo loquens, ait, Propterea ingrediens in mundum, ait, Hostiam et oblationem noluisti, verum corpus adaptasti mihi; ubi cum palam sit eum loqui de mundo in quem ingressus Jesus, sacerdos noster factus est (ut circumstantiae omnes demonstrant) apparet, non de prae-senti, sed de futuro mundo agi, quandoquidem, cap. 8:vet. 4, de Christo dixerat, Si in terris esset, ne sacerdos quidem esset."

items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
Translation: “But what do you answer to the second? — First, that John does not write here that the world was 'created,' but 'made'; for the word which is here read as 'made' does not designate anything other than what is read by John elsewhere where 'made/became' is used: as, for example, in the same chapter, verse 6, and Luke 24:19, 'There was a man sent from God,' etc., and 'Who was a prophet,' etc.”

items.exact_text: "Quid vero per haec, Mundus per cum factus est, intelligis? Duplex eorum sensus dari potest: Prior, quod genus humanum per Christum reformatum, et quasi denuo factum sit, eo quod ille generi humano, quod perierat, et aeternae morti subjectum erat, vitam attulit, eamque sempiternam (quod etiam mundo Johannes exprobrat, qui per Christum ab interitu vindicatus, eum non agnoverit, sed spreverit et rejecerit); is enim mos Hebraici sermonis, quod in ejusmodi loquendi modis, verba facere, creare, idem valeant, quod denuo facere, et denuo creare, idque propterea, quod verbis quae composita vocant ea lingua careat. Posterior vero sensus est, quod illa immortalitas quam expectamus per Christum, quantum ad nos, facta sit; quemadmodum eadem futurum saeculum, habita ratione nostri, vocatur, licet jam Christo et angelis sit praesens." 863

Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
Translation: “But what do you understand by this: 'The world was made through him'? A twofold sense of these words can be given: First, that the entire assembly of men, which is designated by the name 'world,' was raised by him into a more perfect state; second, that through him He made that part of those things which pertain to this world, which pertains to the preaching of the gospel.”

items.exact_text: "E quibus vero testimoniis Scripturae demonstrate conantur Christum (ut loquuntur) incarnatum esse? — Ex iis ubi secundum eorum versionem legitur Verbum caro factum ease, Job. 1:14; Philippians 2:6, 7; 1 Timothy 3:16, etc. "Quomodo ad primum respondes? — Ea ratione, quod in eo testimonio non habeatur Deum (ut loquuntur) incarnatum ease, aut quod natura divina assumpserit humanam. Aliud enim est, Verbum caro factum est, aliud, Deus incarnatus est (ut loquuntur) vel natura divina assumpsit humanam. Praeterea, haec verba, Verbum caro factum est, vel potius, Sermo caro factus est, possunt et debent ita reddi, Sermo caro fuit. Posse its reddi, e testimoniis in quibus vox ἐγένετο (quae hic per factum est translata est) verbo fuit reddita invenitur, apparet; ut in eodem cap., ver. 6, et Luc. 24:19: Fuit homo missus a Deo, etc.; et, Qui fuit vir propheta, etc. Debere vero reddi per verbum fuit, ordo verborum Johannis docet, qui valde inconvenienter loquutas fuisset, Sermonem carnem factum esse, — id est, ut adversarii interpretantur, naturam divinam assumpsisse humanam, — postquam ea jam de illo Sermone exposuisset, quae nativitatem hominis Jesu Christi subsecuta sunt: ut sunt haec, Johannem Baptistam de illo testatum esse; illum in mundo fuisse; a suis non fuisse receptum; quod iis, a quibus receptus fuisset, potestatem dederit, ut filii Dei fierent.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
Translation: “From which testimonies of Scripture indeed do they endeavor to demonstrate that Christ was (as they speak) incarnate? — From those where according to their version it is read: 'The Word was made flesh,' John 1:14; Philippians 2:6, 7; 1 Timothy 3:16, etc. 'How do you answer to the first?' — For the reason that in that testimony it is not held that God (as they speak) was incarnate, or that the divine nature assumed the human. For it is one thing that 'the Word was made flesh,' and another that 'God was incarnate' (as they speak) or 'the divine nature assumed the human.' Furthermore, these words, 'the Word was made flesh,' or rather, 'the Speech was made flesh,' can and ought to be thus rendered: 'the Speech was flesh.' That it can be so rendered is apparent from testimonies in which the word egeneto (which is here translated as 'was made') is found rendered by the verb 'was'; as in the same chapter, verse 6, and Luke 24:19: 'There was a man sent from God,' etc.; and 'Who was a prophet,' etc. That it ought to be rendered by the verb 'was,' the order of John's words teaches, who would have spoken very inconveniently in saying that the Speech was made flesh, — that is, as the adversaries interpret it, that the divine nature assumed the human, — after he had already set forth those things concerning that Speech which followed the birth of the man Jesus Christ: such as these, that John the Baptist bore witness of him; that he was in the world; that he was not received by his own; and that he gave power to those by whom he was received to become the sons of God.”

items.exact_text: "Qua ratione illud intelligendum est, Sermonem carnem fuisse? — Quod is per quem Deus voluntatem suam omnem perfecte exposuisset, et propterea a Johanne Sermo appellatus fuisset, homo fuerit, omnibus miseriis et affiictionibus, ac morti denique subjectus: etenim vocem caro eo sensu Scriptura usurpat, ut ex iis locis perspicuum est, ubi Deus loquitur, Non contendet Spiritus meus cum homine in aeternum, quia caro est, Genesis 6:3; et Petrus, Omnis caro ut foenum, 1 Peter 1:24."
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
Translation: “In what manner is it to be understood that the Word was flesh? — That he through whom God had perfectly set forth His entire will, and was therefore called 'the Word' by John, was a man, subject to all miseries and afflictions, and finally to death; for the Scripture uses the word 'flesh' in that sense, as is clear from those places where God speaks: 'My Spirit shall not strive with man forever, because he is flesh,' Genesis 6:3; and Peter: 'All flesh is as grass,' 1 Peter 1:24.”

items.exact_text: "Ad secundum autem quid respondes? — Neque hic ullam prae- aeternitatis mentionem factam expresse; nam hoc in loco Filium hominis, id est, hominem in coelis fuisse testatur Sriptura, quem citra ullam controversiam prae-aeternum non extitisse certum est."
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
Translation: “But what do you answer to the second? — Neither is any mention of pre-eternity expressly made here; for in this place Scripture testifies that the Son of man, that is, a man, was in heaven, whom it is certain beyond all controversy did not exist from pre-eternity.”

items.exact_text: "Ubi vero Scriptura de Christo ait, quod de coelo descendit, a Patre exivit, et in mundum venit, Joh. 3:13, 10:36, 16:28, 17:18, quid ad haec respondes? — Ex iis non probari divinam naturam hinc apparere, quod 864 primi testimonii verba, Descendit de coelo, possint figurate accipi; quemadmodum, Jac. 1:17, Omne datum bonum et donum perfectum desursum est, descendens a Patre luminum; et Apoc. 21:2, 10, Vidi civitatem sanctam, Hierusalem novam, descendentem de coelo a Deo, etc. Quod si proprie aecipi debeant, quod nos perlibenter admittimus, apparet non de alio illa dicta quam de Filio hominis, qui cum personam humanam necessario habeat, Deus natura esse non potest. Porro, quod Scriptura testatur de Christo, quod Pater eum miserit in mundum, idem de apostolis Christi legimus in iisdem verbis citatis superius: Quemadmodum me misisti in mundum, et ego misi eos in mundum, Joh. 17:18. Ea veto verba, quod Christusm a Patre exierit, idem valent, quod de coelo descendit. Venire vero in mundum, id ejusmodi est, quod Scriptura post nativitatem Christi extitisse ostendit, Joh. 18:37, ubi ipse Dominus ait, Ego in hoc natus sum, et in mundum vent ut testimonium perhibeam veritati; et 1 Joh. 4:1, scriptum est, Multos falsos prophetas exiisse in mundum. Quare ex ejusmodi loquendi modis natura divina in Christo probari non potest. In omnibus vero his locutionibus, quam divinum muneris Christi principium fuerit, duntaxat deseribitur."
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Chapter 1.
Translation: “But where Scripture says of Christ that he descended from heaven, went out from the Father, and came into the world, John 3:13, 10:36, 16:28, 17:18, what do you answer to these? — That the divine nature is not proved from them appears from this, that the words of the first testimony, 'He descended from heaven,' can be taken figuratively; just as in James 1:17, 'Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights'; and Revelation 21:2, 10, 'I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God,' etc. But if they must be taken properly, which we very gladly admit, it appears that those things were said of no other than the Son of man, who since he necessarily has a human person, cannot be God by nature. Furthermore, as to what Scripture testifies of Christ, that the Father sent him into the world, we read the same concerning the apostles of Christ in the very words cited above: 'As you sent me into the world, so have I sent them into the world,' John 17:18. But those words, that Christ 'went out from the Father,' have the same force as 'he descended from heaven.' But 'to come into the world' is of such a kind as the Scripture shows to have occurred after the birth of Christ, John 18:37, where the Lord Himself says: 'For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth'; and in 1 John 4:1 it is written: 'Many false prophets have gone out into the world.' Therefore, a divine nature in Christ cannot be proved from such modes of speaking. In all these expressions, only how divine the origin of Christ's office was is described.”

items.exact_text: "In hoc loco non solum non exprinfitur prae-aeternitas Christi, cum aliud sit, ante Abrahamum fuisse, aliud, prae-aeternum; verum ne hoc quidem expressum est, ipsum ante Mariam Virginem fuisse. Et enim ea verba aliter legi posse (nimirum hac ratione, Amen, amen, dico vobis, Priusquam Abraham fiat, ego sum) apparet ex iis locis apud eundem evangelistam, ubi similis et eadem locutio Graeca habetur, cap. 13:19, Et modo dico vobis, priusquam fiat, ut cum factum fuerit credatis; et cap. 14:29, Et nunc dixi vobis usquam fiat, etc. "Quae vero ejus sententia foret lectionis? — Admodum egregia: etenim admonet Christus Judaeos, qui eum in sermone capere volebant, ut dum tempus haberent, crederent ipsum esse mundi lucem, antequam divina gratia, quam Christus iis offerebat, ab iis tolleretur, et ad Gentes transferretur. Quod vero ea verba, ego sum, sint ad sum modum supplenda, ac si ipse subjecisset iis, Ego sum lux mundi, superius e principio ejus orationis, ver. 12, constat et hinc, quod Christus bis seipsum iisdem verbis, ego sum, lucern mundi vocaverit, ver. 24, 28. Ea vero verba, Priusquam Abraham fiat, id significare quod diximus, e 865 notatione nominis Abraham deprehendi potest; constat inter omnes Abrahamum notare patrem multarum gentium. Cum vero Abram non sit factus prius Abraham, quam Dei gratia, in Christo manifestata, in multas gontes redunda-ret, quippe quod Abrahamus unins tantum gentis antes pater fuerit, apparet sententiara horum verborum, quam attulimus, esse ipsissimam."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “In this place not only is the pre-eternity of Christ not expressed, since it is one thing to have been before Abraham, and another to be pre-eternal; but indeed not even this is expressed, that he was before the Virgin Mary. For that those words can be read differently (namely in this manner, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, Before Abraham is made, I am') is apparent from those passages in the same evangelist, where a similar and the very same Greek expression is found, chapter 13:19, 'And now I tell you before it comes to pass, that when it has happened you may believe'; and chapter 14:29, 'And now I have told you before it happens,' etc. But what would be the meaning of this reading? — Truly excellent: for Christ warns the Jews, who wished to trap him in his speech, that while they had the time, they should believe him to be the light of the world, before the divine grace, which Christ offered to them, was taken away from them, and transferred to the Gentiles. But that those words, 'I am', are to be supplied in this manner, as if he himself had added to them, 'I am the light of the world', from earlier in the beginning of his discourse, verse 12, is clear also from this, that Christ twice called himself the light of the world with the same words, 'I am', verses 24, 28. But that those words, 'Before Abraham is made', signify what we have said, can be grasped from the notation of the name Abraham; it is agreed among all that Abraham denotes the father of many nations. But since Abram was not made Abraham before the grace of God, manifested in Christ, overflowed into many nations, inasmuch as Abraham was previously the father of only one nation, it appears that the meaning of these words, which we have brought forward, is the very truest.”
items.translation_text: Translation: “In this place not only is the pre-eternity of Christ not expressed, since it is one thing to have been before Abraham, and another to be pre-eternal; but indeed not even this is expressed, that he was before the Virgin Mary. For that those words can be read differently (namely in this manner, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, Before Abraham is made, I am') is apparent from those passages in the same evangelist, where a similar and the very same Greek expression is found, chapter 13:19, 'And now I tell you before it comes to pass, that when it has happened you may believe'; and chapter 14:29, 'And now I have told you before it happens,' etc. But what would be the meaning of this reading? — Truly excellent: for Christ warns the Jews, who wished to trap him in his speech, that while they had the time, they should believe him to be the light of the world, before the divine grace, which Christ offered to them, was taken away from them, and transferred to the Gentiles. But that those words, 'I am', are to be supplied in this manner, as if he himself had added to them, 'I am the light of the world', from earlier in the beginning of his discourse, verse 12, is clear also from this, that Christ twice called himself the light of the world with the same words, 'I am', verses 24, 28. But that those words, 'Before Abraham is made', signify what we have said, can be grasped from the notation of the name Abraham; it is agreed among all that Abraham denotes the father of many nations. But since Abram was not made Abraham before the grace of God, manifested in Christ, overflowed into many nations, inasmuch as Abraham was previously the father of only one nation, it appears that the meaning of these words, which we have brought forward, is the very truest.”

items.exact_text: "Fateor me per omnem vitam meam non magis contortam scripturae interpretationem audivisse; ideoque eam penitus improbo." — Eras. Johan. "Cum primum fatendi verbum in tuis verbis animadverti, sperabam to potius nuliam in tua vita scripturae interpretationem audivisse, quae hac sit acutior aut verior; quaeque magis divinum quid sapiat, et a Deo ipso patefactum fuisse prae se ferat. Ego quidem certe non leves conjecturas habeo, ilium, qui primus setate nostra eam in lucem pertulit (hic autem is fuit, qui primus quoque sententiam de Christi origine, quam ego constanter defendo renovavit) precibus multis ab ipso Christo impetrasse. Hoc profecto affirmare ausim, cum Deus illi viro permulta, aliia prorsus tunc temporis incognita, patefecerit, vix quidquam inter ilia omnia esse quod interpretatione hac divinius videri queat." — Socin. Disput. cum Eras. Johan. arg. 4, p. 67.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “'I confess that through all my life I have never heard a more distorted interpretation of scripture; and therefore I thoroughly reject it.' — Erasmus Johannis. 'As soon as I noticed the word 'confess' in your words, I was hoping rather that you had heard no interpretation of scripture in your life which is more astute or truer than this; and which smacks more of something divine, and exhibits itself as having been revealed by God himself. Indeed, I certainly have no slight conjectures that he, who first in our age brought it to light (moreover, this was he who also first renewed the opinion concerning the origin of Christ, which I constantly defend) obtained it by many prayers from Christ himself. I would certainly dare to affirm this, since God revealed very many things to that man, others entirely unknown at that time, there is scarcely anything among all those things which can seem more divine than this interpretation.' — Socinus, Disputation with Erasmus Johannis, argument 4, p. 67.”

items.exact_text: "Quae vero sunt testimonia Scripturae in quibus putant non exprimi quidem prae-aeternitatem Christi, ex iis tamen effici posse? — Ea quae videntur Domino Jesu quasdam res attribuere ab aeterno, quasdam vero tempore certo et definito."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what are the testimonies of Scripture in which they think the pre-eternity of Christ is indeed not expressed, yet it can be inferred from them? — Those which seem to attribute certain things to the Lord Jesus from eternity, but certain others at a fixed and defined time.”

items.exact_text: "Qui vero ad haec testimonia respondendum est? — Antequam ad singula testimonia respondeam, sciendum est, eam ex essentia Patris generationem esse impossibilem; nam si Christus ex essentia Patris genitus fuisset, aut partem essentiae sumpsisset, aut totam. Essentiae partem sumere non potuit, eo quod sit impartibilis divina essentia; neque totam, cum sit una numero, ac proinde incommunicabilis." 866
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But how must these testimonies be answered? — Before I answer the individual testimonies, it must be known that generation from the essence of the Father is impossible; for if Christ had been begotten from the essence of the Father, he would have taken either a part of the essence, or the whole. He could not take a part of the essence, because the divine essence is indivisible; nor the whole, since it is numerically one, and therefore incommunicable.”

items.exact_text: "Nisi Scriptura dixisset, non licuisset dicere, sed ex quo scriptum est dici potent." — Rabb. Ruben. apud Galat. lib 3.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “'Unless Scripture had said it, it would not have been lawful to say it, but since it is written, it can be said.' — Rabbi Reuben, in Galatinus, book 3.”

items.exact_text: "Qui tamen ad primum Scripturae testimonium respondendum est? — Id testimonium de generatione ex essentia Patris nihil prorsus habet; generationem vero prae-aeternam nulla probat ratione: hic enim mentio fit initii et dierum, quae in aeternitate locum non habent. Et verba haec, quae in Vulgata leguntur, a diebus internitatis, in Haebraeo extant, a diebus seculi: dies vero seculi idem quod dies antiqui notant, ut Esau 63:9, 11; Malachi 3:4. Sententia vero loci hujus est, Christum originem nativitatis suae ab ipso principio et annis antiquis ducturum; id est, ab eo tempore, quo Deus in populo suo regem stabilivit, quod reipsa in Davide. factum est, qui et Bethlehemita fult, et autor stirpis et familiae Christi."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “How however must the first testimony of Scripture be answered? — That testimony has absolutely nothing about generation from the essence of the Father; but it proves pre-eternal generation by no reason: for here mention is made of a beginning and of days, which have no place in eternity. And these words, which are read in the Vulgate as 'from the days of eternity', exist in the Hebrew as 'from the days of the age': but the days of the age denote the same thing as days of old, as Isaiah 63:9, 11; Malachi 3:4. But the meaning of this passage is that Christ will trace the origin of his birth from the very beginning and the ancient years; that is, from that time in which God established a king in his people, which in reality was done in David, who was both a Bethlehemite, and the founder of the lineage and family of Christ.”

items.exact_text: עָלַם, latere, abscondere, occultare, 2 Chronicles 9:2, Leviticus 4:18; in niphal latuit, absconditus, occultatus fuit; in hiphil abscondit, celavit, occultavit: inde עַלְמָה, Virgo, quia viro occulta, Genesis 24:43.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “עָלַם (alam), to lie hid, to hide, to conceal, 2 Chronicles 9:2, Leviticus 4:18; in Niphal it lay hid, was hidden, was concealed; in Hiphil he hid, he concealed, he kept secret: thence עַלְמָה (almah), a Virgin, because hidden from a man, Genesis 24:43.”

items.exact_text: "Ad secundum vero quid? — Neque in ea de generatione ex essentia Patris, nec de generatione prae-aeterna prorsus quicquam haberi; etenim vox hodie cum certum tempus designet, prae-aeternitatem denotare non potest. Quod vero Deus eum genuerit, non evincit eum ex essentia ejus genitum; id quod patet ex eo, quod haec eadem verba, Ego hodie genui to, primo sensu de Davide dicantur, quem constat neque ab aeterno, nec ex essentia Dei genitum. Deinde, quod Paulus apostolus eadem verba ad approbandam Christi resurrectionem afferat, Act. 13:33, et autor ad Hebraeos ad glorificationem Domini Jesu citer, Hebrews 1:5, 5:5. Denique, ex ea re, quod constet Deum aliter quam ex essentia generare, dum a Deo genitos credentes Scriptura pronunciat, ut videre est, Johan. 1:13; 1 Johan. 3:9; Jac. 1:18."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what to the second? — Neither in it is there held to be absolutely anything concerning generation from the essence of the Father, nor concerning pre-eternal generation; for indeed the word 'today', since it designates a certain time, cannot denote pre-eternity. But that God begot him does not prove him to be begotten from his essence; which is clear from the fact that these same words, 'Today I have begotten you', are said in the first sense of David, who is agreed to have been begotten neither from eternity, nor from the essence of God. Next, because the apostle Paul adduces the same words to prove the resurrection of Christ, Acts 13:33, and the author to the Hebrews cites them for the glorification of the Lord Jesus, Hebrews 1:5, 5:5. Finally, from this fact, that it is agreed that God begets otherwise than from essence, while Scripture pronounces believers to be begotten by God, as can be seen, John 1:13; 1 John 3:9; James 1:18.”

items.exact_text: "Sensus primus et apertus ad Davidem pertinet; mysticus et abstrusior ad Messiam, ut hic agnoscit David Kimchi, et ad Danielem Saadius Gaon, quo modo sumsere apostoli." — Annot. in ver. 1.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “'The first and open sense pertains to David; the mystical and more abstruse to the Messiah, as David Kimchi acknowledges here, and Saadia Gaon on Daniel, in which manner the apostles took it.' — Annotation on verse 1.”

items.exact_text: "Ad quartum veto quid? — Ut rem melius accipias, scito eos ex hoc loco ad eum modum argumentari: 'Sapientia Dei ab aeterno est genita; Christus est Dei Sapientia: ergo ab aeterno est genitus, 1 Corinthians 1:241 Corinthians 867 1:24.' Id argamentum firmum non csse hinc patet; Primum, quod Solomon agat de sapientia simpliciter et absolute considerata, sine additione vocis Dei; Paulus vero non simpliciter et absolute, sed cum additione, nempe, Dei. Deinde, Solomon agit de sapientia, quae neque est persona, nec esse potest, ut evariis effectis quae huic sapientiae attribuit, apparet, et hoc 7, 8, 9 cap., ex quibus sunt ea, Per me reges regnant, et principies justa decernunt; et initio cap. ix, introducit sapientiam omnes ad se invitantem, et mittentem virgines suae Paulus vero agit de Sapientia quae persona est. Tertio, verba haec, quae sunt reddita ab aeterno, in Hebraeo extant, a seculo: aliud vero ease ab aeterno, aliud a seculo, indicant loci, Esa. 64:4, Jeremiah 2:20, Lue. 1:70, et alii permuiti similes"
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what to the fourth? — So that you may receive the matter better, know that they argue from this passage in this manner: 'The Wisdom of God is begotten from eternity; Christ is the Wisdom of God: therefore he is begotten from eternity, 1 Corinthians 1:24.' That this argument is not firm is clear from this; First, because Solomon treats of wisdom considered simply and absolutely, without the addition of the word 'God'; but Paul treats of it not simply and absolutely, but with the addition, namely, 'of God'. Next, Solomon treats of wisdom which neither is a person, nor can be, as is apparent from the various effects which he attributes to this wisdom, and this in chapters 7, 8, 9, out of which are these, 'By me kings reign, and princes decree justice'; and at the beginning of chapter 9, he introduces wisdom inviting everyone to herself, and sending her maidens. But Paul treats of a Wisdom which is a person. Thirdly, these words, which are rendered 'from eternity', exist in Hebrew as 'from the age': but that it is one thing to be 'from eternity', and another 'from the age', is indicated by passages, Isaiah 64:4, Jeremiah 2:20, Luke 1:70, and very many others similar.”

items.exact_text: "Quid ad hoc respondes? — Neque hinc naturam divinam probari; posse enim aliquem gloriam habere antequam mundus fieret, apud Patrem, nec tamen hinc effici eum ease Deum, apparet, 2 Timothy 1:9, ubi ait apostolus de credentibus, illis datam fuisse gratiam ante tempora secularis. Praeterea, hic scriptum est, Jesum rogare hanc gloriam, quod naturae divinae prorsus repugnat. Loci vero sententia est, Christum togare Deum, ut ei gloriam reipsa det, quam habuerit apud Deum in ipsius decreto antequam mundus fieret."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to this? — Neither is the divine nature proved from this; for that someone can have glory before the world was made, with the Father, and yet it is not hence proven that he is God, is apparent, 2 Timothy 1:9, where the apostle says of believers, that grace was given to them before the secular times. Besides, it is written here that Jesus asks for this glory, which is utterly repugnant to the divine nature. But the meaning of the passage is that Christ asks God to actually give him the glory which he had with God in his decree before the world was made.”
