items.exact_text: "Quid ad hoc respondes? — Neque hine naturam in Christo divinam effici; nam hic Spiritus qui in prophetis erat, Christi dici potest, non quod a Christo datus fuerit, sed quod ea quae Christi fuerunt praenunciarit, ut ibidem Petrus ait, praenuncians illas in Christum passiones, et post haec glorias. Quem loquendi modum etiam, 1 Joh. 4:6, babes, Hinc cognoscimus spiritum veritatis, et spiritum erroris; ubi non propterea spiritus veritatis et erroris spiritus dicitur, quod veritas et error, tanquam personae. eum spiritum conferant; verum eo, quod spiritus veritatis loquatur quae veritatis sunt, et spiritus erroris quae sunt erroris."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to this? — That a divine nature in Christ is not established from this; for this Spirit which was in the prophets can be called the Spirit of Christ, not because he was given by Christ, but because he foretold those things which belonged to Christ, as Peter says in the same place, foretelling the sufferings that would come upon Christ, and the glories to follow. You have a similar manner of speaking in 1 John 4:6: 'By this we know the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error'; where it is not called the spirit of truth and the spirit of error on the grounds that truth and error, as if they were persons, confer that spirit; but because the spirit of truth speaks the things which belong to truth, and the spirit of error the things which belong to error.”

items.exact_text: "Quaenam ea loca Scripturae quae videntur Christo quaedam tempore certo et definito attribnere? — Ea sunt duplicia; quorum alia nomina, alia facta respiciunt, quae Christo a Scriptura attribui opinantur. "Quaenam sunt quae Christi nomina respiciunt? — Ea, ubi arbitrantur Jesum a Scriptura vocari Jehovam; Dominum exercituum; Deum 868 verum; solum verum; Deum magnum; Dominum Deum omnipotentem, qui fuit, qui est, et qui venturus est; Deum qui acquisivit proprio sanguine ecclesiam; Deum qui animam posuit pro nobis. — Jeremiah 23:6; Zechariah 2:8; 1 Joh. 5:20; Jude 4; Titus 2:13; Apoc. 1:8, 4:8; Act. 20:28; 1 Joh. 3:16.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What are those places of Scripture which seem to attribute certain things to Christ at a certain and definite time? — They are twofold; some of which respect names, others deeds, which they think are attributed to Christ by Scripture. What are those which respect the names of Christ? — Those where they judge Jesus to be called by Scripture Jehovah; the Lord of hosts; the true God; the only true [God]; the great God; the Lord God almighty, who was, and is, and is to come; the God who purchased the church with his own blood; the God who laid down his life for us. — Jeremiah 23:6; Zechariah 2:8; 1 John 5:20; Jude 4; Titus 2:13; Rev. 1:8, 4:8; Acts 20:28; 1 John 3:16.”

items.exact_text: "Quid vero tu ad ea ordine respondes, ac ante omnia ad primum? — Primum, quod ex eo confici non possit necessario nomen Jehovae Christo attribui. Ea enim verba, Et hoc eat nomen ejus quo vocabunt eum, Jehovah justita nostra, referri possunt ad Israelem, de quo paulo superius eodem versu loquitur, In diebus ejus aervabitur Juda et Israel habitabit secure, et hoc est nomen ejus, etc., ut e loco simili conspici potest apud eundem prophetam, cap. 33:15, 16, ubi sit, In diebus illis, et in illo tempore, faciam ut existat Davidi Surculus justitiae, et faciet judicium et justitiam in terra. In diebus illis servabitur Juda, et Jerusalem habitabit secure: et hoc (supple nomen) quo vocabunt eam, Jehovam justitae nostra. Etenim in Hebraeo expresse legitur, Vocabunt eam, quam vocem posteriorem ad Hierusalem referri prorsus est necesse, et hoc quidem loco Israeli, qui in priori loco positus eat, respondet. Videtur igitur prorsus verisimile, quod in priori etiam loeo, haec verbc, Voeabunt eam, ad Israelem referantur. At licet concedamus nomen Jehovae ad Christum posse referri, ex altero tamen testimonio apparet asseri non posse Jehovam simpliciter Christum vocari, neque ex eo sequi, Christum reipsa esse Jehovam. Sive igitur de Christo, sive de Israele postrema verba in testimonio Hieremiae accipiantur, sententia ipsorum est, Tum Jehovam unum Deum nostrum nos justificaturum, etenim illo tempore cum Christus appariturus esset Deus id in Israele facturus erat."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what do you answer to these in order, and above all to the first? — First, that it cannot necessarily be proven from it that the name of Jehovah is attributed to Christ. For those words, 'And this is his name by which they shall call him, Jehovah our righteousness,' can be referred to Israel, of which he speaks a little earlier in the same verse: 'In his days Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell securely, and this is his name,' etc., as can be seen from a similar passage in the same prophet, ch. 33:15, 16, where he says: 'In those days, and at that time, I will cause a Branch of righteousness to spring up for David, and he will execute judgment and righteousness in the earth. In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely: and this [supply: is the name] by which they will call her, Jehovah our righteousness.' For in the Hebrew it expressly reads, 'They shall call her,' which latter word must necessarily be referred to Jerusalem, and indeed corresponds in this place to Israel, which is placed in the former text. Therefore it seems quite probable that in the former place also, these words, 'They shall call him,' refer to Israel. But even if we concede that the name Jehovah can be referred to Christ, yet from the other testimony it appears it cannot be asserted that Christ is simply called Jehovah, nor does it follow from it that Christ is in reality Jehovah. Whether therefore the last words in the testimony of Jeremiah be understood of Christ or of Israel, their meaning is: Then Jehovah our one God will justify us, for at that time when Christ was to appear, God was about to do this in Israel.”

items.exact_text: "Quid respondes ad tertium? — In hoc testimonio, Scimus Filium Dei venisse, etc. haec verba, Hic est verus Deus, nego referri ad Dei Filium. Non quod negem Christum esse verum Deum, sed quod is locus ea de Christo accipi non admittat. Etenim hic agitur non solum de vero Deo, sed de illo uno vero Deo, ut articulus in Graeco additus indicat. Christus vero, etsi verus Deus sit, non est tamen ille ex se unus Deus, qui per se et perfectissima ratione Deus est, cum is Deus tantum sit Pater. Nec vero quic-quam juvat adversarios, qui propterea haec ad Christum referri volunt, quod verba, Hic est verus Deus, et Christi mentio proxime antecesserit; etenim pronomina relativa, ut hic et similia, non semper ad proxime antecedentia, verum saepenumero ad id de quo potissimum sermo est referuntur, ut patet ex his locis, Act. 7:19, 20, et 10:6, Joh. 2:7; e quibus locis apparet pronomen relativum hic non ad proximo antecedentes personas, sed ad remotiores referri."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to the third? — In this testimony, 'We know that the Son of God has come,' etc., I deny that these words, 'This is the true God,' refer to the Son of God. Not that I deny Christ is the true God, but that this passage does not allow them to be understood of Christ. For here it treats not only of a true God, but of that one true God, as the article added in the Greek indicates. But Christ, although he is a true God, yet is not of himself that one God, who by himself and in the most perfect manner is God, since this God is only the Father. Nor indeed does it help our adversaries at all, who want these words referred to Christ for the reason that the words, 'This is the true God,' and the mention of Christ, immediately preceded; for relative pronouns, like 'this' and the like, do not always refer to the immediate antecedents, but very often to that which is the primary subject of the discourse, as is clear from these passages: Acts 7:19, 20, and 10:6, 2 John 7; from which passages it appears that the relative pronoun 'this' does not refer to the nearest preceding persons, but to more remote ones.”

items.exact_text: "Ad quintum quid respondes? — Quintum testimonium est, Expectantes beatem spem, etc. Quo in logo epitheton magni Dei ad Christum referri duabus rationibus evincere conantur. Prior est, superius de articulo uno praefixo regula; posterior, quod adventum non expectemus Patris, sod Filii. Verum ad primum argumentum responsum habes in responsione ad quartum testimonium. Ad alterum respondeo, Paulum non dicere, Expectantes adventum magni Dei, verum dicere, Expectantes apparitionem gloriae magni Dei. Posse vero dici gloriam Dei Patris illustratam hi, cum Christus ad judicium venerit, verba Christi ostendunt, cum ait, quod venturus sit in gloria, id est, cum gloria Dei Patris sui, Matthew 16:27; Mark 8:88. Praeterea, quod est inconveniens si dicatur, Deus Pater venturus (prout illi e Vulgata citant) cum Filius ad mundum judicandum venerit? An Christus Dei Patris personam in judicio mundi, tanquam ejus a quo munus judicandi accepit, non sustinebit?" 870
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to the fifth? — The fifth testimony is, 'Looking for the blessed hope,' etc. In which passage they try to prove by two arguments that the epithet of the great God refers to Christ. The first is the rule mentioned above concerning a single prefixed article; the second is that we do not look for the coming of the Father, but of the Son. But you have the answer to the first argument in the response to the fourth testimony. To the other I answer, that Paul does not say, 'Looking for the coming of the great God,' but says, 'Looking for the appearing of the glory of the great God.' But that the glory of God the Father can be said to be illuminated when Christ shall come to judgment, the words of Christ show, when he says that he will come in glory, that is, with the glory of God his Father, Matthew 16:27; Mark 8:38. Besides, what inconsistency is there if it be said that God the Father is to come (as they cite from the Vulgate) when the Son comes to judge the world? Will not Christ sustain the person of God the Father in the judgment of the world, as of him from whom he has received the office of judging?”

items.exact_text: "Quid ad sextum respondes? — Eum vero locum propterea ad Christum referunt, quod arbitrentur neminem venturum, nisi Christum; is enim venturus est ad judicandum vivos et mortuos. Verum tenendum est, eam vocem quam illi reddidere venturus est, reddi aeque posse futurus est, ut Johan. 16:13, ubi Dominus ait de Spiritu, quem apostolis promittebat, quod illis esset futura annunciaturus; et Act. 18:21, ubi legimus, diem festum futurum: in quibus locis duobus, vox Graeca est ἐρχόμενος. Deinde, quis eat qui nesciat, cum prius dictum sit, qui erat, et qui est, et posterius hoc quod additum est per futurum esse reddi debere, et ubique de existentia ea oratio accipiatur, et non in prioribus duobus membris de existentia, in postremo de adventu? Nec est quisquam qui non animadvertat hic describi aeternitatem Dei, quae tempus praeteritum, praesens, et futurum comprehendit. Sed quod crassum errorem hunc detegit, est quod Apoc. 1:4, 5, legimus, Gratia vobis, et pax, ab eo qui est, et qui erat, et qui futurus est; et a septem spiritibus qui sunt ante faciem throni ejus; et a Jesu Christo, qui est testis fidelis. E quo testimonio apparet, Jesum Christum ab eo qui est, qui erat, et qui futurus est, vel, ut illi credunt, venturus, esse longe alium."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to the sixth? — But they refer that passage to Christ for this reason, that they think no one is to come, except Christ; for he is to come to judge the living and the dead. But it must be held, that the word which they have rendered 'is to come' can equally be rendered 'is to be', as in John 16:13, where the Lord says of the Spirit, whom he promised to the apostles, that he would announce things 'that are to be' to them; and Acts 18:21, where we read of a feast day 'that is to be': in both of which places the Greek word is ερχομενος (erchomenos). Next, who is there who does not know that since it was first said, 'who was', and 'who is', that this latter addition ought also to be rendered by 'is to be', and that the whole expression is everywhere taken of existence, and not of existence in the first two clauses, and of coming in the last? Nor is there anyone who does not perceive that the eternity of God is described here, which comprehends past, present, and future time. But what exposes this gross error is that in Rev. 1:4, 5, we read, 'Grace to you, and peace, from him who is, and who was, and who is to be; and from the seven spirits who are before his throne; and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness.' From which testimony it appears that Jesus Christ is entirely distinct from him who is, who was, and who is to be, or, as they believe, is to come.”

items.exact_text: "Quid ad septimum respondes? — Respondeo, nomen Dei hoc loco non referri ad Christum necessario, sect ad ipsum Deum Patrem referri posse, cujus apostolus eum sangninem, quem Christus fudit, sanguinem vocat, eo genere loquendi, et eam ob causam, quo genere loquendi, et quam ob causam propheta ait, Eum qui tangit populum Dei, tangere pupillam oculi Dei ipsius. Etenim summa quae est inter Deum Patrem et Christum conjunctio, etsi essentia sint prorsus diversi, in causa est, cur Christi sanguis, sangnis ipsius Dei Patris dicatur, praesertim si quis expendat quatenus is est pro nobis fusus: etenim Christus est Agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi. Unde sanguis in eum finem fusus, ipsius Dei sangnis jure vocari potest. Nec vero praetereundum est silentio, quod in editione Syriaca loco Dei legatur Christi."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to the seventh? — I answer, that the name of God in this place does not necessarily refer to Christ, but can be referred to God the Father himself, whose blood the apostle calls that blood which Christ shed, by that figure of speech, and for that reason, by which figure of speech and for which reason the prophet says, 'He who touches the people of God, touches the apple of God's own eye.' For the supreme union which exists between God the Father and Christ, although in essence they are entirely different, is the reason why the blood of Christ is called the blood of God the Father himself, especially if one considers the extent to which it was shed for us: for Christ is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. Thus the blood shed for that end can rightly be called the blood of God himself. Nor indeed should it be passed over in silence, that in the Syriac version, instead of 'God', it reads 'Christ'.”

items.exact_text: It is necessary to state that this is far from being correct. Eminent critics, such as Bengel, Matthai, and Scholz, it is true, decide for Θεοῦ, 871 but Griesbach, Lachman. and Tischendorf, give τοῦ Κυρίου as the proper reading. The leading manuscripts A, C, D, E, are in favor of the latter; but Tischendorf has now proved that manuscript B, commonly known as the Vatican manuscript, and formerly supposed to agree with them, on the contrary, has Θεοῦ, a prima manu. All the evidence cannot be weighed and discussed in this note, but the authority for Θεοῦ is, on the whole, sufficient to establish it as the true reading. — ED.

items.exact_text: "Ad octavum veto quid? — Primum igitur sic habeto, neque in Graeca editione uila haec excepta Complutensi), nec in editione Syriaca, vocem Deus haberi. Verum etiamsi vex haberetur in omnibus exemplaribus, num idcireo ea vex the ad Deum erit referenda? Non certe; non solum ob eam causam quam paulo superius attulimus, in responsione ad testimonium tertium, quod verba ejusmodi non semper ad propinquiores personas referantur, verum etiam quod ἐκεῖνος vocem Graecum Johannes in hac epistola saepe ad eum refert, qui longe antea nominatus fuerat, ut et 3, 5, et 7, versu ejusdem capitis in Graeco apparet."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what to the eighth? — First, therefore, understand this, that neither in any Greek edition (except the Complutensian), nor in the Syriac edition, is the word 'God' found. But even if the word were found in all copies, must that word therefore be referred to God? Certainly not; not only for that reason which we brought forward a little above, in the answer to the third testimony, that words of this kind do not always refer to the nearer persons, but also because John often refers the Greek word εκεῖνος (that one) in this epistle to him who had been named long before, as is apparent in the Greek in verses 3, 5, and 7 of the same chapter.”

items.exact_text: "Quid ad tertium? — Praeter id, quod et hoc testimonium loquatur de Christo tanquam media et secunda causa, verbum creata sunt, non solum de vetere, verum etiam de nova creatione in Scriptura usurpari constat; cujus rei exempla habes, Ephesians 2:10,15, Jac. 1:18. Praeterea ea verbs, Omnia in coelis et in terra, non usurpari pro omnibus prorsus, apparet non solum ex verbis paulo inferius subjectis, ver. 20, ubi apostolus ait, quod per eum reconciliata sint omnia in coelis et in terra, verum etiam ex iis ipsis verbis, in quibus apostolus non ait, coelum et terram creata esse, verum ea omnia quae in coelis et in terra aunt. "Qui vero istud testimonium intelligis? — Ad eum modum quo per Christum omnia quae sunt in coelis et in terra postquam eum Deus a mortuis excitavit, reformata sunt, et in alium statum et conditionem translata; id vero cum Deus et angelis et hominibus Christum caput dederit, qui antea tantum Deum solum pro domino agnoverunt." 872
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What to the third? — Besides this, that this testimony also speaks of Christ as the mediating and secondary cause, it is certain that the word 'were created' is used in Scripture not only of the old, but also of the new creation; examples of which you have in Eph. 2:10, 15, James 1:18. Furthermore, it is apparent that these words, 'All things in heaven and on earth', are not used for absolutely all things, not only from the words subjoined a little lower, in verse 20, where the apostle says that 'through him all things in heaven and on earth were reconciled', but also from those very words, in which the apostle does not say that heaven and earth were created, but 'all those things which are in heaven and on earth'. How then do you understand that testimony? — In the way in which, through Christ, all things which are in heaven and on earth, after God raised him from the dead, were reformed, and translated into another state and condition; and that indeed when God gave Christ as head both to angels and to men, who previously acknowledged only God alone as Lord.”

items.exact_text: "Ea quae in coelis sunt personae (quae subjecae sunt Christo), sunt angeli, iique tam boni quam mali: quae in coelis sunt, et personae non sunt, omnia ilia continent quaecunque extra angelos vel sunt, vel etiam esse possunt.." — Smalc, de Divin. Christi, cap. 16 de regno Christi super angelos.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Those persons which are in heaven (which are subject to Christ), are angels, and those both good and bad: the things which are in heaven, and are not persons, contain all those things whatsoever, outside of the angels, either are, or even can be.” — Valentinus Smalcius, De Divinitate Christi (On the Divinity of Christ), ch. 16, Concerning the kingdom of Christ over the angels.

items.exact_text: "Certum est per Verbum creata omnia; sed quae praecedunt, ostendunt hic de Christo agi, quod hominis est nomen; quomodo etiam Chrysostomus hunc accepit locum. Sed hle intelligit mundum creatum propter Christum, sensu non malo: sed propter id quod praecessit, rectius est ἐκτίσθη hic interpretari, ordinata sunt, — novum quendam statum sunt consecuta." — Grotius in Colossians 1:16.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “It is certain that all things were created by the Word; but what precedes shows that it here treats of Christ, which is the name of a man; in which manner Chrysostom also understood this passage. But he understands the world to have been created for the sake of Christ, in no bad sense: but on account of what preceded, it is more correct to interpret εκτίσθη (were created) here as 'were ordered' — they obtained a certain new state.” — Hugo Grotius on Colossians 1:16.

items.exact_text: "Qui respondes ad quartum testimonium? — Eo pacto, quod hic palam scripture sit, non Christum fecisse, sed Deum per Christum fecisse secula Vocem vero secula non solum praesentia et praeterita, verum etiam futura significare posse, in confesso est. Hic vero de futuris agi id demonstrat, quod idem autor affirmet per eum quem haeredem universorum constituerit Deus, etiam secula eese condita; nam Jesus Nazarenus non prius constitutus haeres universorum fuit, quam eum Deus a mortuis ex-citavit, quod hinc patet, quod tum demum omnis potestas in coelo et in terra eidem data a Deo Patre fuerit, cujus potestatis donatione, et non alia re, ista universorum haereditas continetur."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to the fourth testimony? — In this manner, that here it is openly written, not that Christ made, but that God made the worlds through Christ. But it is confessed that the word 'worlds' can signify not only present and past things, but also future things. But that future things are treated of here is demonstrated by the fact that the same author asserts that the worlds were also established by him whom God appointed heir of all things; for Jesus of Nazareth was not appointed heir of all things before God raised him from the dead, which is evident from this, that only then was all power in heaven and on earth given to him by God the Father, in the donation of which power, and in nothing else, does that inheritance of all things consist.”

items.exact_text: "Ad quintum quid respondes? — Ad id testimonium id respondeo, quod non de Christo, verum de Deo accipiendum sit. Quia vero idem scriptor illud ad Filium Dei referat, expendcndum est sermonem in testimonio, non de una re sed de duabus, potissimum haberi expresse. Una est coeli et terrae creatio: altera rerum creatarum abolitio. Quod vero is autor priorem ad Christum non referat, hinc perspicuum est, quod in eo capite praestantiam Christi demonstrare sibi proposuerit; non cam quam a seipso habeat, verum eam quam haereditavit, et qua praestantior angelis effectus sit, ut e ver. 4, cuivis planum est; cujus generis praestantia, cum creatio coeli et terrae non sit, nec esse possit, apparet manifeste non in eum finem testimonium ab co scriptore allatum, ut Christum creasse coelum et terram probaret. Cum igitur prior ad Christum referri nequeat, apparet posteriorcm tantum ad eum referendam esse, id veto propterea quod Dcus coelum et terram per 873 cum aboliturus sit, tum cum judicium extremum per ipsum est executurus, quo quidem tantopere praestantia Christi prae angelis conspicua futura est, ut ipsi angeli sint ei ca ipsa in re ministraturi. Quae posterior orstio, cum sine verbis superioribus, in quibus fit coeli terraeque mentio, intelligi non potuerit, cum sit cum iis per vocem ipsi conjuncta, et eadem illa verba priora idem autor commemorare necesse habuit. Nam si alii scriptores sacri ad eum modum citant testimonia Scripture, nulla adacti necessitate, multo magis huic, necessitate compulso, id faciendum fuit. "Ubi vero scriptores sacri id fecerunt? — Inter alia multa testimonia, habes Matthew 12:18-21, ubi nimis apertum est versiculum 19, tantum ad propositum evangelistae Matthaei pertinere, cum id voluerit probare cur Christus, ne palam fieret, interdiceret. Deinde, Acts 2:17-21, ubi etiam tantum, ver. 17, 18, ad propesitum Petri apostoli faciunt, quod quidem est, ut Spiritum Sanctum ease effusum supra discipulos doceat; et ibidem ver. 25-28, ubi palam est, versum tantum 27, ad propesitum facere, quan-doquidem id approbet apostolus, Christum a morte detinere fuisse impessibile. Deniquo, in hoc ipso capite, ver. 9, ubi verba haec, Dilexisti justitiam, et odio habuisti iniquitatem, apparet, nihil pertinere ad rem quam probat apostolus, quae est, Christum praestantiorem factum angelis."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to the fifth? — To that testimony I answer this, that it is to be understood not of Christ, but of God. But because the same writer refers it to the Son of God, it must be considered that the discourse in the testimony is expressly held not primarily concerning one thing, but two. One is the creation of heaven and earth: the other is the abolition of created things. But that this author does not refer the former to Christ is clear from this, that in that chapter he set out to demonstrate the excellence of Christ; not that which he has from himself, but that which he inherited, and by which he was made more excellent than the angels, as is plain to anyone from verse 4; of which kind of excellence, since the creation of heaven and earth is not, nor can be, it manifestly appears that the testimony was not adduced by that writer to this end, that he might prove Christ created heaven and earth. Since therefore the former cannot be referred to Christ, it appears that the latter only is to be referred to him, and this indeed because God will abolish heaven and earth through him, then when he executes the final judgment through him, in which indeed the excellence of Christ above the angels will be so conspicuous that the angels themselves will minister to him in that very matter. Which latter statement, since it could not be understood without the preceding words, in which mention is made of heaven and earth, since it is joined with them by the word 'they', the same author found it necessary to commemorate those same preceding words. For if other sacred writers cite testimonies of Scripture in this manner, driven by no necessity, much more was it to be done by this one, compelled by necessity. Where indeed have the sacred writers done this? — Among many other testimonies, you have Matthew 12:18-21, where it is very clear that only verse 19 pertains to the purpose of the evangelist Matthew, since he wished to prove why Christ forbade that he should be made known. Next, Acts 2:17-21, where also only verses 17 and 18 make for the purpose of the apostle Peter, which indeed is that he might teach that the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the disciples; and in the same place, verses 25-28, where it is evident that only verse 27 makes for the purpose, since the apostle proves this, that it was impossible for Christ to be held by death. Finally, in this very chapter, verse 9, where it is apparent that these words, 'You have loved righteousness, and hated iniquity,' do not pertain at all to the matter which the apostle proves, which is that Christ was made more excellent than the angels.”

items.exact_text: "Rursum, quod de Deo dictum fuerat Messiae aptat; quia constabat inter Hebraeos, et Mundum hunc Messiae causa conditum (unde ἐθεμελίωσας recte intelligi putem, Causa fuisti cur fundaretur, et opus manuum tuarum; id est, propter to factum: יַל רָד Hebraeis et Chaldaeis etiam propter sigaificat), et fore, ut novus meliorquo Mundus condatur per ipsum."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Again, what had been spoken of God he applies to the Messiah; because it was agreed among the Hebrews, both that this world was founded for the sake of the Messiah (whence I think εθεμελίωσας [you founded] is rightly understood as, 'You were the cause why it was founded', and 'the work of your hands'; that is, made for your sake: for ‏עַל יַד‏ [by the hand of] signifies also 'on account of' to the Hebrews and Chaldeans), and that it would be that a new and better world should be founded by him.”

items.exact_text: "Hic verbum, omnia, non minus quam in pluribus aliis locis, non omnia in universum sine ulla exceptione designare, verum ad ea tantum quae ad Christi regnum pertineant referri; de quibus vere dici potest, Dominum Jesum omnia verbo virtutis suae portare, id est, conservare. Quod vero vox, onmia, hoc loco ad ea duntaxat referatur, ex ipsa materia subjecta satis apparet. Praeterea, verbum quo hic utitur scriptor, portare, magis gubernandi vel administrandi rationem quam conservandi significat, quemadmodum illa quae annexa sunt, verbo virtutis suae, innuere videntur." 874
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Here the word 'all things', no less than in many other places, does not designate all things in the universe without any exception, but is referred only to those things which pertain to the kingdom of Christ; concerning which it can truly be said, that the Lord Jesus upholds all things by the word of his power, that is, preserves them. But that the word 'all things' in this place refers to those things alone, appears sufficiently from the subject matter itself. Furthermore, the word which the writer uses here, 'to uphold' (portare), signifies a manner of governing or administrating rather than of preserving, just as those words which are annexed, 'by the word of his power', seem to hint.”

items.exact_text: "Ex iis verbis doceri non potest, apostolum affirmare, Christum in deserto revera tentatum fuisse; ut e simili oratione, siquis ita diceret, deprehendi potest. 'Ne sitis refractarii magistratui, quemadmodum quidam majorum nostrorum fuerunt;' non illico concluderes eundem numero magistratum utrobique designari. Quod si reperiuntur in Scripturis ejusmodi loquendi modi, in quibus similis oratio ad eum cujus nomen paulo ante expressum est, sine ulla illius ejusdem repetitione referatur, tum hoc ibi sit, ubi ullus alius praeter cum cujus expressum est nomen, subintelligi possit: ut exemplum ejus rei habes in illo testimonio, Deuteronomy 6:16, Nos tentabis Dominum Deum tuum, quemadmodum tentasti in loco tentationis. Verum in ea oratione apostoli, de qua agimus, potest subintelligi alias praeter Christum, ut Moses, Aaron, etc.; de quo vide Numbers 21:5."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “It cannot be taught from those words that the apostle affirms that Christ was truly tempted in the desert; as can be understood from a similar sentence, if someone were to say thus: 'Do not be disobedient to the magistrate, as some of our ancestors were;' you would not immediately conclude that the numerically same magistrate is designated in both cases. But if manners of speaking of this kind are found in the Scriptures, in which a similar expression refers to him whose name was expressed a little before, without any repetition of that same name, then let this be so where anyone else, besides him whose name is expressed, could be understood: as you have an example of this thing in that testimony, Deut. 6:16: 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God, as you tempted him in the place of temptation.' But in that sentence of the apostle which we are treating, another besides Christ can be understood, such as Moses, Aaron, etc.; concerning which see Num. 21:5.”

items.exact_text: "Primum, ea verba ad Christum non necessario referri hinc apparet, quod de Deo Patre accipi possint; etenim verba paulo superiors de eodem dicuntur, excaecavit, induravit, sanavit. Deinde, gloriam quam Esaias vidit poterat esse, imo erat, non praesens, sed futura; etenim proprium est vatibus futura videre, unde etiam videntes appellati fuere, 1 Samuel 9:9. Denique, etiamsi de gloria ea quae tum praescus erat, Esaiae visa, haec verba accipias, longe tamen aliud est gloriam alicujus videre, et aliud ipsummet videre. Et in gloria illius modus Dei vidit etiam Esaias gloriam Christi Domini. Ait enim ibidem vates, Plena est terra glora Dei, Esa 6:8. Tum autem hoe reipsa factum est, cum Jesus Christus illi populo primum apparuit, et post toti mundo annunciatus est."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “First, it appears from this that these words are not necessarily referred to Christ, because they can be understood of God the Father; for the words slightly above are spoken of the same person, ‘he has blinded, hardened, healed’. Then, the glory which Isaiah saw could be, or rather was, not present, but future; for it is proper to prophets to see future things, whence they were also called seers, 1 Samuel 9:9. Finally, even if you accept these words concerning the glory which was then present, seen by Isaiah, it is far different to see the glory of someone, and another thing to see the person himself. And in that manner of the glory of God Isaiah also saw the glory of Christ the Lord. For the prophet says in the same place, ‘The earth is full of the glory of God,’ Isa. 6:8. But this in fact happened, when Jesus Christ first appeared to that people, and afterwards was announced to the whole world.”

items.exact_text: "E quibus testimoniis Scripturae demonstrare conantur Christum (ut loquuntur) incarnatum esse? — Ex iis ubi secundum eorum versionem legitur, Verbum caro factum est, Johan. 1:14; Et qui (Christus) cum esset in forma Dei, etc.; Philippians 2:6, 7; 1 Timothy 3:16; Hebrews 2:16; 1 Johan. 4:2, 8; Hebrews 10:5."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “From what testimonies of Scripture do they try to demonstrate that Christ was incarnated (as they say)? — From those where according to their version it is read, ‘The Word became flesh,’ John 1:14; ‘And who (Christ) although he was in the form of God, etc.’; Philippians 2:6, 7; 1 Timothy 3:16; Hebrews 2:16; 1 John 4:2, 8; Hebrews 10:5.”

items.exact_text: "Ad secundum quid respondes? — Neque hic extare quod adversa pars confectum velit. Aliud enim est quod hic apostolus ait, Cum in forma 875 Dei esset, forman servi assumpsit; aliud vero natura divina assumpsit humanam. Etenim hic forma Dei de-signare non potest Dei naturam, cum apostolus scribat eam formam Christum exin-anivisse. Deus vero naturam suam nullo mode exinanire potest; nec vero forma servi denotat naturam humanam, cum servum esse ad fortunam et conditionem hominis referatur. At ne id quoque dissimulandum est, scripta Novi Testamenuti hanc vocem forma semel fortassis tantum alibi usurpare, Marc. 16:12, idque eo sensu quo non naturam, sed exteriorem speciem significat, cum ait, Jesum duobus discipulis suis apparuisse alia forma. "Ex iis vero verbis, quae apostolus paulo post subjecit, Habitu inventus est ut homo, nonne apparet eum (ut loquuntur) incarnstum esse? — Nullo modo; etenim ea oratio nihil in se habet ejusmodi. De Samsone enim in literis sacris legimus, quod idem futurus erat ut homo, Judic. 16:7, 11; et Psalm 82., Asaph iis hominibus quos deos et filios Altissimi, vocaverat, denunciat, quod essent morituri ut homines; de quibus certum est non posse dici eos (ut adversarii dicunt) incarnatos fuisse. "Qua ratione locum hunc totum intelligis? — Ad eum modum, quod Christus, qui in mundo, instar Dei, opera Dei efficiebat, et cui, sicut Deo, omnia parebant, et cui divina adoratio exhibebatur, — ita volente Deo, et hominum salute exigente, — factus est tanquam servus et mancipium, et tanqusm unus ex aliis vulgaribus hominibus, cum ultro se capi, vinciri, caedi, et occidi permiserat."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you answer to the second? — That there is nothing here which the opposing party wishes to conclude. For it is one thing which the apostle here says, ‘Although he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant’; but another thing [to say] that the divine nature assumed the human. For here the ‘form of God’ cannot designate the nature of God, since the apostle writes that Christ emptied himself of that form. But God can in no way empty himself of his nature; nor does the ‘form of a servant’ denote human nature, since being a servant refers to the fortune and condition of a man. But neither is it to be concealed, that the writings of the New Testament use this word ‘form’ perhaps only once elsewhere, Mark 16:12, and in that sense in which it signifies not nature, but outward appearance, when it says that Jesus appeared to two of his disciples ‘in another form.’ — ‘But from those words which the apostle added shortly after, “Being found in fashion as a man,” does it not appear that he was (as they say) incarnated?’ — By no means; for that speech has nothing of such a kind in itself. For concerning Samson we read in the sacred letters, that he was to be ‘as a man,’ Judg. 16:7, 11; and in Psalm 82, Asaph announces to those men whom he had called gods and sons of the Most High, that they would die ‘like men’; of whom it is certain that it cannot be said that they (as the adversaries say) were incarnated. — ‘In what way do you understand this whole passage?’ — In this manner, that Christ, who in the world, like God, was performing the works of God, and whom, just as God, all things obeyed, and to whom divine adoration was shown, — God so willing, and the salvation of men demanding it, — became like a servant and a slave, and like one of the other common men, when he voluntarily allowed himself to be taken, bound, beaten, and killed.”

items.exact_text: "Qui porro ad ea loca respondes, etc.? — Quod Christus sit aequalis Deo, id divinam in eo naturam hullo modo probat: imo hinc res adversa colligitur; nam si Christus Deo, qui natura Deus est, aequalis est, efficitur, quod is idem Deus esse non possit. AEqualitas vero Christi cum Deo in eo est, quod ea virtute quam in eum contulit Deus, ea omnia efficeret, et efficiat, quae ipsius Dei sunt, tanquam Deus ipse.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Furthermore, what do you answer to those passages, etc.? — That Christ is equal to God in no way proves the divine nature in him: rather from this the opposite is gathered; for if Christ is equal to God, who by nature is God, it follows that he cannot be that same God. But the equality of Christ with God consists in this, that by that power which God conferred upon him, he accomplished, and does accomplish, all those things which belong to God himself, just as God himself.”

items.exact_text: "Ad tertium vero quid respondes? — Primum quidem, quod in multis exemplaribus vetustis, et in ipsa Vulgata, non legatur vox Deus; quare ex eo loco certum nihil concludi potest. Deinde, etiamsi ea vox legeretur, nullam esse causam cur ad Patrem referri non possit, cum haec de Patre affirmari possint, eum apparuisse in Christo, et apostolis, qui caro fuerunt. Quod autem inferius legitur, secundum 876 usitatam versionem, Receptus est in gloriam, id in Graeco habetur, Receptus est in gloria, — id est, cum gloria, aut gloriose. "Quae vero futura eat hujus testimonii sentontis? — Religionem Christi plenam esse mysteriis: nam Deus, id est, voluntas ipsius de servandis hominibus, per homines infirmos et mortales perfecte patefacta eat; et nihilominus tamen propter miracula et Tirtutes varias quae per homines illos infirmos et mortales edita fuerant, pro vera eat agnita; eadem ab ipsis angelis fuit demum perspecta; non solum Judaeis, verum etiam Gentibus fuit praedicata: omnes ei crediderunt, et insignem in modum, et summa cum gloria recepta fuit."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what do you answer to the third? — First indeed, that in many ancient copies, and in the Vulgate itself, the word ‘God’ is not read; wherefore from that passage nothing certain can be concluded. Next, even if that word were read, there is no reason why it could not be referred to the Father, since these things can be affirmed of the Father, that he appeared in Christ, and in the apostles, who were flesh. Moreover, what is read further down, according to the usual version, ‘Received up into glory,’ that in Greek is had, ‘Received up in glory,’ — that is, with glory, or gloriously. — ‘But what will be the meaning of this testimony?’ — That the religion of Christ is full of mysteries: for God, that is, his will concerning the saving of men, was perfectly manifested by weak and mortal men; and nevertheless, on account of the miracles and various powers which were produced by those weak and mortal men, it was acknowledged as true; the same was at length perceived by the angels themselves; it was preached not only to the Jews, but also to the Gentiles: all believed it, and it was received in a remarkable manner, and with the greatest glory.”

items.exact_text: Griesbach, Lachman, and Tischendorf, have decided for ὅς as the true reading. Knapp, Tittmann, Scholz, Henderson, Bloomfield, and Moses Stuart, abide by Θεός. Tischendorf refers to seven manuscripts, — four of them being in uncial characters, — as his authority for ὅς. Upwards of one hundred and fifty manuscripts have Θεὸς. It is a question, however, to be determined not by the number of the manuscripts merely, but by their value and authority; and the reader is referred on this subject to Dr Henderson's dissertation, "The Great Mystery of Godliness Incontrovertible," and the second edition of Tischendorf's New Testament, — ED.

items.exact_text: "In eo ne similitudinem quidem incarnationis (ut vocant) apparere, cum is scriptor non dicat, Christum assumpisse (ut quidam reddunt, et vulgo eo sensu accipiunt) sed assumere. Nec dicit, naturam humanam, sed semen Abrahae, quod in literis sacris notat cos qui in Christum crediderunt, ut Galatians 3:29, videre est. "Quid vero sensus hujus erit loci? — Id sibi vult is scriptor, Christum non esse Ser-vatorem angelorum, sed hominum credentium, qui quoniam et afflictionibus et morti subjecti sunt (quam rem superius expressit per participationem carnis et sanguinis), propterea Christus ultro illis se submisit, ut fideles suos a mortis metu liberaret, et in omni afflictione iisdem opern afferret." 877
items.modern_reference: Translation: “In that [passage] not even a likeness of the incarnation (as they call it) appears, since that writer does not say that Christ ‘has assumed’ (as some render it, and commonly accept it in that sense) but ‘assumes’. Nor does he say ‘human nature,’ but the ‘seed of Abraham,’ which in the sacred letters denotes those who have believed in Christ, as can be seen in Galatians 3:29. — ‘But what will be the sense of this passage?’ — That writer means this, that Christ is not the Savior of angels, but of believing men, who, since they are subject both to afflictions and to death (which thing he previously expressed by the sharing of flesh and blood), therefore Christ voluntarily submitted himself to them, that he might free his faithful ones from the fear of death, and bring help to them in every affliction.”

items.exact_text: "Etiam in eo nihil prorsus de incarnatione (quam vocant) haberi; etenim quod apud quoedam legitur, Venit in carnem, in Graeco habetur, In carne venit. Propterea non scribit Johannes, quod spiritus qui confitetur Jesum Christum, qui in carne venit, ex Deo est; verum quod ille spiritus qui confitetur Jesum Christum in carne venisse ex Deo est. Quorum verborum seusus est, eum spiritum ex Deo esse qui confitetur Jesum ilium, qui munus suum in terris sine ulla pompa et ostentatione mundana, summa cum humilitate (quoad exteriorem speciem) summoque cum contemptu obiverit, mortem denique ignominiosam oppetierit, esse Christum, et populi Dei Regem."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Also in that [passage] there is contained absolutely nothing concerning the incarnation (which they call it); for because it is read in some, ‘He came into the flesh,’ in Greek it is had, ‘He came in the flesh.’ Therefore John does not write, that the spirit which confesses Jesus Christ, who came in the flesh, is of God; but that the spirit which confesses that Jesus Christ came in the flesh is of God. The sense of which words is, that that spirit is of God which confesses that that Jesus—who discharged his office on earth without any pomp and worldly ostentation, with the greatest humility (as to outward appearance) and with the greatest contempt, and finally met an ignominious death—is the Christ, and the King of the people of God.”

items.exact_text: "Ne hic quidem de incarnatione (ut vocant) ullam mentionem factam, cum is mundus, in quem ingressum Jesum is autor ait, sit ille mundus futuras, ut superius demonstratum eat; unde etiam ingredi in illum mundum, non nasci in mundum, sed in coelum ingredi significat. Deinde, illis verbis, Corpus aptasti mihi, corporis vex (ut ex eo apparuit ubi de ingressu hoc in mundum actum est) pro corpore immortali accipi potest. "Quae sententia ejus est? — Deum Jesu tale corpus aptasse, postquam in coelum est ngressus, quod ad obeundum munus pontificis summi aptum et accommodatum foret."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Not even here is any mention made of the incarnation (as they call it), since that world, into which this author says Jesus entered, is that future world, as was previously demonstrated; whence also ‘to enter into that world’ signifies not to be born into the world, but to enter into heaven. Next, by those words, ‘A body thou hast prepared for me,’ the word ‘body’ (as appeared from that [place] where his entry into the world was discussed) can be accepted for an immortal body. — ‘What is the meaning of it?’ — That God prepared such a body for Jesus, after he entered into heaven, which would be fit and suited for discharging the office of high priest.”

items.exact_text: "In quibus scripturis Christus vocatur Deus? — Johan. 1:1, Et Verbum fuit Deus, et cap. 20:28, Thomas ad Christum ait, Dominus meus et Deus meus; et Romans 9:5, apostolus scribit Christum Deum (esse) supra omnes benedicturn in secula. "Quid his testimoniis effici potest? — Naturam divinam in Christo ex iis demonstrari non posse, praeter ea quae superius allata sunt, hint manifestum est, quod in primo tes-timonio agatur de Verbo, quod Johannes testatur apud ilium Deum fuisse; in secundo, Thomas eum appellat Deum, in cujus pedibus et manibus, clavorum, in latere lanceae vestigia deprehendit; et Paulus eum qui secundum carnem a patribus erat, Deum supra omnia benedictum vocat. Quae omnia dici de eo qui natura Deus sit, nullo mode posse, planum est, etenim ex illo sequeretur duos esse Deos, quorum alter apud alterum fuerit. Haec vero, vestigia vulnerum habere, eque patribus esse, hominis sunt prorsus, quae ei, qui natura Deus sit, ascribi nimis absonum esset. Quod si illud distinctionis naturarum velum quis praetendat, jam 878 superius illud amovimus, et docuimus hanc dis-tinctionem nullo modo posse sustineri."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “In what scriptures is Christ called God? — John 1:1, ‘And the Word was God’; and chap. 20:28, Thomas says to Christ, ‘My Lord and my God’; and Romans 9:5, the apostle writes that Christ is God over all, blessed forever. — ‘What can be proven by these testimonies?’ — That the divine nature in Christ cannot be demonstrated from them, besides those things which were alleged previously, is evident from this, that in the first testimony it is treated of the Word, which John testifies was with that God; in the second, Thomas calls him God, in whose feet and hands he found the marks of the nails, and in whose side the spear; and Paul calls him who according to the flesh was from the fathers, God blessed over all. All of which things it is clear can in no way be said of him who by nature is God, for from that it would follow that there are two Gods, one of whom was with the other. But these things, to have the marks of wounds, and to be from the fathers, are entirely of a man, which it would be too absurd to ascribe to him who by nature is God. But if anyone puts forward that veil of the distinction of natures, we have already removed it previously, and taught that this distinction can in no way be sustained.”

items.exact_text: "Ubi vero Scriptura testatur Christum cum Patre esse unum? — Jonah 10:29-31, ubi Dominus ait, Pater, qui mihi (oves) dedit, major omnibus est; et nemo eas rapere potest e manibus Patris mei. Ego et Pater unum sumus. "Qua ratione respondes ad id testimonium? — Ex eo, quod dicatur Christus esse cum Patre unum, efiiei non posse esse unum cum co nature, verba Christi, quae ad Patrem de discipulis habuit, demonstrant: Johan. 17:11, Pater sancte, serve illos in nomine tuo, ut sint unum, quemadmodum et nos unum sumus; et paulo inferius, ver. 22, Ego gloriam, quam dedisti mihi, dedi illis; ut sint unum, quemadmodum nos unum surnus. Quod veto Christus sit unum cum Patre, hoc aut de voluntate aut de potentia in salutis nostrae ratione accipi debet. Unde naturam divinam non probari ex eodem loco constat ubi Christus air, Pattern omnibus esse majorem, ac proinde etiam ipso Domino, quemadmo-dum idem Dominus expresse fatetur, et quod eas oves ei dederit, Johan. 14:28."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But where does Scripture testify that Christ is one with the Father? — John 10:29-31, where the Lord says, ‘The Father, who gave me the sheep, is greater than all; and no one can snatch them out of my Father’s hands. I and the Father are one.’ — ‘In what way do you answer to that testimony?’ — That from this, that Christ is said to be one with the Father, it cannot be proven that he is one with him in nature, the words of Christ, which he had to the Father concerning the disciples, demonstrate: John 17:11, ‘Holy Father, keep them in your name, that they may be one, just as we are one’; and slightly lower, ver. 22, ‘The glory which you gave me, I have given them; that they may be one, just as we are one.’ But that Christ is one with the Father, this ought to be understood either of will or of power in the matter of our salvation. Whence it is certain that the divine nature is not proven from the same passage where Christ says, that the Father is greater than all, and therefore also than the Lord himself, just as the same Lord expressly confesses, and that he gave those sheep to him, John 14:28.”

items.exact_text: "Filium autem Dei viventis, Filium Dei proprium et unigenitum esse Christum, ubi habetur? — De hoc Matthew 16:16, legimus, ubi Petrus ait, Tu es Christus, Filius Dei viventis; et Romans 8:32, ubi apostolus ait, Qui (Deus) proprio Filio, non pepercit, verum cum propter nos tradidit; et Johan. 3:16, Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum genitum daret; et ver. 18, Nomen unigeniti Filii Dei. "Quomodo vero ad haec loca respondetur? — Ex iis omnibus attributis Christi hullo modo probari posse naturam ejus divinam; nam quod ad primum attinet, notissimum est Petrum fateri, quod Filius hominis sit Christus, et Filius Dei viventis, quem constat divinam naturam, qualem illi comminiscuntur, non habuisse. Praeterea, testatur Scriptura de aliis hominibus quod sint filii Dei viventis, ut ex Hosea, Romans 9:26, Et erit loco ejus, ubi eis dictum est, Non populus meus (estis) vos, illic vocabuntur filii Dei viventis. Quod vero secundum et tertium locum attinet, in his legimus pro-prium et unigenitum Dei Filium in mortem traditum, quod eo qui natura Deus sit, dici non potest. Imo vero ex eo quod Christus Dei Filius sit, apparet Deum illum non esse, alioquin sibi ipsi Filius esset. Causa vero cur Christo ista attributa competant 879 haec est, quod inter onmes Dei filios et praecipuus sit et Deo charissimus, quemadmodum Isaac, quia Abahamo charissimus et haeres exstitit, unigenitus vocatus est, Hebrews 11:17, licet fratrem Ismaelem habuerit; et Solomon unigenitus coram matre sua, licet plures ex eadem matre fratres fuerint, 1 Paral. 3:1-6, etc, Proverbs 4:3."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But where is it held that Christ is the Son of the living God, the proper and only-begotten Son of God? — Concerning this we read in Matthew 16:16, where Peter says, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’; and Romans 8:32, where the apostle says, ‘Who (God) did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us’; and John 3:16, ‘For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son’; and ver. 18, ‘The name of the only begotten Son of God.’ — ‘But how is it answered to these passages?’ — That from all these attributes of Christ his divine nature can in no way be proven; for as pertains to the first, it is most well known that Peter confesses that Christ is the Son of man, and the Son of the living God, who it is certain did not have a divine nature, such as they invent. Moreover, Scripture testifies concerning other men that they are sons of the living God, as from Hosea, Romans 9:26, ‘And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” there they shall be called sons of the living God.’ But concerning the second and third passage, in these we read that the proper and only begotten Son of God was delivered to death, which cannot be said of him who by nature is God. Rather indeed from the fact that Christ is the Son of God, it appears that he is not that God, otherwise he would be a Son to himself. But the reason why these attributes belong to Christ is this, that among all the sons of God he is both the foremost and dearest to God, just as Isaac, because he was dearest to Abraham and stood as heir, is called only begotten, Hebrews 11:17, although he had a brother Ishmael; and Solomon is only begotten before his mother, although there were several brothers from the same mother, 1 Chron. 3:1-6, etc., Prov. 4:3.”

items.exact_text: "Quae scriptura eum vocat primogenitum omnis creaturae? — Colossians 1:15. "Quid ad eam respondes? — Neque hinc naturam divinam Christum habere exsculpi posse, etenim cum Christus primogenitus omnis creaturae sit, eum unum e numero creaturarum esse oportere necesse est; ea enim in Scripturis vis est primogeniti, ut primogenitum unum ex eorum genere, quorum primogenitus est, esse necesse sit, Colossians 1:18; Romans 8:29; Apoc. 1:5. Ut vero unus e rebus conditis creationis veteris existat Dominus Jesus, nec adversarii quidem concedent, nisi Ariani esse velint. Unum igitur esse e novae creationis genere Dominum Jesum concedant oportet. Unde non solum divina Christi natura effici non potest, verum etiam quod nunam divinam naturam Christus habeat firmiter conficitur. Quod vero eo nomine vocatur ab apostolo Jesus, eo fit, quod tempore et praestantia res onmes novae creationis longe antecedat."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What scripture calls him the firstborn of every creature? — Colossians 1:15. — ‘What do you answer to it?’ — Neither from this can it be extorted that Christ has a divine nature, for since Christ is the firstborn of every creature, it is necessary that he must be one of the number of creatures; for this is the force of ‘firstborn’ in the Scriptures, that the firstborn must be one of the kind of those of whom he is the firstborn, Colossians 1:18; Romans 8:29; Rev. 1:5. But that the Lord Jesus stands as one of the created things of the old creation, not even the adversaries will concede, unless they wish to be Arians. Therefore they must concede that the Lord Jesus is one of the kind of the new creation. Whence not only can the divine nature of Christ not be proven, but it is also firmly established that Christ does not have a divine nature. But that Jesus is called by that name by the apostle, it comes about for this reason, that he far precedes all things of the new creation in time and excellence.”

items.exact_text: "Ubi vero scriptura eum omnia quae Pater habeat habere asserit? — John 16:15, Christus sit, Omnia quae Pater habet mea sunt; et infra capite 17:10, Mea omnia tua sunt, et tua mea. "Quid tu ad haec? — Vox omnia, ad subjectam materiam ut superius aliquoties de-monstravimus fere semper refertur; quare ex ejusmodi locis non potest ullo modo quod volunt effici. Materia vero subjecta, cap. 16, est, id nimirum, quod Spiritus Sanctus apostolis ad Christi regnum spectans revelaturus erat; et 17 cap. constat apertissime agi de discipulis ipsius Jesu quos ipsi Deus dederat, uncle eos etiam suos vocat. Praeterea, cum quicquid Christus habeat, habcat Patris dono, non autem a seipso, hinc apparet, ipsum divinam naturam habere hullo modo posse, cum natura Deus omnia a seipso habeat."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But where does scripture assert that he has all things which the Father has? — John 16:15, Christ says, ‘All things which the Father has are mine’; and below in chapter 17:10, ‘All mine are yours, and yours are mine.’ — ‘What do you say to these?’ — The word ‘all’ is almost always referred to the subject matter, as we have previously demonstrated a few times; wherefore from such passages what they wish can in no way be proven. But the subject matter in chap. 16 is this, namely, what the Holy Spirit was to reveal to the apostles pertaining to Christ’s kingdom; and in chap. 17 it is most clearly established that it is treating of the disciples of Jesus himself, whom God had given to him, whence he also calls them his own. Besides, since whatever Christ has, he has by the gift of the Father, and not from himself, from this it appears that he can in no way have a divine nature, since God by nature has all things from himself.”

items.exact_text: "At quae scriptura Christum Patrem aeternitatis vocat? — Isaiah 9:6. 880 "Tu vero quid ad haec? — Ex eo naturam divinam probari non posse, cum certain ob causam Pater aeternitatis Christus sit vocatus, ex ipsis verbis ibidem paulo superius expressis videre est. Mirum veto est adversarios hunc locum, ubi agitur de Patre aeterno, ad Filium referre, quem constat secundum cos ipsos Patrem non esse. Pater vero aeternitatis aut futuri seculi propterea dictus est Christus, quod sit princeps et autor vitae aeternae, quae futura est."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what scripture calls Christ the Father of eternity? — Isaiah 9:6. — ‘But what do you say to these?’ — That the divine nature cannot be proven from this, since for a certain cause Christ is called the Father of eternity, can be seen from the very words expressed there slightly above. But it is strange that the adversaries refer this passage, where it is treated of the eternal Father, to the Son, who it is certain according to themselves is not the Father. But Christ is called the Father of eternity or of the future age for this reason, that he is the prince and author of eternal life, which is to come.”

items.exact_text: "Ex eo quod Verbum Dei sit Christus doceri divina in Christo natura non potest, imo adversum potius colligitur, cum enim ipsius unius Dei Verbum sit, apparet eum non esse ipsum unum Deum. Quod etiam ad singula haec testimonia simul responderi potest. Verbum vero, vel Sermo Dei Jesus ideo nuncupatur, quod omnem Dei voluntatem nobis exposuerit, ut ibidem Johannes inferius exposuit, Johan. 1:18. Quemadmodum etiam eodem sensu et vita et veritas dicitur.'
items.modern_reference: Translation: “From the fact that Christ is the Word of God, a divine nature in Christ cannot be taught, rather the opposite is gathered, for since he is the Word of the one God himself, it appears that he is not the one God himself. Which also can be answered at the same time to each of these testimonies. But Jesus is named the Word, or Speech of God for this reason, because he expounded to us all the will of God, as John expounded lower in the same place, John 1:18. Just as also in the same sense he is called both the life and the truth.”

Just as also in the same sense he is called both the life and the truth.”

items.exact_text: "Quod vero attinet ad dictum Domini Jesu, Qui me videt videt Patrem, nequehinc naturam divinam probari certum cuique esse potest, cum ea ratio videndi non possit de essentia Dei accipi, quae invisibilis sit prorsus, verum de cognitione eorum, quae dixit et fecit Christus."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But as pertains to the saying of the Lord Jesus, ‘He who sees me sees the Father,’ it can be certain to anyone that the divine nature is not proven from this, since that manner of seeing cannot be taken of the essence of God, which is altogether invisible, but of the knowledge of those things which Christ said and did.”

items.exact_text: "Nec illis denique verbia, quod plenitudo divinitatis in eo habitat corporaliter, probatur natura divina. Primum enim, vox haec divinitas designate potest voluntatem Dei. Eamque orationem cum apostolus opponat non personis, sed philosophiae et legi, hinc perspicuum est, eam de doctrina Domini Jesu non de persona accipi. De hac vero voce corporaliter, quid ea notet, inferius suo loco audies."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Nor finally by those words, that ‘the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily,’ is the divine nature proven. For first, this word ‘Godhead’ can designate the will of God. And since the apostle opposes that speech not to persons, but to philosophy and the law, it is clear from this that it is understood of the doctrine of the Lord Jesus, not of his person. But concerning this word ‘bodily’, what it denotes, you will hear below in its proper place.”

items.exact_text: "Ex eo quod Christum apostolus Dominum suum vocet, natura divina effici nequit; nam eum primo manitfeste ab illo Patre, quem ibidem Deum unum fatetur, secernit, quum solum natura Deum esse superius docuimua Deinde, hoc ipsum quod de eo dicit, omnia per ipsum, eum natura Deum esse non ostendit, cum, ut superius demonstratum est, 881 hac particula per non primam verum secundam causam designari constet, quod de eo qui natura Deus est dici nullo mode petest. Et licet de Patre Scriptura interdum loquatur, Per eum omnia, aliter tamen haec de Patre quam de Christo accipiuntur. De Patre enim haec ideo dici constat, quod omnes causae mediae per quas fit aliquid, non aliunde sint, nisi ab ipso, nec sint ejusmodi, ut sine iis ille agere non possit; de Christo vero dicuntur, quod per eum alius quis, nempe Deus omnia operetur, ut Ephesians 3:9 expresse habetur. Ne commemorandum mihi sit verbum omnia (uti superius ostensum est) ad subjectam materiam referri; quod ita habere inde apparet, quod apostolus agit de iis omnibus rebus quae ad populum Christianum pertinent, ut duo haec verba demonstrant, nobis, et Pater. Unde efficitur Christum non simpliciter et absolute, verum certa de causa vocatum Dominum unum, per quem omnia Quare hinc natura divina non probatur."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “From the fact that the apostle calls Christ his Lord, a divine nature cannot be proven; for first he clearly distinguishes him from that Father, whom he there confesses to be the one God, since we have taught above that He alone is God by nature. Then, this very thing which he says of him, ‘all things by him,’ does not show him to be God by nature, since, as was demonstrated above, by this particle ‘by’ (per) not the primary but the secondary cause is established to be designated, which cannot in any way be said of Him who is God by nature. And although Scripture sometimes speaks of the Father, ‘By him are all things,’ yet these things are understood differently of the Father than of Christ. For it is established that this is said of the Father because all mediate causes by which anything is done are from nowhere else but from Him, nor are they such that without them He could not act; but they are said of Christ, because by him someone else, namely God, works all things, as Ephesians 3:9 expressly states. Nor need I mention that the word ‘all things’ (as was shown above) is to be referred to the subject matter; which is apparent from this, that the apostle is dealing with all those things which pertain to the Christian people, as these two words demonstrate, ‘to us’ and ‘the Father.’ Whence it is established that Christ is not simply and absolutely, but for a certain cause called ‘one Lord, by whom are all things.’ Wherefore a divine nature is not proved from this.”

items.exact_text: "Cum in eo agatur de eo qui crueifixus sit, apparet ex eo naturam divinam non probari, cum de hac illud dici nequeat, verum de heroine, qui ideo Dominus gloriae dicitur, hoc est, Dominus gloriosus, quod a Deo gloria et honore coronatus sit."

items.exact_text: "In tertio testimonio, cum agatur de eo qui Agnus est, et qui vestimenta ha Revelation bet quem et occisum, et sanguine suo nos redimisse, apertissime idem Johannes fatetur, quae referri ad divinam naturam nulla ratione poassunt, apparet eo naturam divinam Christi astrui non posse. Omnia veto quae hic Christo in iis testimoniis tribuuntur, singularem ipsius potestatem quam Deus Christo in iis quae ad novum foedus pertinent, dedit, arguunt."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “In the third testimony, since it treats of him who is the Lamb, and who has garments, whom the same John most clearly confesses to be both slain, and to have redeemed us by his blood, things which can by no means be referred to the divine nature, it appears that the divine nature of Christ cannot be established thereby. But all the things which are here attributed to Christ in these testimonies prove his singular power which God gave to Christ in those things which pertain to the new covenant.”

items.exact_text: "Ad omnia ita responderi potest, ut appareat nullo modo ex iis effici divinam in Christo esse naturam; etenim aliam ob causam ea quae de Deo dicta sunt sub lege, dici potuerunt de Christo sub evangelio, quemadmodum et dicta sunt, nimirum propter illam summam quae inter Deum et Christum est, ratione imperii, potestatis, atque muneris, conjunctionem, quae onmia illum Dei dono consecutum esse scripturae Novi Testamenti passim testantur. Quod si Scriptura ea tradit de Mose, eum Israelem ex AEgypto eduxisse, Exodus 32:7, et quod redempter illius populi fuerit, Acts 7:35, et de aliis idem quod de ipso Deo apertissime scriptum erat, cum nec Moses neque alli tantam cum Deo conjunctionem haberent, quanta inter Deum et Christum 882 intercessit, multo justius haec quae de Deo primo respectu dicta sunt, Christo accommo-dari possunt, propter summam illam et arctissimam inter Deum et Christum conjunctionem."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “To all these things it can be answered thus, so that it may appear that in no way is it proven from them that there is a divine nature in Christ; for another reason those things which are said of God under the law could be said of Christ under the gospel, even as they are said, namely because of that highest conjunction which is between God and Christ, by reason of empire, power, and office, all which things the Scriptures of the New Testament everywhere testify that he obtained by the gift of God. But if Scripture relates these things of Moses, that he led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 32:7), and that he was the redeemer of that people (Acts 7:35), and of others the same thing which was most clearly written of God Himself, although neither Moses nor others had so great a conjunction with God as that which intervened between God and Christ, much more justly can these things which are said of God in the first respect be accommodated to Christ, on account of that highest and closest conjunction between God and Christ.”

items.exact_text: "Nota quod in locis innumeris in Talmud hoc expenitur de Messia, et nunquam de alio, ab aliquo qui alicujus apud Hebraeos authoritatis sit. Quare pater quod errant, nimium judaizantes nostri, qui hoe de Josia ad literam non verentur expenere. De solo quippe Messia hoc intelligendum fore ostenditur per R. Solomon, qui hoc de ipso non de Josia exponit; quod juxta morem suum nunquam, egisset, si absque injuria sui Talmud et Targum, et sine praedecessorum suorum omnium praejudicio, aliter exponere potuisset." — Raymund. Martin. Pug. Fid. p. 3, d. 1, c. xi.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Raymundus Martinus, Pugio Fidei, Part 3, dist. 1, ch. 11.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Raymundus Martinus, Pugio Fidei, Part 3, dist. 1, ch. 11.
Translation: “Note that in countless places in the Talmud this is expounded of the Messiah, and never of anyone else, by anyone who is of any authority among the Hebrews. Wherefore it is evident that our overly Judaizing scholars err, who do not fear to expound this literally of Josiah. For it is shown by R. Solomon that this is to be understood of the Messiah alone, who expounds this of him, not of Josiah; which according to his custom he would never have done, if without injury to his Talmud and Targum, and without the prejudice of all his predecessors, he could have expounded it otherwise.”

items.exact_text: "Tradunt de prophets quod die quodam dixerit Gabrieli, O Gabriel, optem to in specie figurnae turn magnae videre, secundum quam Deus creavit to. Dixit Gabriel, O dilecte Deo, est figura mea valde terribilis; nemo eam poterit videre, et sic neque tu, quin animi deliquium passus concidat. Reponit Mahumed, Etsi maxime ita sit, velim tamen to videre in figura majori. Respondit ergo Gabriel, O dilecte Deo, ubi me videre desideras? Extra urbem Meccam, respondit Mahumed, in villa lapidosA. Dixit Gabriel, Villa ista me non capiet. Ergo respondit Mahumed, In monte Orphath. Hic, inquit Gabriel, locus aptior erit et capacior. Abiit ergo Mahumed in montem Orphath, et ecce Gabriel, cum magno fragore et strepitu, totum figura sua operiens horizontem; quod cum propheta vidisset, concidit, deliquium passus, in terram. Ubi vero Gabriel, super quo pax, ad priorem rediisset figuram, accessit ad prophetam, eumque amplexus et osculatus, ita compellavit, Ne timeas, O dilecte Deo, sum enim frater tuus Gabriel. Dixit propheta, Vera dixisti, O frater mi Gabriel: nunquam existimassem ullum esse Dei creaturam tanta praeditam figura. Respondit Gabriel, O dilecte Deo, quid si igitur videres figuram Europhil angeli? " — Kessaeus Vit. Patr. p. 12, Interpret. Hotting.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Al-Kisa'i, Vitae Patrum (Qisas al-Anbiya), trans. J.H. Hottinger.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Al-Kisa'i, Vitae Patrum (Qisas al-Anbiya), trans. J.H. Hottinger.
Translation: “They relate concerning the prophet that on a certain day he said to Gabriel, ‘O Gabriel, I would desire to see you in the appearance of that great figure according to which God created you.’ Gabriel said, ‘O beloved of God, my figure is very terrible; no one can see it, and thus neither you, without falling down in a swoon.’ Mohammed replied, ‘Although it be so to the greatest degree, yet I would wish to see you in your greater figure.’ Therefore Gabriel replied, ‘O beloved of God, where do you desire to see me?’ ‘Outside the city of Mecca,’ answered Mohammed, ‘in the stony village.’ Gabriel said, ‘That village will not contain me.’ Therefore Mohammed replied, ‘On Mount Arafat.’ ‘Here,’ said Gabriel, ‘the place will be more fitting and more capacious.’ Therefore Mohammed went away to Mount Arafat, and behold Gabriel, with a great crash and noise, covering the whole horizon with his figure; which when the prophet had seen, he fell down, suffering a swoon, to the earth. But when Gabriel, upon whom be peace, had returned to his former figure, he approached the prophet, and having embraced and kissed him, addressed him thus, ‘Do not fear, O beloved of God, for I am your brother Gabriel.’ The prophet said, ‘You have spoken true things, O my brother Gabriel: I would never have thought that there was any creature of God endowed with so great a figure.’ Gabriel replied, ‘O beloved of God, what if you should then see the figure of the angel Israfil?’”

items.exact_text: "Unde apparet Christum nobis Dei voluntatem perfecte manifestasse? — Hinc, quod ipse Jesus perfectissima ratione eam a Deo in coelis sit edoctus, et ad eam hominibus publicandam e coelo magnifice sit missus, et eam perfecte iisdem annuntiavit. "Ubi vero scriptum est Christum fuisse in coelo, etc.coelo missum? — Johan. 6:38, 3:13." — Cat. Rac. de offic. Christi prophetico, q. 4, 5.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Of the Prophetic Office of Christ, q. 4, 5.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Of the Prophetic Office of Christ, q. 4, 5.
Translation: “Whence does it appear that Christ perfectly manifested the will of God to us? — From this, that Jesus himself was in the most perfect manner taught it by God in heaven, and was magnificently sent from heaven to publish it to men, and he perfectly announced it to them. ‘But where is it written that Christ was in heaven, and was sent from heaven?’ — John 6:38, 3:13.”

items.exact_text: "Aut verba Christi sine ullo prorsus tropo interpretanda sunt, et proinde ex ipsis ducta argumentatio vestra, penitus dissolvetur: aut si tropus aliquis in Christi verbis, admittendus eat, non videmus cur non potius dicamus, ideo dixisse Christum filium hominis fuisse in coelo 884 antequam post resurrectionem eo ascenderet, quia jam ante iliad tempus, non modo in coelo mente, et cogitatione perpetuo versabatur, verum etiam omnia coelestia, id est arcana quaeque divinissima, et ipsa omnia quae in coelo sunt, et fiunt, adeo cognita et perspecta habebat, ut ea tanquam praesentia intueretur: et ita quamvis in terris degens, in ipso tamen coelo commorari dici possit, Nam in coelo antequara moreretur revera esse potuit, postquam ex Maria natus est: nec solum potuit, sed (ut ita dicamus) debuit; si enim homo ille Paulus Christi servus, ad tertium usque coelum ante mortem raptus est, nullo pacto nobis verisimile sit, Christum ipsum ants mortem in coelo non fuisse." — Socin. Resp. prior, ad Par. Vol. pp. 38-40.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, Responsio prior ad Paraenesim Andreae Volani, pp. 38-40.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, Responsio prior ad Paraenesim Andreae Volani, pp. 38-40.
Translation: “Either the words of Christ are to be interpreted entirely without any trope, and therefore your argumentation drawn from them will be thoroughly dissolved: or if some trope is to be admitted in the words of Christ, we do not see why we should not rather say that Christ therefore said that the Son of Man had been in heaven before he ascended there after the resurrection, because already before that time, he was not only perpetually dwelling in heaven in mind and thought, but he also had all heavenly things, that is, all the most divine secrets, and all those things themselves which are and are done in heaven, so known and clearly perceived, that he beheld them as if present: and thus although living on earth, he can yet be said to tarry in heaven itself. For he could indeed have been in heaven before he died, after he was born of Mary: and not only could he, but (so to speak) he ought to have been; for if that man Paul, the servant of Christ, was caught up even to the third heaven before his death, it could by no means be likely to us that Christ himself was not in heaven before his death.”

items.exact_text: a "Quaenam sunt perfecta mandata Dei per Christum patefacta? — Pars eorum con-tinetur in praeceptis a Mose traditis, una cum iis quae sunt eis in novo foedere addita; pars veto continetur in iis quae peculiariter ipse Christus praescripsit."

items.exact_text: "Primtun igitur quod attinet ad priorem rationem dico, diversam illam lectionem non extare, ut arbitror, neque in ullo probato codice, neque apud ullum probatum scriptorem, quod vel ex eo constare potest, quod Erasmus in suis Annotatioaibus quamvis de hoc ipso loco agat, ejus rei nullam prorsus mentionem facit. Qui Erasmus, cure hoe in genere nusquam non diligentissime versatur; tum in omnibus locis in quibus Christus Deus appellari videtur, adeo diligenter omnia verba expendit, atque examinat, ut non immerito et Trinitariis Arianismi suspectus fuerit, et ab Antitrini-tariis inter eos relatus, qui subobscure Trinitati reclamaverint." — Faust. Socin. Ep. ad Franc. David. pp. 186, 187.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, Epistola ad Franciscum Davidis, pp. 186, 187.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, Epistola ad Franciscum Davidis, pp. 186, 187.
Translation: “First therefore, as to what pertains to the former reason, I say, that diverse reading does not exist, as I think, neither in any approved codex, nor in any approved writer, which can be established even from this, that Erasmus in his Annotations, although he deals with this very passage, makes no mention at all of this matter. Which Erasmus, since he is nowhere not most diligent in this kind of thing; then in all passages in which Christ seems to be called God, he so diligently weighs and examines all words, that not unmeritedly he was both suspected of Arianism by Trinitarians, and numbered by Anti-Trinitarians among those who somewhat obscurely protested against the Trinity.”

items.exact_text: "Exemplum denique affert nostrorum, Thes. 108. Quomodo se gesserint in Transylvania in negotio Francisci Davidis, quomodo semetipsos in actu illo inter se reos agant vafriciae, perfidiae, crudelitatis, sanguinariae proditionis, etc., sed his primum regero: non exemplis, sed legibus judicandum esse: si nostri ita se gesserunt ut scribit Frantzius, etc. Deinde dico falso ista objecta fuisse sb autoribus scripti, quod citat Frantzius nostris: nec enim fraterne tractarunt Franciscum Davidem, usque ad ipsum agonem, quanquam eum ut fratrem tractare non tenebantur, qui in Jesu Christi veram divinitatem tam impie involabat, ut dicere non dubitaret, tantum peccatum esse eum invocare, quantum est, si Virgo Maria invocetur," etc. — Smalc. Refut. Thes. Franz. disput. 9, p. 298.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Finally, he brings forward an example of our people, Thesis 108: How they conducted themselves in Transylvania in the affair of Francis David; how in that act they make themselves mutually guilty of craftiness, perfidy, cruelty, and bloody betrayal, etc. But to these things I reply first: we must judge not by examples, but by laws; if our people acted thus, as Franzius writes, etc. Next, I say that these things were falsely objected by the authors of the writing which Franzius cites against our people: for they did not treat Francis David fraternally, even up to his death agony, although they were not bound to treat him as a brother, who attacked the true divinity of Jesus Christ so impiously that he did not hesitate to say it is as great a sin to invoke Him as it is if the Virgin Mary is invoked,” etc.

items.exact_text: "Recte igitur existimasti, mlhl quoque verisimile videri, eum qui Dominum Jesum Christum invocare non vult, aut non audet, vix Christiani nomine dignum esse: nisi quod non modo vix, sed ne vix quidem, et non modo verisimile id mihi videtur, sed persuasissimum mihi est."

items.exact_text: "Quid vero sentis de iis hominibus qui Christum non invocant, nec invocandum censent? — Prorsus non esse Christianos,sentio: cum reipsa Christum non habeant, et licet verbis id negare non audeant, repsa tamen negent." — Cat. Rac. De praecept. Christi. cap. 1:p. 126. 886
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what do you think of those men who do not invoke Christ, nor judge that He ought to be invoked? — I think that they are absolutely not Christians: since in reality they do not have Christ, and although they may not dare to deny it in words, nevertheless they deny it in reality.”

items.exact_text: "Video enim nihil hodie edi posse in tota Christiana religione majoris momenti quam hoc sit, demonstratio, videlicet, quod Christo licet creaturae tamen invocatio et adoratio seu cultus divinus conveniat." — Socin. Ep. 3 ad Rad. p. 143.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “For I see that nothing can be published today in the whole Christian religion of greater importance than this, namely, the demonstration that invocation and adoration, or divine worship, belongs to Christ, even though He is a creature.”
