items.exact_text: "Si enim hoc demonstratum fuerit, concident omnes Trinitariorum munitiones, quae revera uno hoc fundamento nituntur adhuc, quod Christo adoratio et invocatio conveniunt, quae solius Dei illius altissimi omni ratione videtur esse propria." — Id ibid.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “For if this is demonstrated, all the fortifications of the Trinitarians will fall, which in truth still rest on this one foundation: that adoration and invocation belong to Christ, which by all reason seems to be proper to that most high God alone.”

items.exact_text: "Hic primum adorationem cum invocatione confundis, quod tamen fieri non debet, cum utriusque sit diversa quaedam ratio, adeo ut ego, quamvis nihil prorsus dubitem, praeceptum extare de adorando Christo, et etiamsi non extaret, tamen eum a nobis ado-rari omnino debere, non idem tamen existimem de eodem invocando, cum videlicet invocatio pro ipsa opis imploratione, et directione precum nostrarum accipitur. Hic enim statuo id quidem merito a nobis fieri posse, id est, posse nos jure ad ipsum Chris-tum preces noetras dirigere, nihil tamen esse quod nos id facere cogat." — Socin. Ep. 3 ad Rad. p. 151.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Here first you confuse adoration with invocation, which nevertheless ought not to be done, since there is a certain different reason for each; so much so that I, although I doubt nothing at all that there exists a precept concerning the adoring of Christ, and even if it did not exist, yet He ought to be absolutely adored by us, yet I would not think the same concerning invoking Him, since clearly invocation is taken for the very imploring of help, and the directing of our prayers. For here I determine that this indeed can deservedly be done by us—that is, we can by right direct our prayers to Christ Himself—yet there is nothing which compels us to do it.”

items.exact_text: "Legi quoque diligenter responsionem tuam ad argumenta Francisci Davidis, ubi Christi Domini invocationem honoremque nomini ejus sacrosancto convenientem asseris, ac contra calumnias Francisci Davidis defendis. Attamen videris mihi, paucis verbis, optimam sententiam non tantum obscurasse, sed quasi in dubium revocasse, adver-sariosque in errore confirmasse. Quaeris quid sit quod tantum malum secum importare possit? Breviter respondeo, verba ilia quae saepius addis, Christum Dominum invocaro posaumus, sed non debemus, sive non tenemur, etc., ruinam negotio, causaeque tuae minantur. Non possum perclpere quomodo haec conciliari possint: non 887 debemus, sed possumus, quasi in negotio salutis nostrae liberum sit facere vel omittere, prout nobis aliquid magis necessarium, vel e contra visum fuerit." — Niemojevius, Ep. 1 ad Faust. Socin. anno 1587.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I have also diligently read your response to the arguments of Francis David, where you assert the invocation of Christ the Lord and the honor fitting for His sacrosanct name, and defend it against the calumnies of Francis David. Nevertheless, you seem to me, in a few words, not only to have obscured an excellent opinion, but as it were to have called it into doubt, and to have confirmed the adversaries in their error. You ask what it is that could bring such a great evil with it? I respond briefly, those words which you quite often add: ‘We are able to invoke Christ the Lord, but we do not have to, or are not bound to,’ etc., threaten ruin to your enterprise and cause. I cannot perceive how these can be reconciled: ‘we do not have to, but we are able to,’ as if in the business of our salvation it is free to do or omit, according to as something has seemed to us more necessary, or the contrary.”

items.exact_text: "Videtur autem hoc imprimis modo diabolus insidias struere Domino Jesu, dum scilicet tales excitat, qui non dubitant affirmare Dominum Jesum nunc plane esse otiosum in coelis, et res humanas vel salutem hominum non aliter curare, quam Moses curat salutem Judaeorum. Qui quidem homines, professione videri volunt Christiani, interne veto Christum abnegarunt, et spiritu judaico, qui semper Christo fuit inimicissimus, infiati sunt; et si quis jure cum eis agere velit, indigni plane sunt, qui inter Christianos numerentur, quantumvis ore tenus Christum profiteantur, et multa de eo garriant; adeo ut multo tolerabilior sit error illorum qui Christum pro illo uno Deo habent et colunt, quam istorum: et praestet, ex duobus malis minus quod aiunt eli-gendo, Trinitarium quam hujusmodi blasphemum esse." — Smalc, de Ver. Christi Divin. cap. 15:De regn. Christi moderno.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But the devil seems in this way especially to construct snares for the Lord Jesus, while clearly he raises up such men, who do not hesitate to affirm that the Lord Jesus is now entirely idle in the heavens, and does not care for human affairs or the salvation of men otherwise than Moses cares for the salvation of the Jews. Which men indeed, by profession wish to be seen as Christians, but internally they have denied Christ, and are puffed up with a Judaic spirit, which was always most hostile to Christ; and if anyone wishes to deal with them by right, they are plainly unworthy to be numbered among Christians, however much by word of mouth they may profess Christ, and chatter many things about Him; so much so that the error of those who hold and worship Christ as that one God is much more tolerable than theirs: and it is better, by choosing the lesser of two evils as they say, to be a Trinitarian than a blasphemer of this kind.”

items.exact_text: "Respondeo particulis istis exclusivis, qualis et solus, et similis, cum de Deo usurpantur, nunquam cos simpliciter excludi, qui a Deo, in ea re de qua agitur, dependent. Sic dicitur solus Deus sapiens, solus potens, solus immortalis, neque tamen simpliciter a sapientia, a potentia, ab immortalitate excludi debent et alii, qui istarum rerum participes sunt effecti. Quare jam cum solus Deus adorandus aut invocandus esse dicitur, excludi simpliciter non debet is, qui hac in parte a Deo pendet, propter divinum ab ipso in cuncta acceptum imperium, sed potius tacite simul includendus est." — Schlichting. ad Meisner. artic, de Deo, pp. 206, 207.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I answer that by those exclusive particles, such as both ‘alone’ and the like, when they are used of God, those are never absolutely excluded who depend on God in that matter concerning which it is being treated. Thus it is said God alone is wise, alone powerful, alone immortal, and yet others who are made partakers of those things ought not to be absolutely excluded from wisdom, from power, from immortality. Wherefore now when God alone is said to be adored or invoked, he ought not to be absolutely excluded who in this part depends on God, on account of the divine empire over all things received from Him, but rather is to be tacitly included at the same time.”

items.exact_text: "Sed cur quaeso absurdum est affirmare septem illos spiritus a Johanne fuisse in-vocatos? An quia solus Deus est invocandus? Atqui hanc rationem nihili ease tota ilia disputatione demonstratur, non modo quia nunquam diserte interdictum est, quem-quam alium praeter Deum ipsum invocare, sed etiam, et multo magis, quia ejusmodi interdictiones (ut sic loquar) nunquam cos excludunt qui ipsi Deo sunt subordinati." — Socin. Ep. 3 ad Volk.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But why, I ask, is it absurd to affirm that those seven spirits were invoked by John? Or is it because God alone is to be invoked? But that this reason is of no value is demonstrated in that whole disputation, not only because it is never expressly forbidden to invoke anyone else besides God Himself, but also, and much more, because such interdictions (so to speak) never exclude those who are subordinated to God Himself.”

items.exact_text: "Quanta distantia inter Creatorem eat et creaturam, tanta esse debet differentia inter honorem qui Creatori exhibetur et qui creaturae tribuitur. Atqui inter Creatorem et creaturam maxima est distantia, sive essentiam et naturam spectes, sive digni-tatem et excellentiam, ergo et maxima esse debet differentia inter honorem Dei et creaturae. At honor qui praecipue debetur Deo est religiosa adoratio; ergo haec non est tribuenda creaturae, ergo neque Christo, quem tu puram esse creaturam fateris." — De Adorat. Christi, Disput. cum Christoph. Fran., p. 4.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “As great a distance as there is between the Creator and the creature, so great ought to be the difference between the honor which is exhibited to the Creator and that which is attributed to the creature. But between the Creator and the creature there is the greatest distance, whether you consider essence and nature, or dignity and excellence; therefore there ought also to be the greatest difference between the honor of God and that of the creature. But the honor which is principally due to God is religious adoration; therefore this is not to be attributed to a creature, and therefore neither to Christ, whom you confess to be a pure creature.”

items.exact_text: "Etsi summa est inter Deum et creaturam distantia, non tamen necesse est, tan-tam esse differentiam inter honorem Dei et creaturae; nam potest Deus cui vult commu-nicare honorem suum, Christo prsesertim, qui dignus est tali honore, quique non sine gravissimis causis adorari jubetur in sacris literis." — Disput, de Adorat. Christi, p. 6.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Although the distance between God and a creature is supreme, nevertheless it is not necessary that there be so great a difference between the honor of God and of the creature; for God can communicate his honor to whom he wills, especially to Christ, who is worthy of such honor, and who is not without the most weighty reasons commanded to be adored in the sacred letters.”

items.exact_text: 'Quodnam eat discrimen inter veteris, et novi foederis peceatorum expiationem? Ñ peccatorum sub novo fodere non solum distat ab expiatione peccatorum sub vetere plurimum, verum etiam longe praestantior et excellentior est: id vero duabus potissimum de causis. Prior est, quod sub vetere foedere, iis tantum peccatis expiatio, per illa legalia sacrificia, constituta fuit, quae per imprudentiam vel per infirmitatem admissa fuere, unde etiam infirmitates et ignorantiae nuncupabantur. Verum pro peccatis gravioribus, quae transgressiones erant mandati Dei manifestsae, nulla sacrificia instituta fuerant, sed mortis poena fuit propesita. Quod si talia Deus alicui condonabat, id non vi foederis fiebat, sed misericordia Dei singulari, quam Deus citra foedus, et quando et cui libuit exhibebat. Sub novo vero foedere peccata expiantur, non solum per imprudentiam et infirmitatem admissa, verum etiam ea quae apertissimorum Dei mandatorum sunt transgressiones, dummodo is cui labi ad eum modum contigerit, in eo non perseveret, verum per veram poenitentiam resipiscat, nec ad illud peccatum amplius relabatur. Posterior vero causa est, quod sub prisco foedere ad eum modum peccatorum expiatio peragebatur, ut poena temporaria tantum ab iis quorum peccata expiabantur tolleretur; sub novo vero ea est expiatio, ut non solum poenas temporarias, verum etiam aeternas amoveat, et loco poenarum, aeternam vitam, in foedere promissam, iis quorum peccata fuerint expiata, offerat."
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Christopher Ostorod and Andrzej Wojdowski, Compendium Religionis.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Christopher Ostorod and Andrzej Wojdowski, Compendium Religionis.
Translation: “What is the difference between the expiation of sins of the old and the new covenant? — The expiation of sins under the new covenant not only differs greatly from the expiation of sins under the old, but is also far more excellent and outstanding; and that chiefly for two reasons. The first is, that under the old covenant, expiation through those legal sacrifices was established only for those sins which were committed through ignorance or weakness, whence they were also called infirmities and ignorances. But for more serious sins, which were manifest transgressions of the commandment of God, no sacrifices had been established, but the penalty of death was set forth. But if God pardoned such things in anyone, it did not happen by virtue of the covenant, but by a singular mercy of God, which God exhibited apart from the covenant, both when and to whom He pleased. But under the new covenant, sins are expiated not only when committed through ignorance and weakness, but also those which are transgressions of the most open commandments of God, provided that he to whom it happens to fall in that manner does not persevere in it, but repents through true repentance, and does not fall back into that sin any further. The latter reason is, that under the ancient covenant, the expiation of sins was performed in such a way that only a temporary punishment was removed from those whose sins were expiated; but under the new, the expiation is such that it removes not only temporary but also eternal punishments, and in place of punishments, offers eternal life, promised in the covenant, to those whose sins have been expiated.”

items.exact_text: "Qua ratione vero utrumque demonstras? — Peccata quae sub vetere foedere ex-piari non potuere omnia sub novo expiari, testatur apostolus Paulus in Act. cap. 13:38, 39, idem habetur, Romans 3:25, Hebrews 9:15. Quod vero ea ratione expientur peccata sub novo foedere ut etiam aeterna poena amoveatur, et vita aeterna donetur, habetur Hebrews 9:12, ubi sup." — Q. 6.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But by what reasoning do you prove both? — The apostle Paul testifies in Acts 13:38, 39 that all sins which could not be expiated under the old covenant are expiated under the new; the same is maintained in Romans 3:25, Hebrews 9:15. But that sins are so expiated under the new covenant that even eternal punishment is removed and eternal life given, is maintained in Hebrews 9:12, ubi supra.” — Question 6.

Christi, p. 146. 893

items.exact_text: "Puniendis peccatis tres esse debere causas existimatum est. Una est quae νουθεσία vel κόλασις vel παραίνεσις dicitur; cum poena adhibetur castigandi atque emendandi gratia, ut is qui fortuito deliquit, attentior fiat, correctiorque. Altera est, quam ii, qui vocabula ista curiosius diviserunt, τιμωρίαν appellant, ea causa animadvertendi est, quum dignitas authoritasque ejus, in quem est peccatum tuenda est, ne praetermissa animadversio contemptum ejus pariat, et honorem elevet," etc. — Vid. A. Gell. lib. 6:cap. xxiv.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “It has been thought that there ought to be three reasons for punishing offenses. One is what is called nouthesia [admonition], or kolasis [chastisement], or parainesis [exhortation]; when punishment is applied for the sake of correction and amendment, so that he who has offended by chance may become more careful and better. The second is what those who have divided these words more carefully call timōria [retribution]; this reason for punishing is when the dignity and authority of him against whom the offense is committed must be protected, lest the omission of punishment produce contempt for him and diminish his honor,” etc. — See Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 6, chap. 24.

items.exact_text: "Porro libri istius, unde haec sectio in Esaiam desumpta est, Author perhibetur D. Simeon, concionatorum princeps, qui Francofurti olim degebat. Hic e Judaeorum vetustissimis scriptis, secundum bibliorum seriem, dicta et explicationes plurimas: magna diligentia et labore collegit: unde libri suo nomen וליט ac si peram dicas [mallet:] quia ut in pera reconduntur plurima." — L'Emper.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Furthermore, the author of this book, from which this section on Isaiah is taken, is said to be Rabbi Simeon, the prince of preachers, who formerly lived in Frankfurt. He collected with great diligence and labor from the most ancient writings of the Jews, according to the order of the Bibles, many sayings and explanations: whence the name of his book is Yalkut [ילקוט], as if you would say a wallet: because as in a wallet, very many things are stored.” — L'Empereur.

items.exact_text: "Σκελοκοπία seu crucifragium ut crux ipsa, servorum quasi peculiare supplicium fuit." — Lipsias. "Sublimes extra ordinem aliquae statuebantur cruces; si exempla edenda forent in famosa persona, et ob atrox facinus, aut si hoc supplicio veniret afficiendus ille, cujus odium erat apud omnes flagrantissimum." — Salmas, de Cruce. Which seems to be the case in the cross of Christ, between those of the thieves. - Bene addit crucem, nam servorum non civium crucis erat supplicium." — Nannius, in Terent. And. Acts 8:1Acts 8, 5, 15. — "Noli minitari scio crucem Futuram mihi sepulchrum: ibi enim mei majores sunt siti, Pater, avus, proavus, abavua — "Servus apud Plaut. Mil. Glor. 2:4,19. Vid. Trach. Histor. lib. U. 27; Vulcat. in Avid. Cassio, cap. iv.; Capitolin. in Macrin. Cap. xii.; Luc. Florus, lib. in. cap. xix.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Skelokopia or crucifragium [breaking of the legs], like the cross itself, was a punishment almost peculiar to slaves.” — Lipsius. “Some extraordinarily high crosses were erected, if examples were to be made in a famous person, and on account of an atrocious crime, or if he who was to be afflicted with this punishment was one whose hatred was most burning among all.” — Salmasius, De Cruce. items.exact_text: "Vidi ego dum plaustro per ora vulgi traducitur, illudentem theologo e Franciscanis, cujus cura mollire ferocitatem animi obstinati. Lucilius ferocitate contumax, dum in patibulum traditus, monachi solarium aspernatus objectam crucem aversatur, Christoque illudit in haec eadem verba: ' Illi in extremis prae timore imbellis sudor, ego imperterritus 895 morior.' Falso sane imperterritum se dixit scelestus homo, quem vidimus dejectum animo, philosophia uti pessime, cujus se mentiebatur professorem. Erat illi in extremis aspectus ferox et horridus, inquieta mens, anxium quodcunque loquebatur; et quanquam philosophice mori se clamabat identidem, finiisse ut brutum nemo negaverit. Antequam rogosubderetur ignis; jussus sacrilegam linguam cultro submittere, negat, neque exerit, nisi forcipum vi apprehensam carnifex ferro abscindit: non alias vociferatio horridior: diceres mugire ictum bovem, etc. Hic Lucilii Vanini finis, cui quanta constantia fuerit, probat belluinus in morte clamor. Vidi ego in custodia, vidi in patibulo, videram antequam subiret vincula: flagitiosus in libertate, et voluptatum sectator avidus, in carcere Catholicus, in extremis onmi philosophize praesidio destitutus, amens moritur." — Gramon. Hist. Galatians lib. 3:ad anno 1619.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “I saw him, while being led in a cart before the faces of the mob, mocking a theologian of the Franciscans, whose care it was to soften the ferocity of his obstinate mind. Lucilius, stubborn in his ferocity, while handed over to the gibbet, despising the monk's comfort, turns away from the cross offered to him, and mocks Christ in these very words: 'In his last moments he had an unwarlike sweat out of fear, I die fearless.' Falsely indeed did the wicked man call himself fearless, whom we saw cast down in spirit, making the worst use of philosophy, of which he falsely claimed to be a professor. In his last moments his appearance was fierce and horrid, his mind restless, whatever he spoke was anxious; and although he repeatedly shouted that he was dying philosophically, no one could deny that he ended like a brute. Before the fire was applied to the pyre, ordered to submit his sacrilegious tongue to the knife, he refuses, nor does he stick it out, unless the executioner cuts it off with iron after grasping it with the force of tongs: at no other time was there a more horrid outcry: you would say a struck ox was bellowing, etc. This was the end of Lucilio Vanini, whose degree of constancy is proven by his beastly clamor in death. I saw him in custody, I saw him on the gibbet, I had seen him before he went into bonds: flagitious in liberty, and an avid follower of pleasures, in prison a Catholic, in his last moments destitute of all the protection of philosophy, he dies insane.” — Gramond, Historiarum Galliae, book 3, at the year 1619.

items.exact_text: "Fecialis sumpto in manibus lapide, postquam de foedere inter partes convenerat, haec verba dixit, Si recte ac sine dolo malo, hoc foedus atque hoc jusjurandum facio, dii mihi cuncta felicia praestent; sin aliter aut ago, aut cogito, caeteris omnibus salvis, in propriis legibus, in propriis laribus, in propriis templis, in propriis sepulchris, solus ego peream, ut hic lapis de manibus meis decidet." — Polyb, lib. 3:"' Audi Jupiter; audi pater patrate; ut ilia palam prima postrema ex illis tabulis cerave recitata sunt sine dolo malo, utique ea hic hodie rectissime intellecta sunt, illis legibus papulus Romanus prior non deficiet. Si prior defexit publico consilio, dolo malo; tu illo Diespiter, populum Romaaum sic ferito, ut ego hunc porcum hie hodie feriam: tantoque magis ferito quanto magis potes pollesque.' Id ubi dixit, porcum saxo silice percussit." — Livius, lib. 1:cap. 24. 896 "Armati, Jovis ante aras, paterasque tenentes Stabant: et caesa jungebant foedera porca" — Virg. AEn. 8:640. "Ad quem locum Servius: ' Foedera dicta sunt, a porca foede et crudeliter occisa: nam cum ante gladiis configeretur, a fecialibus inventum ut silice feriretur, ea causa quod antiquum Jovis signum, lapidem silicem putaverunt esse.'"

items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Polybius, Histories, Book 3; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita, Book 1, Chapter 24; Virgil, Aeneid, Book 8, Line 640, with Servius' Commentary.
Translation: “The herald [fetial], taking a stone in his hands, after he had agreed on the treaty between the parties, spoke these words: 'If I make this treaty and this oath rightly and without deceit, may the gods grant me all things happy; but if I act or think otherwise, all others being safe, in my own laws, in my own house, in my own temples, in my own tombs, may I alone perish, as this stone falls from my hands.' — Polybius, Book 3. 'Hear, O Jupiter; hear, O father patrate; as those things have been publicly recited from first to last from those tablets or wax without deceit, and as they have been today most correctly understood here, the Roman people will not be the first to depart from those laws. If they depart first by public counsel and with evil intent, then do you, O Jupiter, strike the Roman people just as I strike this pig here today; and strike them so much the more as you are more able and powerful.' When he said this, he struck the pig with a flint stone. — Livy, Book 1, Chapter 24. 'Armed, they stood before the altars of Jupiter, holding cups, and joined treaties over a slain sow.' — Virgil, Aeneid, 8:640. To which place Servius: 'Treaties [foedera] are named from a sow slain in a foul [foede] and cruel manner; for whereas before they were pierced with swords, it was invented by the heralds that they should be struck with a flint, for the reason that they thought the flint stone was an ancient statue of Jupiter.'”

items.exact_text: "Quid ad ea testimonia quae nos a Christo testantur redemptos respondes? — Resp. E verbo redimendi non posse efiici satisfactionem hanc, hinc est planum, quod de ipso Deo et in novo et in prisco foedere scribitur, eum redemisse populum suum ex AEgypto, eum fecisse redemptionem populo suo. Deinde cum scriptum sit quod Deus redemit Abrahamum et Davidem, et quod Moses fuerit redemptor, et quod simus redempti e nostris iniquitatibus, aut e vana conversatione nostra, et e maledictione legis; certum autem est Deum nemini satisfecisse, nec vero aut iniquitatibus, aut conversationi vanae, aut legi satisfactum esse dici posse."
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore, Book 1, Part 2, Chapter 1 [Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, 2:124].
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore, Book 1, Part 2, Chapter 1 [Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, 2:124].
Translation: “'What do you answer to those testimonies which witness that we are redeemed by Christ?' — Answer: 'That this satisfaction cannot be derived from the word “redeem” is clear from this, that it is written of God Himself both in the New and in the Old Covenant that He redeemed His people out of Egypt, and made redemption for His people. Then, since it is written that God redeemed Abraham and David, and that Moses was a redeemer, and that we are redeemed from our iniquities, or from our vain conversation, and from the curse of the law; but it is certain that God satisfied no one, nor indeed can it be said that satisfaction was made either to our iniquities, or to our vain conversation, or to the law.'”

items.exact_text: "Requiritur et is qui captivum detineat, alioqui captivus non esset. Huic in liberatione nostra, si exactius rem ipsam considerare velimus, respondent multA. Multa siquidem nos tanquam captivos detinebant; ea autem sunt peccatum, diabolus, mundus, et quae peccatum consequuntur, mortis aeternae reatus, seu mortis aeternae nobis decretum supplicium." — De Servat, lib. 1 cap. 2.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore, Book 1, Chapter 2 [Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, 2:125].
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore, Book 1, Chapter 2 [Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, 2:125].
Translation: “'There is also required he who holds the captive, otherwise he would not be a captive. In our liberation, if we wish to consider the matter more precisely, many things correspond to this. For indeed many things were holding us as captives; and those are sin, the devil, the world, and those things which follow sin, the guilt of eternal death, or the punishment of eternal death decreed for us.'”

items.exact_text: "Nihil in hac liberatione desideratur, ut omnino verae redemptioni respondeat, nisi ut is qui captivum detinebat pretium accipiat. Quamvis autem quibusdam videatur dici posse diabolum, pretium quod in nostra liberatione intervenit, accepisse, quemadmodum antiquiores theologi, inter quos Ambrosius et Augustinus, ausi sunt dicere, tamen id perabsurdum videri debet, et recte est neminem id pretium accepisse affirmare. Ea siquidem ratione potissimum, non vera sed metaphorica redemptio, liberatio nostra est, quocirca in ea nemo est qui pretium accipiat; si enim id quod in ipso pretii loco est acceptum (ab eo scilicet 897 qui captivum hominem detinebat) fuisset, jam non metaphoricum sed verum pretium intervenisset, et propterea vera redemptio esset."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Nothing is lacking in this liberation, so that it entirely corresponds to a true redemption, except that he who held the captive should receive the price. But although it may seem to some that it can be said that the devil received the price that intervened in our liberation, as older theologians, among them Ambrose and Augustine, dared to say, yet this must seem thoroughly absurd, and it is correct to affirm that no one received that price. By that reason primarily, our liberation is not a true but a metaphorical redemption, on which account there is no one in it who receives a price; for if that which is accepted in place of the price itself had been received (namely from him who held man captive), then a true price, not a metaphorical one, would have intervened, and therefore it would be a true redemption.”

items.exact_text: "Christus per obedientiam suam (maxime in morte) et preces ei accedentes, hoc a Patre obtinuit, ne is humanum genus gravibus peccatis immersum desereret atque obduraret, sed viam illis daret ad justitiam perveniendi per Christum, Esau 53:4, ita et ἀπολυτροῦν aut ποιεῖν λύτρωσιν, Luc. 1:68. גָּאַל aut פָדָה, id est, liberare, nempe a necessitate moriendi in peccatis, vista patefaciendo per quam exire ista liceret."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Christ, by his obedience (especially in death) and the prayers accompanying it, obtained this from the Father, that he would not forsake and harden the human race immersed in heavy sins, but would give them a way of arriving at righteousness through Christ, Isaiah 53:4; so also [Greek: apolytroun] ‘to redeem’ or [Greek: poiein lytrōsin] ‘to accomplish redemption,’ Luke 1:68. [Hebrew: ga'al] or [Hebrew: padah], that is, to liberate, namely from the necessity of dying in sins, by opening a way through which it would be permitted to escape.”

items.exact_text: "Interventus sanguinis Christi, licet Deum ad liberationem hanc a peccatorum nostrorum poena nobis concedendum movere non potuerit, movit tamen nos ad eam nobis oblatam accipiendam, et Christo fidem habendam." — Socin, ubi sup.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore (Of Jesus Christ the Savior), Part I, Chapter I.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore (Of Jesus Christ the Savior), Part I, Chapter I.
Translation: “The intervention of the blood of Christ, although it could not move God to grant us this liberation from the penalty of our sins, nonetheless moved us to receive it when offered to us, and to have faith in Christ.”

items.exact_text: "Si in eo sita est dilectio, quod Deus nos dilexerit et Filium suum miserit ἱλασμόν, pro peccatis nostris, quomodo Christus morte sua demum iram Dei adversus nos incensam placarit? nam cum dilectio illa Dei quae plane fuit summa, causa fuit cur Deus Filium suum charissimum miserit, necesse est ut iram jam suam adversus nos deposuerit; nonne aliter eodem tempore et impense amabit et non amabit? Si Deus etiam tum potuit nobis irasci cum Filium suum charissimum supremae nostrae felicitatis causa morti acerbissimae objiceret, quod satis magnum argumentum erit ex effectu ejus petitum, 898 unde cognoscamus Deum nobis non irasci amplius." — Crell. Defen Socin. con. Grot. part. 6.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Johannes Crellius, Defensio Socini contra Grotium (Defense of Socinus against Grotius), Part 6.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Johannes Crellius, Defensio Socini contra Grotium (Defense of Socinus against Grotius), Part 6.
Translation: “If love is situated in this, that God loved us and sent his Son to be a [Greek: hilasmon] propitiation for our sins, how did Christ by his death finally appease the anger of God kindled against us? For since that love of God, which was clearly supreme, was the reason why God sent his most dear Son, it is necessary that he had already laid aside his anger against us; otherwise, will he not at the same time both love immensely and not love? If God could still be angry with us when he subjected his most beloved Son to the most bitter death for the sake of our supreme happiness, what sufficiently great proof will be sought from its effect, from which we may know that God is no longer angry with us?”

items.exact_text: "Ad haec vero quod nos Deo reconciliarit quid affers? — Primum, nusquam Scripturam asserere Deum nobis a Christo reconciliatum, verum id tantum, quod nos per Christum, aut mortem ejus, simus reconciliati, vel Deo reconciliati, ut ex omnibus locis quae de hac reconciliatione agunt videre est. Quare nullo modo ex iis omnibus locis ea satisfactio extrui potest. Deinde vero quod aperte in Scripturis extat, Deum nos sibi reconciliasse, id opinionem adversariorum prorsus falsam esse evincit, 2 Corinthians 5:18, Colossians 1:20-22."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But regarding this, what do you adduce to show that he reconciled us to God? — First, that Scripture nowhere asserts that God was reconciled to us by Christ, but only this, that we through Christ, or his death, were reconciled, or reconciled to God, as can be seen from all the passages that treat of this reconciliation. Therefore in no way can that satisfaction be built from all those passages. Furthermore, what is plainly in the Scriptures, that God reconciled us to himself, proves the opinion of the adversaries to be entirely false, 2 Corinthians 5:18, Colossians 1:20–22.”

items.exact_text: "Quid veto de hac reconciliatione sentis? — Christum Jesum nobis, qui propter peccata nostra Dei inimici eramus et ab eo abalienati, viam ostendisse, quemadmodum nos ad Deum converti, atque ad eum modum ei reconciliari oporteat."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What then do you think of this reconciliation? — That Christ Jesus showed us, who because of our sins were enemies of God and alienated from him, the way in which we ought to be converted to God, and in that manner be reconciled to him.”

items.exact_text: "Non est etiam aliqua alia morris Christi causa? — Nulla prorsus. Etsi nuno vulgo Christiani sentiunt, Christum morte sua nobis salutem meruisse, et pro peccatis nos-tris plenarie satisfecisse, quae sententia fallax est et erronea, et admodum peraiciosa" — Cat. Rac. de mot. Chria cap. 8 q. 12.
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Section 5, Chapter 8, Question 12.
items.translation_text:
Modern Citation: Racovian Catechism, Section 5, Chapter 8, Question 12.
Translation: “Is there also any other cause of the death of Christ? — None whatsoever. Although now Christians commonly think that Christ by his death merited salvation for us, and fully satisfied for our sins, which opinion is deceptive and erroneous, and exceedingly pernicious.”

items.exact_text: "Qua ratione? — Quod ad id quod fallax sit et erronea, attinct, id hinc perspicuum est, quod non solum de ea nihil extet in Scripturis, verum etiam Scripturis et sanae rationi repugnat?"
items.modern_reference: Translation: “By what reasoning? — As to the fact that it is deceptive and erroneous, it is clear from this, that not only is there nothing about it in the Scriptures, but it is also repugnant to the Scriptures and to sound reason.”

items.exact_text: "Demonstra id ordine? — Id non haberi in Scripturis argumento est, quod istius opinionis assertores nunquam perspicuas scripturas afferunt ad probandam istam opinionem, verum quasdam consecutiones nectunt quibus quod asserunt efficere conantur; quas ut admittere sequum est cum ex Scripturis necessario adstruuntur, ita ubi Scripturis repugnant eas nullum vim habere certum est." — Ques. 15.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Demonstrate it in order. — That it is not found in the Scriptures is proven by the fact that the assertors of this opinion never adduce clear scriptures to prove that opinion, but weave together certain consequences by which they attempt to establish what they assert; which, as it is equitable to admit them when they are necessarily built upon the Scriptures, so when they are repugnant to the Scriptures it is certain they have no force.”

items.exact_text: "Qui vero Scripturae repugnat? — Ad eum modum, quod Scripturae passim Deum peccata hominibus gratuito remittere testentur, 2 Corinthians 5:19, Romans 3:24, 25; potissimum vero sub novo foedere, Ephesians 2:8, Matthew 18:23, etc. At remissioni gratuitae nihil adversatur magis quam sstisfactio. Cui enim creditori satisfit vel ab ipso debitore, vel ab alio debitoris nomine, de eo dlci non potest vere eum debitum gratuito ex ipsa gratis remisisse." 899
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But how is it repugnant to Scripture? — In this way, that the Scriptures everywhere testify that God freely forgives sins to men, 2 Corinthians 5:19, Romans 3:24, 25; but especially under the new covenant, Ephesians 2:8, Matthew 18:23, etc. But nothing is more opposed to free remission than satisfaction. For whatever creditor is satisfied, whether by the debtor himself or by another in the debtor’s name, of him it cannot be truly said that he freely remitted the debt out of sheer grace.”

items.exact_text: "Cedo qui istud rationi repugnat? — Id quidem hinc perspicuum est, quod sequeretur Christum aeternam mortem subiisae, si Deo pro peccatis nostris satisfecisset, cum constet poenam quam homines peccatis meruerant aetornam mortem esse. Deinde consequeretur nos Christo quam Dee ipsi devinctiores ease, quippe qui satisfactione multum gratiae nobis ostendisset; Deus veto exacta satisfactione, nulla prorsus gratia nos prosecutus fuisset."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Tell me, how is that repugnant to reason? — That indeed is clear from this, that it would follow that Christ underwent eternal death, if he had satisfied God for our sins, since it is evident that the punishment which men had merited by sins is eternal death. Furthermore, it would follow that we are more bound to Christ than to God himself, inasmuch as he by his satisfaction would have shown us much grace; but God, having exacted satisfaction, would have bestowed upon us no grace whatsoever.”

items.exact_text: "Cedo etiam qui haec opinio est perniciosa? — Ad eum modum, quod hominibus fenestram ad peccandi licentiam aperiat, aut certe ad socordiam in pietate colenda eos invitet. Scriptura vero testatur, cum inter alios Christi mortis finem esse, ut redimeremur ab omni iniquitate, ex hoc seculo nequam eriperemur, et redimeremur ex vana conversatione a patribus tradita, et mundaremur conscientia a mortuis operibus ad serviendum Deo viventi, Titus 2:14; Galatians 1:4; 1 Peter 1:18; Hebrews 9:14.'
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Tell me also, how is this opinion pernicious? — In this way, that it opens a window to a license for sinning for men, or at least invites them to sloth in cultivating piety. But Scripture testifies that among other things, the purpose of Christ’s death is that we might be redeemed from all iniquity, snatched from this evil age, and redeemed from the vain conduct handed down by our fathers, and that we might be cleansed in conscience from dead works to serve the living God, Titus 2:14; Galatians 1:4; 1 Peter 1:18; Hebrews 9:14.”

items.exact_text: "Quae vero sunt scripturae e quibus illi opinionem suam adatruere conantur? — Eae quae testantur Christum vel pro peccatis nostris mortuum, deinde, quod nos redemit, ant dedit semetipsum et animam suam redemptionem pro multis; tum quod noster mediator est. Porro quod nos reconciliarit Deo, et sit propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Deniquc, ex illis sacrificiis quae mortum Christi seu figurae adumbraverunt."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But what are the scriptures from which they attempt to build their opinion? — Those which testify that Christ died either for our sins, next, that he redeemed us, or gave himself and his life as a redemption for many; then that he is our mediator. Furthermore that he reconciled us to God, and is the propitiation for our sins. Finally, from those sacrifices which, as figures, foreshadowed the death of Christ.”

items.exact_text: "Quod attinet ad ilia testimonia in quibus habetur Christum pro nobis mortuum, ex iis satisfactionem adstrui necessario non posse hinc manifestum est, quod Scriptura testetur etiam nos pro fratribus animas ponere debere, 1 John 3:16; et Paulus de se scribat, Colossians 1:24,.Nunc gaudeo, etc. Certum autem est, nec fideles pro fratribus cuiquam satisfacere, neque Paulum cuiquam pro ecclesia satisfecisse. "At horum verborum, Christum pro nobis esse mortuum, qui sensus est? — Is, quod haec verba pro nobis non significent loco vel vice nostri, verum propter nos, uti etiam apostolus expresse loquitur, 1 Corinthians 8:11, quod etiam similia verba indicant, cum Scriptura loquitur pro peccatis nostris mortuum esse Christum, quae verba eum sensum habere nequeunt, loco seu vice nostrorum peccatorum mortuum esse, verum propter peccata nostra esse mortuum, uti 900 Romans 4:25, manifeste scriptum legimus. Ea porro verba, Christum pro nobis mortuum esse, hanc habent vim, eum idcirco mortuum, ut nos salutem aeternam quam is nobis coelitus attulit amplecteremur et consequemur, quod qua ratione fiat paulo superius accepisti."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Regarding those testimonies in which it is held that Christ died for us, it is evident from this that satisfaction cannot necessarily be built from them, because Scripture testifies that we also ought to lay down our lives for the brothers, 1 John 3:16; and Paul writes of himself, Colossians 1:24, ‘Now I rejoice,’ etc. But it is certain that neither do believers satisfy anyone for the brothers, nor did Paul satisfy anyone for the church. But what is the sense of these words, that Christ died for us? — This, that these words ‘for us’ do not signify in our place or stead, but on account of us, as the apostle also expressly speaks, 1 Corinthians 8:11, which similar words also indicate, when Scripture says that Christ died for our sins, which words cannot have this sense, that he died in place or stead of our sins, but rather that he died on account of our sins, as we read plainly written in Romans 4:25. Furthermore, these words, that Christ died for us, have this force, that he died for this reason, that we might embrace and obtain the eternal salvation which he brought to us from heaven, the manner of which you received a little earlier.”

items.exact_text: "Quid ad haec dicis, quod Christus sit mediator inter Deum et homines, aut novo foederis? — Cum legatur Moses fuisse mediator, Galatians 3:19 (puta inter Deum et populum Israel aut prisoi foederis), neque eum satisfecisse Deo ullo modo constet, ne hinc quidem, quod mediator Dei et hominum Christus sit, colligi certo poterit eum satisfac-tionem aliquam qua Deo pro peccatis nostris satisfieret peregisse."
items.modern_reference: Translation: “What do you say to this, that Christ is the mediator between God and men, or of the new covenant? — Since it is read that Moses was a mediator, Galatians 3:19 (namely, between God and the people of Israel or of the former covenant), and it is not established that he satisfied God in any way, not even from this, that Christ is the mediator of God and men, will it be able to be inferred with certainty that he accomplished some satisfaction by which he satisfied God for our sins.”

items.exact_text: "Deinde negant resurrectionem carnis, hoc est, hujus ipsius corporis, quod carne ac sanguine praeditum est, etsi fateantur corpora esse resurrectura, h. e. ipsos homines fideles; qui tunc novis corporibus coelestibus induendi sunt." — Compend. Doct. Ecclesiastes in Polon.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Then they deny the resurrection of the flesh, that is, of this very body, which is endowed with flesh and blood, although they confess that bodies will rise, i.e. the faithful men themselves; who then are to be clothed with new celestial bodies.”

items.exact_text: "Itaque negant cruciatus impiorum et diabolorum duraturos esse in seternum, verum omnes simul penitus esse abolendos; adeo ut mors et infernus ipse dicantur conjiciendi in stagnum illud ardens, Apoc. 20:14. Rationem addunt, quod absurdum sit, Deum irasci in aeternum; et peccata creaturarum finita, poenis infinitis mulctare: pracaertim cum hinc nulla ipsius gloria illustretur." — Compend. Doct. Ecclesiastes in Polon.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “And so they deny that the torments of the wicked and of devils will last into eternity, but that all alike are to be utterly abolished; so much so that death and hell itself are said to be cast into that burning lake, Rev. 20:14. They add the reason, that it is absurd that God should be angry for eternity; and to punish the finite sins of creatures with infinite punishments: especially since from this no glory of His is illustrated.”

items.exact_text: "Nam quod ais, ea ibi, tum de Christianorum resurrectione, tum de morte impiorum paessim contineri, quae a multis sine magna offensione, tum nostris tum aliis, legi non possint; scio equidem ea ibi contineri, sed meo judicio nec passim, nec ita aperte (cavi enim istud quantum potui) ut quisquam vir pius facile offendi possit, adeo ut quod nominatim attinet ad impiorum mortem, in quo dogmate majus est multo offensionis periculum, ea potius ex iis colligi possit, quae ibi disputantur, quam expresse literis consignata extet; adeo ut lector, qui alioqui sententiam meam adversus Puccium de mortalitate primi 901 hominis, quae toto libro agitatur, quaeque ob non paucos quos habet fautores parum aut nihil offensionis parere potest, probandam censeat, prius sentiat doctrinam istam sibi jam persuasam esse quam suaderi animadvertat." — Faust. Socin. Ep. ad Johan Volkel. 6, p. 491.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “For as to what you say, that those things there, both concerning the resurrection of Christians, and concerning the death of the wicked, are contained here and there, which cannot be read by many without great offense, both ours and others; I know indeed that they are contained there, but in my judgment neither here and there, nor so openly (for I guarded against that as much as I could) that any pious man could easily be offended, so much so that what specifically pertains to the death of the wicked, in which dogma there is a much greater danger of offense, it can rather be gathered from those things which are disputed there, than that it exists expressly committed to writing; so that a reader, who otherwise would think that my opinion against Puccius concerning the mortality of the first man should be approved, which is discussed in the whole book, and which on account of not a few supporters which it has can produce little or no offense, would first feel that this doctrine has already persuaded him than that he would notice that it is being persuaded to him.”

items.exact_text: Αλλ ἔστι καὶ τῷ ὄντι καὶ τὸ ἀναβιώσκεσθαι καὶ ἐκ τῶν τεθνεώτων τοὺς ζῶντας γίγνεσθαι καὶ τὰς τῶν τεθνεώτων ψυχὰς εῖναι καὶ ταῖς μὲν ἀγαθαῖς ἄμεινον εῖναι ταῖς δὲ κακαῖς κάκιον,. — Plato in Phaedone, 17.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “But in reality there is both coming back to life and the living being born from the dead and the souls of the dead existing, and it being better for the good ones and worse for the bad ones.”

items.exact_text: "A. Ita jocaris, quasi ego dicam, eos esse miseros, qui nati non sunt, et non eos miseros, qui mortui sunt. M. Esse ergo eos dicis. A. Immo, quia non sunt, cum fuerint, eos miseros esse. M. Pugnantia to loqui non vides? quid enim tam pugnat, quam non modo miserum, sed omnino quidquam esse qui non sit. . . . A. Quoniam me verbo premis, posthac non ira dicam, miseros esse, sed tantum, miseros, ob id ipsum quia non sunt. M. Non dicis igitur, miser est M. Crassus, seal tautum, miser M. Crassus. A. Ita plane. M. Quasi non necesse sit, quicquid isto modo pronunties, id ant ease, ant non esse. An tu dialecticis ne imbutus quidem es," etc. — Cicer. Tuscul. Quest. lib. 1:7.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “A. You are joking as if I were saying that those who are not born are miserable, and not that those who are dead are miserable. M. You say therefore that they exist. A. Nay, rather, because they do not exist, when they once did, that they are miserable. M. Do you not see that you are speaking contradictions? For what is so contradictory, as that one who does not exist should not only be miserable, but should be anything at all? ... A. Since you press me on a word, hereafter I will not say 'they are miserable', but only 'miserable', for the very reason that they do not exist. M. You do not say therefore, 'M. Crassus is miserable', but only, 'miserable M. Crassus'. A. Exactly so. M. As if it were not necessary, whatever you pronounce in that way, that it either exists or does not exist. Are you not even imbued with dialectics?” etc.

items.exact_text: "Bene et composite Caesar . . . . disseruit, falsa, credo, existimans, quae de infernis memorantur; diverso itinere malos a bonis loca tetra, inculta, festa atque formidolosa, habere." — Cato, apud Sallust. Bell Catilin. 52.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Well and carefully has Caesar . . . discussed, judging to be false, I believe, what is related concerning the infernal regions; that the bad, by a different path from the good, inhabit places foul, uncultivated, horrid, and fearful.”

items.modern_reference: Translation: “A man devises evil for himself when he devises evil for another; this evil counsel is worst for the one who counseled it.”
